en: Preface to the *Zhengfan* (Orthodox Model for Transmitting the Precepts).
How excellent are the words of Liu Hedong: "The Confucians establish benevolence and righteousness through ritual; the Buddhists maintain meditative concentration and wisdom through the Vinaya.

Thus, when our World-Honored One proclaimed the teachings during the five periods, he placed the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* first among all the scriptures. When his radiance faded beneath the twin trees, he entrusted these golden words [to us].
The study of the precepts serves as the eyes for humanity and the bridge across the celestial river; this has been the undisputed teaching of both the ordinary and the sage.
Alas, as the Dharma grew old and corruptions proliferated, the ordination platforms became sealed and restricted.

Fortunately, our ancestors—the two elders Linggu and Qianhua—relied on the power of their great vows to reclaim this vast wilderness once more, so that from the distant reaches of the oceans to the remote corners of the land, all came to know how to uphold and receive them. Thus, the Way of Nanshan flourished once again.

However, following the Restoration and the passing of my late teacher to the West, there was no one to preside over the Vinaya; the Three Studies were in a state of flux, and no one knew whom to revere as their master.
My original teacher, the Venerable Jianyue Ti, possessed an iron-and-stone heart and was endowed with adamantine bones.

He had mastered the five divisions of the Vinaya in depth and was the successor to the "Thousand-Petaled Flower" (the Vinaya lineage). He lamented that within the realm today, the conferral of precepts had been abandoned, yet wherever altars were opened, they were numerous. Upon examining this...

Regarding the precepts, they were ignorant and lacked learning; observing their ritual conduct, they were lax and failed to meet the standard. In a frantic seven days, the three altars were completed;

no distinction was made between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, nor was there any differentiation between the monastic orders of monks and nuns. Their hearts were frivolous as they performed the confession of exposed transgressions.

Regarding the *karmavācanā*, they treat it as mere ancient text, failing to comprehend what is permitted and what is prohibited. When questioned, they offer only superficial excuses to stave off inquiry; thus, for a single period, the assembly is dissolved.

Their names are merely attached to their saffron robes, while their three karmas are utterly derelict. The *Prātimokṣa* has been relegated to high shelves, leaving the precepts of the successive sages [unpracticed].

[This] is equivalent to child’s play, and thus the Vinaya has fallen into great ruin. The Upādhyāya took pity on this; internally he placed great weight on personal practice, while externally he strictly observed the formal procedures.
Furthermore, he was diligent in his writings to benefit those who would come after. Beyond the monastic conduct prescribed by the two-vehicle *poṣadha* regulations, [he established further rules].

Furthermore, he compiled the *Zhuanjie Zhengfan* (Orthodox Model for the Transmission of Precepts) and the *Sandan Guize* (Rules for the Three Altars). These works are systematic in their great and small details;
the ritual protocols for the seven classes of followers are precise and orderly. In his diligent instruction, he poured the essence of nectar upon both the wise and the ignorant;

in his careful performance of the *karmavācanā*, he distinguished between light and heavy offenses with the precision of a hair’s breadth. Without deviating from ancient texts, he produced new models, such as the "Seven Matters" of the Hutuo River, which were like armor and weaponry [for the Dharma].

Suddenly renewed! The three armies of Wang Guangbi saw their banners and pennants undergo a transformation; it was truly like the southern chariot for those wandering in the wilderness, and the brilliant sun for Mokṣaka.

This text shall be circulated and adopted as a standard code, not only to provide strict regulations for those who specialize in the propagation of the Vinaya, but so that even those who practice both Chan and Vinaya may all know the proper measure.
From this point forward, the ritual methods for the ordination platform shall be compiled and perfected. Furthermore—
It is not merely a continuation of the ancient *mianzuo* (temporary ritual enclosures). As the ancients said, "The rites and music of the Three Dynasties are all contained herein.

Those who occupy these positions and ascend this altar should, if their hearts harbor dualistic interests, admire the precision and solemnity of the Vinaya assemblies; and if they fear the seven transgressions of the Dharma, loathe the simplicity and meagerness of contemporary masters.
Holding fast to this principle, one may proceed.
Written on the Shangsi (3rd) day of the first month of the Gengzi year of the Shunzhi reign, by the fellow-disciple and precept-recipient Jie Xian,

Compiled by the Vinaya Master Śramaṇa Duti of Mount Baohua, Jinling.
The Ritual for Invoking the Precepts and Repenting Prior to Bestowing the Śrāmaṇera Precepts on the First Altar, from the *Jingtang jijun* (Assembly in the Hall of Purity), Part One:

Whenever one intends to perform the ritual procedures, it is necessary first to establish the boundary (*sīmā*). If the characteristics of the threefold boundary are established according to the Dharma, there will be no obstacles.
Thus one is able to accomplish all things, namely the monastic regulations for communal residence, which must necessarily rely upon the formal demarcation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*).

How could the Sangha’s propagation of these regulations ever transcend this? When those who have first resolved their minds come to enter a monastery and request the precepts from the Sangha, they should first assemble the Sangha and perform the formal proclamation to establish the boundary.
Subsequently, they should formally invite the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) to grant permission for the date, whereupon the invitation is announced.
One should pay respects to the preceptor. Then, one should assemble the community in a clean hall. Next, one must formally address both *ācāryas* before entering the room to request [the precepts].
At the time of delimiting the boundary (*sīmābandha*), those newly seeking the precepts must be driven out to a place where they are visible but beyond earshot.
If it is a site for long-standing practice of the Vinaya and the boundary field has been established for a long time, it is unnecessary to chant the directions at each session.

(A few days prior to the conferral of the śrāmaṇera precepts, the ritual master instructs the attendants to sweep and clean the Dharma Hall, arranging a single seat within it and providing offerings of incense and candles. When the time arrives, he orders the attendants to strike the *ghanṭī* [wooden mallet]; if there are no attendants, a śrāmaṇera may do so.

Regarding the number of strikes for the mallet, one follows the standard regulations for the monastic rules (*vinaya*). Since we are currently assembling only a small group, only three strikes are permitted; the rest is as prescribed by the *vinaya* and need not be explained in detail here.

Once those seeking the precepts have gathered upon hearing the sound, four individuals first proceed to the ritual master’s position and perform a prostration with touching heads (*praṇāma*). Upon reaching the Dharma Hall, the entire assembly of those seeking the precepts performs three prostrations together, then stands up. The leader places his palms together at chest height and says:)
We, [Name] and others, have now resolved our minds and aspire to seek the pure precepts; yet, as our worldly passions have long obscured us, we lack the means to advance toward them.
We only pray that the various masters who guide the ceremony will, out of tireless compassion for others, graciously provide us with instruction and guidance.
The ritual master said:
"Excellent; so be it. Since you, the assembly, have newly entered the gateway of the Vinaya and are not yet familiar with its protocols, I shall now inform the two masters on your behalf.
We shall respectfully proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to invite the Upādhyāya to provide preliminary instruction for the occasion."
Ascending the seat, I shall bestow upon you, the śrāmaṇeras, the ten precepts. From among the assembly, four of the leaders shall step forward from the ranks and, following me, request two masters;
the others shall remain standing in their places.
(The assembly again bows together toward the Ritual Master once, then rises and stands to the left and right.
The General Announcement:
Regarding the second matter, according to the Vinaya regulations for bestowing the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, we request only the Upādhyāya and the Karmavācanā-Ācārya.

Regarding the *ācārya* who requests instruction, there is no such teaching. However, according to the Vinaya regulations for the ordination of a śrāmaṇera into the ten precepts, there are three categories:
first, those from seven to thirteen years of age, who are classified as "crow-chasers";
second, those from fourteen to nineteen years of age, who are properly considered "those who accord with the Dharma."
Third, if one is twenty years of age or older, both [stages] belong to the category of "name" (nāman). Now, those who seek ordination are already at the stage of "name" in terms of their age;
since their original intention is to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) to become a monk, they rely upon the status of a *śrāmaṇera* to advance to the great precepts of a *bhikṣu*.

If there were no instructor (*śāstṛ*), one would not be familiar with the proper deportment (*īryāpatha*). Therefore, it is necessary to request both [the *śrāmaṇera* and *bhikṣu* precepts]; should this be otherwise...
Regarding the two aforementioned methods for receiving the śrāmaṇera precepts, one should still follow the orthodox regulations.
When the two masters descend from the hall to and fro, they must not mingle with one another, so as to facilitate the admonition and instruction of beginners.

(1) The ritual attendant leads the two individuals to the quarters of the *karmācārya*. Upon arrival, the ritual attendant first performs a single prostration with a touch toward the master, then stands to his left and calls the other two to perform three prostrations. Once the master has accepted the invitation, they proceed together to the Dharma Hall;
the same procedure applies to the invitation of the *śikṣācārya*.
The ritual master says:
"All you sons of good family, prostrate together three times. Kneeling long with palms joined (the ritual master speaks on their behalf):
These [individuals, named] so-and-so, wish to receive the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera tomorrow morning. We now request the *karmavācanā* master to attend."
Recently, we arrived together at the Abbot’s quarters and addressed the Preceptor: "Your great compassion extends to us in our distress;
we only pray that the Karmadāna will deign to grant his skillful means and graciously accept our humble sincerity."
The Karmācārya says:
"Virtuous sons, the mind of faith and precepts is difficult to arouse, and the resolve to maintain them is even more difficult.

Since you have already aroused the aspiration to receive the precepts and desire to practice them with purity, it is because you have planted roots of goodness in the past that you now encounter this opportunity."
In this sublime assembly, I shall go to the abbot’s quarters on behalf of you all to inform the Preceptor and, with sincere entreaty,
request that he confer upon you the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
The ritual attendant says:
"All stand up together. Upon hearing the sound of the *qing*, perform three prostrations and divide into ranks.

(The one who has performed the invitation escorts the *karmadāna* back to his quarters and then invites the *śikṣācārya*. The ceremonial protocol is as described above; however, in the formal announcement, simply change the two characters for "instructor" [to "preceptor"].)
The Preceptor said:
"Noble sons, faith is the source for entering the Path, and precepts are the foundation for accomplishing goodness.

Since you have already grown weary of worldly life and left the household to seek the reception of the pure precepts, you possess a firm basis for that source and foundation; thus, supramundane merit will naturally arise."
You must apply yourselves with diligent effort and be careful from beginning to end. This is indeed a rare and auspicious opportunity, made possible by the seeds of merit planted over many lifetimes.

I shall now respectfully proceed to the Abbot’s quarters on your behalf to inform the Master of your sincere request, so that he may confer upon you the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera (the same applies to the prostrations).

Regarding the third point on the exhortation for receiving the precepts, the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first preach the Dharma to them to guide and enlighten their understanding;
the purpose is to stimulate their resolve so that they may recognize the essential aim and ultimate goal of the precepts. Now, [the text] simply uses the robes...

Regarding the characteristics of the alms bowl, to perform the entire ritual of receiving and transmitting the precept-body (śīla-ātman) based solely on these is truly to say that the officiant has misunderstood the principle.

One must realize that the essential point is to strictly maintain the characteristics of the robe and bowl; this precisely manifests the function of cessation and action. If one can thus inwardly discipline the precept-body, [the ritual is perfected].
Defiled karma is naturally severed; by relying externally upon robes and alms bowls, one’s deportment finally attains tranquility.

Only then are both nature and characteristics fully realized, such that the internal and external become as one. In this way, concentration and wisdom may be expected, and the holy life (*brahmacarya*) may be perfected. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For a son of the Śākya, receiving the prohibitive precepts is his nature, while shaving the head and wearing the patched robes are his characteristics. This refers precisely to this.
This is what is meant. Therefore, before receiving the śrāmaṇera precepts, one pays homage and requests the upādhyāya, who provides preliminary instruction;
however, the formal ritual for the actual request occurs at the time of the transmission and reception of the precepts, and thus will not be described here in advance.

(When inviting the Abbot, nine persons are employed. One acts as the leader, holding incense and proceeding ahead. The Ritual Master sounds the *yin-磬* (guiding chime), leading eight others who follow behind. The two masters are at the very rear.

Upon reaching the Abbot’s quarters, the Ritual Master and the inviters stand facing each other. After the two masters have prostrated to the Abbot, they stand to the left and right respectively. The inviters perform three prostrations with their heads to the ground. They escort the Abbot to the Dharma Hall to ascend the seat. The two masters first prostrate to the Abbot three times and then take their places.)
The Master of Ceremonies says:
"Offer incense. Return to your positions and line up facing upward in unison. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, prostrate three times, then kneel long with palms joined.
The Karmavācanā Master says:
"Virtuous sons, since you have all given rise to faith and seek to receive the pure precepts,
let the one who leads perform the formal announcement with utmost sincerity regarding the words of the request for ordination (the leader makes the announcement as follows)."

I respectfully address the Venerable Master. May you compassionately receive us. We, your disciples [Name] and others, though we have long since left the household life, regret that we have not yet been moistened by the Dharma of the precepts.
Merely bearing the empty name of "sons of the Śākya," we have presumptuously joined the ranks of the Saṃgha; therefore, we now prostrate ourselves before your seat.
We pray that you will deign to show us compassion and bestow upon us, your disciples [Name] and others, the precepts of pure discipline.

May we cultivate them with dharma-accordant diligence and practice them in accordance with your instructions, dedicating the merit toward the three realms of existence. We, your humble servants, are moved by the utmost sincerity in our earnest entreaty. (The Ritual Master says:
Prostrate once.
The Master struck the sounding block and said:

"Originally, for both those living at home and those who have left home, there is fundamentally no duality within. Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, not even a hair’s breadth is stirred therein.
Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are none other than the pure Dharma-body; light and darkness, form and emptiness—all are entirely the Perfect [Enlightenment]."
The wondrous land of fusion is fully present in every person; it is thus for each and all alike.

Since there is no distinction between defilement and purity, how could there be any characteristics of acceptance or rejection? Why, then, seek further liberation within that which is already free from bondage and attachment?

Alas, sentient beings are deluded and obstructed; their cognitive nature is clouded and ignorant. They mistakenly divide the wondrous essence of the single truth into the bodies of "self" and "other."
Taking the field of non-dual awakening, they delusively conceive of it as a dwelling for self and others. Due to this entanglement, they indulge in craving and give rein to hatred and ignorance;
submerged in the toil of worldly dust, their cycle of rebirth knows no end. From delusion to accumulated delusion, they do not contemplate returning to self-illumination;
entering suffering through suffering, they never grow weary of or seek to leave it. Therefore, all Buddhas appear in the world out of compassion for those who are sinking and drowning.

To rescue and deliver these beings, [the Buddha] knew that sentient beings’ greed and desire mostly arise from having a home; therefore, he showed them the path of distancing oneself and caused them to leave the household life.
Knowing that sentient beings’ entanglements all stem from affection and love, he showed them the path of liberation and caused them to renounce such love.
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "If there are those who do not understand the Dharma of leaving the household life and instead delight in and cling to birth and death..."
They do not seek liberation. For this reason, the Bodhisattva renounces his kingdom and wealth, leaving the household life to seek tranquility. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"There is no such thing as practicing and cultivating the path to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment while remaining a householder. Why is this? Because householders are attached to accumulation."
The householder renounces [the world], while the one who has gone forth is detached from the "self" of the householder. The householder is subject to defilement;
the one who has gone forth is tranquil. The householder is gathered by evil; the one who has gone forth is gathered by the good. The householder is submerged in the mud of craving and desire;
the one who has gone forth is pulled out from the mud of craving and desire. By this, it is known that those who seek the Noble Path must first go forth. Therefore, I, Śākyamuni—

"World-Honored One, you manifested your traces in the Middle Kingdom; at midnight, you leaped over the city walls. You spurred your white horse to traverse the void and went to the Green Mountains to sever your hair.
Once the thunderous voice had resounded, the 'Welcome' formula first initiated the five men.

As soon as the rain of Dharma moistened them, the *karmavācanā* rituals flourished throughout the four seas. To this day, all people receive its bounty. Good sons, your excellent causes lie in past lives..."
I, Zhi, have now encountered the Imperial Grace; having left worldly desires behind to enter the monastic life, I have attained the outward appearance of a monk.

Yet, if one who ascends the altar with a sincere heart to receive the precepts does not understand what the meaning of those precepts is, they possess only the name of ascending the altar while lacking the reality of receiving the precepts.
Such a person’s entire life will be spent in vain, their very being remaining that of a layman (*śuklāmbaram*). Therefore, before receiving the precepts, I pointed out—
I shall demonstrate to you, the śrāmaṇeras, the fourfold meaning of the precepts: the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*), the practice of the precepts, and the characteristics of the precepts.

This is to ensure that your minds attain clear understanding, so that you may receive and transmit them according to the Dharma, practice and maintain them with proper method, and not contravene the Vinaya regulations.
What is called the "precept-method" refers to the ten branches of purity established by the Buddha when he commanded Śāriputra to ordain Rāhula into the homeless life for the first time.

This refers to the twenty-four categories of monastic rules (*vinaya*), as well as the extensive formulation of training precepts (*śikṣāpada*) for *bhikṣus* who have no worldly affairs over the course of twelve years, along with the regulations governing all the conduct of *śrāmaṇeras* in accordance with the Vinaya. Regarding the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-bhāva*):

it is when you, at the very moment of receiving the precepts, employ the sixth consciousness—the mental consciousness—present before you, to direct your thoughts toward the Triple Gem until the ritual is completed.
At that time, one universally takes as objects of focus all sentient and non-sentient things;

upon these objects, one initiates the function of vowing to prevent evil and vowing to cultivate goodness. You all must not delight in ease and shun toil, nor loathe complexity while seeking simplicity.
Now that you have entered the initial stage of the Path, you must first practice the etiquette of serving a teacher, and next...
Regarding the labors of the Saṃgha, from the activities of morning and evening to the most subtle of actions, all are performed in accordance with the precepts;

therefore, they are called "precept-conduct" (śīla-carita). You all were not born into the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and your physical forms are identical to those of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Now, fortunately, you have ascended to the rank of the precepts; internally, you possess the virtue of compassion and harmony, and externally, you wear the black and white robes.
As for robes, furthermore, one’s dwelling is the same as that of the great assembly; in all movements and comings and goings, one values dignified decorum.

The supramundane path of practice is accomplished only through the precepts. Even the slightest transgression is termed a violation. Therefore, they are called the "characteristics of the precepts" (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*).

If you are able to hear them with faith and contemplate them, and having contemplated them, receive and uphold them—reverently following the monastic regulations and protecting and cultivating the root of virtue—then you may, at best, [attain the goal].

The Tathāgata established the precepts with the intent of gathering and sustaining all living beings; those who receive them below must not bring shame upon themselves, for they bear the name of compassionate salvation from defilement.
Can you all truly receive these with utmost sincerity and practice them according to the Dharma? (They respond in unison: "We shall practice according to the teachings. (The Upādhyāya says:
"Since you can practice according to the teachings, I now dispatch the ritual attendants to first request the *Ācārya* of Instruction on your behalf."
Lí: "Examine the robes and alms bowls. Next, invite the Karmācārya to purify the bodies and minds of you all through confession.

If your robes and bowls are in accordance with the Dharma and your persons are free from obstacles, tomorrow you shall ascend the platform to receive the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, which serves as the preliminary stage for the bhikṣu precepts."
The ritual master says:
"All sons of good family, stand up together. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations in gratitude.
Those who previously went out to welcome shall step forward from their ranks to escort the Abbot back to his quarters."

(Once the two masters have performed three prostrations at the lower level, they join the ritual master in leading the assembly to escort the Abbot back to his quarters. They then return to the Dharma Hall, perform another set of prostrations before the two masters, and after the prostrations are complete, escort the two masters back to their own quarters.

Next, having finished paying respects and offering thanks to all the ritual masters, the assembly disperses in an orderly manner to await the *kāṣāya-vastra-karman* [the formal rite for the transmission of the robe].)
Section Four: Examining the Robe and Alms Bowl.
Regarding the style of robes for *śrāmaṇeras*, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is said that a *śrāmaṇera* may possess two types of upper and lower garments:
one should be an *antarvāsaka* and the other an *uttarāsaṅga*. These are intended for entering [the monastic community] in a state of purity.
The assembly, as well as when traveling or arriving, wear it. Furthermore, the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya states:

"When a śrāmaṇera receives the antaravāsaka (inner robe), if he has reached the age of twenty, he may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). The preceptor shall seek for him the three robes and the alms bowl.
As for what is meant by 'proper,' it is not the same as the five-strip robe of a bhikṣu; rather, it is a seven-strip robe with one long and one short panel, cut into pieces."

It is sewn together like the ridges and furrows of a field; it merely adopts the name of "five or seven" [patches] for the purpose of formal acceptance, but does not employ the actual characteristics of five or seven patches.
As for what is called "plain" (*maṇḍala*), it means that there is no pattern. This refers to the robe sought from the preceptor at the time of full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
Regarding the practice of cutting and piecing together the marks of the robes, this accords with the regulations of the Vinaya and its commentaries; generally, it is as described above.
However, as for the current practice where the three types of śrāmaṇeras indiscriminately wear the three robes with field-patterned seams, it is unclear from what time this originated.
Since these practices have been followed for so long, they cannot be reformed all at once. From the year Bingxu, when I received the precepts, I have gradually expounded upon the Vinaya;

it was only in the winter of Jiawu that I began to reverse the present customs and honor the ancient traditions. Although I strive to implement the orthodox regulations, there are still certain expedient means within them:
for those between the ages of seven and nineteen who wish to receive the śrāmaṇera precepts, it is strictly required—

Regarding the *man-yi* (plain robe): if one has reached the age of twenty or older and resolves to ascend the three tiers of ordination platforms, it is not restricted solely to maintaining the practices of a *śrāmaṇera*;
however, there is nothing better than advancing through the stages gradually without skipping over their respective levels.

Therefore, within the original realm, it was provisionally permitted to accept and maintain two robes according to the characteristics of the field [of practice], with the sole exception that wearing the *saṃghāṭī* was not allowed.
For this reason, when the *śrāmaṇera* precepts are currently being conferred, one may not be without one of the three robes;
only after the formal ritual for requesting the precepts has been completed does the *upādhyāya* first instruct the candidate to request a *śikṣācārya* to verify the robes and bowl. Next...
He instructed that the *karmācārya* (preceptor for the ritual) should purify his physical vessel.

According to the Vinaya, when receiving the *bhikṣu* precepts, a *śikṣācārya* (instructor) is appointed to question the candidate in a private place, asking: "Do these three robes and one alms bowl belong to you?
This is called the "verification of the robes and bowl. To verify them at the stage of the *śrāmaṇera* precepts seems premature; however, due to [the following circumstances]...
The times are no longer those of antiquity; among people, those who are hypocritical and deceitful have become increasingly numerous.
Originally intending to borrow robes and bowls, they answer when asked that they already possess them. Yet, after receiving them, they subsequently return them to their original owners.

This disrupts the bequeathed regulations of the former sages and deceives the pure assembly within the hall. Unless one conducts a preliminary examination, the fault will lie with both teacher and disciple.
Since both [the preceptor and the candidate] are difficult to exempt from this responsibility, establishing this ritual now is an urgent necessity.

(After the Preceptor has finished his exhortation, he rests for a short while. Then, the *gandī* is struck again. Those seeking the precepts for the first time each take their robes and bowls and proceed to the place of formal action. The ritual master leads them to stand in order. They then place their robes and bowls upon the table.)

Recognize your own robe and station and take your place; do not cause confusion or lose proper decorum. Second, the ritual master leads five persons to invite the teacher: one person holds incense and four follow behind. Once they have reached the hall and taken their seats—
The ritual master says:
"Offer incense. Return to your positions and face upward together. Upon hearing the sound of the *qing*, perform three prostrations with full obeisance.
Kneel long with palms joined (the two ritual masters perform a *wenshun* toward the upper direction, return to their positions, and join their hands, saying): [Text continues...]
Good sons, although your outward forms are those of śrāmaṇeras, your minds have not yet been moistened by the precepts and dharmas.
Since you now seek the disciplinary chapters for calming and compassion, you ought to don the dharma robes that transcend the world.
Therefore, in accordance with the instructions of the Upādhyāya, I have been requested to examine your robes and bowls as your teachers; you must each listen attentively to all the words I speak.
The Master struck the sounding block and said:

"Now, the ultimate essential of leaving the household life is that preceptual conduct comes first. The primary condition for receiving the precepts is the monastic robes, and the foundation is the bowl.

This is because the physical appearance and deportment of a Śākyaputra are utterly distinct from those of the secular world, and the mental capacity of a Śākyaputra does not resemble the sentiments of ordinary people. Only when the three robes are complete..."
The manifest characteristics and essential nature [of the robes and bowl] support one another; they must not be separated from a single alms-bowl.

Only when one’s needs are thus minimized can one cultivate the Way. You who now seek the precepts: if you lack robes and a bowl and borrow them from others, even if you have received the ordination, you will not possess the precepts.
If the preceptor knows this yet intentionally confers the precepts upon you, he falls into unrighteousness. Therefore:

Before you have received the precepts, I shall examine each of you one by one. If your formal conditions are fully met and your appearance as renunciants is complete, it may be said that you are in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and following the Buddha’s instructions; thus, I shall cause all of you to obtain the pure precepts.
(True sons of the Śākya—*clapping the ruler once*). As for the robes and alms bowls currently present here, have you all prepared them yourselves?
(The assembly answers: Yes. (The Master says: Since you have them, that is very good; however, I fear that because they are mixed together, your three robes (*tricīvara*) will be spoiled.

As for the five types of high-quality fabrics such as silk and brocade: although it is currently permitted for śrāmaṇeras to possess only two robes, since you have all reached the required age and will soon ascend the precious altar to receive full ordination, it is necessary to conduct a preliminary inspection now so that no haste or confusion occurs at the last moment.
Furthermore, regarding the alms bowls you have prepared, ensure they strictly conform to the prescribed standards before you take possession of them.
If, upon first leaving the dust of the world to receive the precepts, one immediately dons old and tattered *kāṣāyas*, it is known that the causal mind seeking the precepts was not superior.

If, at the very beginning of wearying of the secular life and abandoning the household, one immediately seeks out precious silk and brocade, it must be that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of fondness for such things have not yet been eliminated.
This is just as Mahākāśyapa wore his three robes with a hundred patches, and Kauṇḍinya wore cloth garments worth only five coins.
As for Mount Heng, one spent their entire life in coarse hemp; on the Southern Mountains, silk and brocade were forever abandoned.

Since the patriarchs of India and this eastern land were so pure and frugal, how could we common folk not emulate them? Now I shall step out of my station to investigate each point in detail, so that I may report back to the Master.
The ritual attendant says:
"Virtuous sons, prostrate once and then rise. Each shall go to the place of his own robe and bowl and await the Master’s personal arrival for detailed examination."

(The Master steps out of his position. The various ritual attendants follow him, examining each item in detail. Should there be any items that are damaged, borrowed, or made of high-quality silk such as *zhou* or *ling*, the Master should instruct them with kind words to inspire joy in them, so that they may be replaced according to the Vinaya.)

If one follows one's own emotions in repenting for violations of the Vinaya, it does not conform to the model of a teacher. Those who understand the Dharma should not fail to be cautious. (Upon completion of the examination, the Master leads all according to protocol back to their respective positions.)
The Master struck the sounding block and said:
"I have examined your robes and bowls for you all. Fortunately, your robes and bowls are complete;
thus, the conditions for the Dharma are fulfilled, and it is possible for you to receive the pure precepts. Tonight, you must repent with utmost sincerity, so that when the time comes tomorrow,"
The Ordination Platform.
The ritual master says:
"Virtuous sons, all form a single row. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations and then stand up to divide into ranks."
The one who received the invitation escorts the Master back to his quarters.

The others stand in formation (as usual, after the escort has departed, they return to the location where the robes were kept). They collectively bow once to the assembly and the Preceptor of Ceremonies (*yinyili*), then each identifies their own robes and bowl. They proceed in order to carry them back to their respective halls (the Preceptor of Ceremonies departing last).
The purpose of verifying the robes and alms bowl is to prevent the acquisition of non-Dharmic requisites; it does not establish a prohibition based on the robes and bowl of a deceased monk.
Lately, there has been a false tradition claiming that those who survive a monk’s death should not wear or possess his robes and bowl.

This is entirely due to a lack of training in the Vinaya and ignorance of its underlying principles. According to the *Vinaya*, there is a formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the distribution of a deceased monk’s belongings.
It is said: "In general, although all bhikṣus have left the household life in reliance upon the Triple Gem, wealth and property are necessarily acquired through the Saṃgha;
they do not belong to the Buddha or the Dharma. Therefore, they enter into the two types of Saṃgha and should be divided according to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

If one takes them privately before the *karmavācanā*, one incurs an offense against the Saṃgha of the ten directions. If one takes them privately at the time of the actual *karmavācanā*, one incurs an offense against the present Saṃgha. If...
When this Saṃgha has assembled in harmony and grants [the robe] through a formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) in accordance with the Dharma, who would say it should not be used?

If the deceased’s robe is not to be used, then what of the discarded clothes of corpses in cemeteries? The Buddha commanded those practicing *dhūta* austerities to wash, clean, patch, and mend them to make *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) garments.
How, then, can this intention be reconciled? It is truly because the property of a deceased monk is rarely...
This is rarely seen and seldom heard. One should follow the *karmavācanā* of the Vinaya and maintain pure conduct.

Nowadays, I frequently observe that when a preceptor passes away, those who act as disciples treat the remaining robes and belongings as their own paternal inheritance, refusing to share them with the community.

Little do they realize that this constitutes stealing monastic property and treating it as private wealth; it is like administering poison to others while claiming it to be nectar. This is truly [lamentable].
How lamentable it is! Because this has been erroneously transmitted throughout the world, I have appended these arguments for clarification.

Regarding the fifth section, the "Exposure of Faults and Repentance by a New Ordinee," there are four principles for weighing persons and dharmas as the circumstances differ: first, the initial stage.
First, those who have left the household life and immediately seek to receive the precepts. Second, those who have been tonsured for a long time but only now seek the precepts.
Third, those who have been in the monastic order for years and have only received the five precepts, but now, desiring further cultivation, seek the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

Fourth, those who, while still in the household life, previously received the five precepts or the bodhisattva and upāsaka precepts, and now, having again left the household life, beg for the great precepts.
Among these four types, when performing the ritual according to the specific occasion, one must distinguish three categories;
they must not be treated as a single uniform whole, lest the medicine and the ailment conflict, resulting in the failure of all three—person, rite, and matter.

Regarding the first type of seeker who seeks the precepts: if one follows the method for receiving the ten precepts according to the *Nanshan Jieben* (The Nanshan Vinaya Rite), one should inquire about the prohibitions and obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

In this case, only the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are questioned as being "obstructions to the precepts" (*śīlāvaraṇa*). If such a person exists, they are immediately barred and expelled; the Vinaya regulations do not permit them.
As for the four root offenses (*catur-āpatti*), such as killing one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*), there is no need to inquire about them universally. Why is this?

When he first left the household life, he immediately sought to receive the precepts; however, since the three masters had not yet been formally invited and the four parājikas had not yet been undertaken, there was no master to kill and no precepts to break.
Thus, one need only examine the five *ānantarya* offenses and need not inquire about the seven *ānantarya* offenses.

Examining the second type of seeker of the precepts: regarding the obstacles to the precepts they inquire about, although the number does not reach seven *ānantarya* offenses, in terms of meaning there are six.
This is because, having long since left secular life and having served their teacher for many years, according to the Vinaya, one must add the question concerning the murder of an *ācārya*.
Furthermore, among the five types of *ācāryas* mentioned in the Vinaya, the tonsure-master (*keśa-cchedaka-ācārya*) stands at the head. If [such a case occurs]...
To commit such transgressions is something the Dharma cannot tolerate; logically, they ought to be excluded.

Upon examining the third and fourth types of those seeking ordination, according to various sūtras and vinayas, those who have committed the seven grave offenses (ānantarya-karma) or the four root defeats (pārājika) should be strictly interrogated.
Since they were previously monastics or laypeople who had ascended the ranks of the precepts, their *upādhyāya*...
Every person has their preceptors (*ācārya*). As for the four root offenses (*pārājika*), one must receive and uphold them in every detail.
Since this case does not resemble the two previous types of persons, it should be categorized separately and examined.
The four types of inquiries presented above strictly follow the regulations of the Vinaya. However, the present age is not the era of the Buddha;

the five turbidities contend with one another, and there may be those who interfere with state prohibitions under the guise of the Dharma-gate. Unless one carefully examines and rigorously investigates them, how can they be said to be protected within the Dharma-gate?
Therefore, I now provide a general outline of these categories and add detailed inquiries regarding the ten evil deeds for all those who preside over grave matters.
Those in charge should be especially cautious in this matter.
Regarding the ritual for repentance (*pratikramaṇa*), it may be performed on the same day or the preceding night.

If the ordination hall is secluded and far from the dust of the marketplace, and there are few seekers of the precepts with no other distractions, then the rite should be held on that very day. First, have them undergo a thorough examination and repentance, and subsequently receive the precepts.
Regarding the Dharma of Precepts: Even if the ordination hall is situated in a remote and secluded place, those seeking the precepts may number in the thousands or even double that amount;
in such cases involving the causes and conditions of the Triple Gem, one may perform repentance overnight and receive the precepts the following morning.
If the ordination hall is adjacent to a village or city, regardless of whether the number of seekers is large or small, one must simply...
One should gauge the capacity and suitability of the practitioners; whether on the same day or the night before, one may perform the ritual according to convenience.
If it is a formal confession held the night before, at the beginning of the first watch of the night, a seat shall be prepared within the *karmadhara* hall and adorned with incense and flowers.
Furthermore, a side table shall be set up behind the main seat to await the scribe and the person responsible for recording the proceedings.
One must ensure that the lamps and candles shine brilliantly, their radiance like that of day; the incense smoke is fragrant and dense, its swirling patterns like clouds.

Relying on such magnificent adornments, one can cause the hearts of people to be struck with awe and trepidation, so that past transgressions naturally cannot be concealed and all faults are laid bare.
During the performance of the ritual, if there should be laypeople who enter and mingle with the assembly, it is the duty of the ritual master (the guide) to [deal with them].
One should employ skillful means to dismiss [the distractions] and cause [the assembly] to give rise to joy.

When the time arrives, strike the wooden mallet to assemble those seeking the precepts. The ritual protocol for requesting the *karmavācanā* master is as usual. Once the master has entered the hall, paid homage to the Buddha, and ascended the seat, he takes up the incense, offers praise for the incense, and recites the eulogy.
The Ritual Attendant says:
"Offering Incense. Those who are to invite [the deities] step forward from their ranks, perform three prostrations, and return to their positions.
With palms joined, you all should follow my voice and chant the Great Compassion Divine Mantra in unison. Relying on the power of this mantra, purify the altar.
Altar. To distance oneself from all demonic obstacles.

(When reciting the mantra, by no means remain silent for the sake of personal ease; one must know that every person has their own altar and their own demonic obstacles. If one does not recite with utmost sincerity and clarity, it will instead increase those transgressions. Having finished the recitation of the mantra, [raise the chant].
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amṛtarāja (Recite three times).
The ritual master says:
"Virtuous sons and daughters, line up together facing upward. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations with full length.
Kneel with palms joined and listen attentively to these words; do not harbor other thoughts or perceptions.

Now, the Venerable Master has appointed us to adorn and purify the Dharma Hall, burn incense, and arrange the seats, to respectfully invite [Name] Vinaya Master to serve as the *ācārya* for your assembly to perform the ritual of examining and repenting for transgressions.
*Ācārya* in Sanskrit means "model" (*guǐfàn*) and is also translated as "right practice" (*zhèngxíng*). Model.
"Those who are capable of serving as models for later students, being worthy of emulation and worthy of following because they practice with diligence;
those who are capable of correcting their disciples, possessing a straightforward mind and straightforward conduct because they proceed toward the Truth;

who wash away the ordinary body to become vessels for the Path and clear away the weeds of craving to cause the flower of the Bodhicitta to bloom—all this is due to such a teacher guiding according to the Vinaya and performing repentance according to the Dharma. If there were none..."
This master purifies the three karmas and assists in manifesting the True Cause. Thus, regarding the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, one might have retreated in awe;
now that we have fortunately encountered him, it is like a sick person meeting a physician. For this reason, with utmost sincerity and earnest devotion, we extend our request.

As for the words of requesting the master, you ought to state them yourself; fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, I shall now instruct you. (Each should recite his own Dharma-name [the assembly recites the names together]). As for the remaining words:
[The] words: "All follow my path.
Venerable One, attend with one-pointed mind. I, the disciple [Name], and others, now request the Venerable One to act as our Preceptor for Examining Offenses and Confession (*ālocanā-ācārya*).
May the Venerable One act as our Preceptor for Examining Offenses and Confession. We rely upon the Venerable One."
"Therefore, you may perform the repentance according to the Dharma. Out of compassion [I grant this]. (Having made this request three times, bowing the head three times.
The Master strikes the sounding block and says:

'The essence of nature is perfectly luminous and fundamentally free from arising or ceasing. It is because it is shrouded by the dust of deluded emotions that there are distinctions between the holy and the ordinary. Therefore, [one must] act with urgency...'"
One must awaken early so as to be able to advance in practice by seizing the opportune moment. However, the initial gateway to entering the Way lies in transforming defilement into purity.
If the defiled mind is not severed, evil karma will arise; only when pure mindfulness manifests can the holy life (*brahmacarya*) be established.

Now that I stand before this hall, performing repentance for your three karmas on your behalf is precisely the method for transforming defilement into purity. Indeed, throughout the four continents and the six...
The Way: Only among the humans of Jambudvīpa in the south is the human path most excellent; their nature is close to the stage of Buddhahood, making it easy to cultivate progress.

Now that you have fortunately been able to join this superior company, you may hope to find ground for transcendent advancement. Yet, I fear that from the time of your birth until now, within the various realms of existence, you may have created causes for karma that is profoundly unwholesome.
Such karma not only obstructs the Great Path that leads beyond the world, but also contravenes the reception of the precepts.
This is a supreme condition. One must first cleanse the crystal vase thoroughly before it can be fit to hold lion’s milk.
At this time, before the Hall of Repentance, you are like the bright sun shining in the sky; no shadow may be hidden. With a clear mirror set upon its stand, every brow and eye is fully revealed.
Each of you must hollow out your hearts and drain your very gall, reforming the past and following anew, and before me, one by one, pour forth your sincerity.
If one knows of their transgression yet feels shame, remaining silent and concealing it, then even if they receive [the precepts], they do not attain them. Why?
Because when defilement and purity intermingle, and sin and merit are mixed together, this is of no benefit for the Path; from where could realization be attained?

As for what is called repentance (*pratikramana*), its essential requirement is to possess the power of great faith and to give rise to great shame and remorse. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "There are two pure dharmas."

They are able to save sentient beings through two qualities: first, shame (*hrī*); second, remorse (*apatrāpya*). Shame is internal self-reproach; remorse is the disclosure of one's faults to others. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
"If the world were devoid of these two dharmas of shame and remorse, it would transgress the path of purity and head toward birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Therefore, one should give rise to shame and remorse, and have deep faith in the retribution of karma. You have now entered the Vinaya for the first time.
Gate: You do not know the names and characteristics of the obstacles to the precepts. Not knowing their names and characteristics is equivalent to not asking at all.
Therefore, I shall first follow the Sūtras and Vinaya to analyze and point them out for you. Each of you should listen attentively and reflect deeply, examining whether these obstacles exist or not.
After a short while, they shall take their places in order one after another and confess according to reality (striking the ruler once).
As for what is called an obstruction to the precepts, it refers to you all who, from time immemorial, have maintained them within the faculty of the mind.

The five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*) constitute the most grievous karmic offenses; this is the general heading for the first type of person [examined here]. (In the subsequent explanatory text, the numbered figures from the diagrams shall be taken and combined with this general heading.)

The six perversions and the ten evil deeds are the most grievous karmic offenses; these constitute the general heading for the second type of person (the numbers within pointed brackets in the subsequent explanatory text are to be combined with this general heading).

The seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*), the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala-karma-patha*), and the four kinds of fundamental grave sins (this is a general heading for the three and four types of persons discussed below;
it is used throughout the subsequent explanations in accordance with the text, rather than as a formal enumeration).

If there are those who have committed each of these transgressions, it is termed an "obstruction to the precepts" (*śīlāvaraṇa*). This is a prohibition established by the Vinaya, whereby they are not permitted to receive the precepts.

Although there may be extenuating circumstances that allow for their rescue, one must still distinguish between the capacities of the practitioners and the teachings to correspond with the gates of repentance.

If one possesses sharp faculties and superior wisdom, one must necessarily cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) deeply to give rise to the illumination of fundamental wisdom, contemplating the body and mind as illusory, such that subject and object...

Both are empty. One realizes that self-nature is true and eternal, and that all phenomena are unreal. In a single thought-moment of resonance, one accords with the principle of suchness and enters into non-arising.

This inclusion of the gate of wisdom as the ritual of repentance for the ultimate principle means that it is not merely a matter of the afflictions temporarily subsiding and claiming to have ascended to the field of liberation, nor is it the case that because the nature of karma is not yet empty, one can be called to have entered the ocean of nirvana. One must ensure that the contemplation of the ultimate principle is refined and pure; truly...

Only upon realizing non-arising do the flowers of transgression wither and fall away. As for those of middling or inferior capacity, they must follow the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras to cultivate the methods of repentance (*chánfǎ*).

They should contemplate the emptiness of the essence of the three wheels, cease the conditioned shadows of the six sense-objects, and advance toward the Way according to a fixed schedule—whether for seven days, fourteen days, or even months and years—seeking to behold auspicious signs (*hǎoxiàng*).
If they do not see such auspicious signs, they should increase their efforts with even greater intensity and sincerity.
Increase your earnest sincerity; even if it requires the remainder of your entire life, you must take the vision of [the Buddha] as your appointed goal.
This gate of meditative concentration for the rite of repentance pertains to both phenomena and principle. It does not mean that while the body performs prostrations, the mind remains distracted.

How could one escape the gravest and most evil karmic retribution through the slight merit of a few days? As for what is called "the five, six, or seven rebellions," "rebellion" means to be contrary to principle and to turn one's back on kindness while forgetting it.

If one instead commits acts of opposition and harm against those virtues, then both worldly and world-transcending laws are difficult to evade. (The following text enumerates the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) in order; however, if one examines the five heinous offenses (*pañcānantarya*) and the six heinous offenses, they should be selected separately according to their specific names and numbers for practical application.)
First: Shedding the Buddha’s Blood (This is the fifth among the five heinous acts and the first among the six heinous acts). The Buddha is the God among gods and the Sage among sages;

adorned with myriad virtues and fully endowed with the ten titles, he has, throughout immeasurable kalpas for the sake of sentient beings, realized the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma through his practice.
With kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, he universally rescues all living beings and causes them to attain the three [refuges].
Throughout the nine realms, there are those who equally attain the path of enlightenment; the four modes of birth and the six destinies are forever severed from saṃsāra.
This would mean that Mount Sumeru could be toppled and the great ocean could be exhausted, yet the profound grace of the Dharma King is such that it cannot be repaid even throughout kalpas.

If one fails to recognize this kindness and repay this virtue by instead bearing [the Buddha] upon one’s head with offerings, or conversely, commits acts of rebellion and harm—such as shedding the blood of a Buddha—then the transgression is beyond salvation. Therefore, the Buddha...
It is said that shedding the blood of a Buddha is termed an obstruction to the precepts (*śīlāvaraṇa*).

According to various sūtras and vinayas, this *ānantarya* offense is generally attributed to Devadatta, who, out of malice, hurled a stone at the Buddha; a small fragment thereof struck and wounded the Buddha’s toe.

Now that the Master has long since passed away and his radiance is hidden, I still maintain my former inquiry regarding repentance. Even if a mind of anger and evil were to arise, it would destroy everything.
To damage images of the Buddha, as well as stupas containing the Buddha’s relics, and to destroy various Mahāyāna sūtras, constitutes the same offense and is likewise termed an "extremely evil" act.

Second is the killing of one’s father; third is the killing of one’s mother (among the five heinous crimes, these occupy the first and second positions; among the six heinous crimes, they occupy the second and third).

"Murder" refers to killing one who is superior by means of one who is inferior. Parents are the "heaven" of their children; in principle, a child ought to exert all their strength in filial piety and obedience, never contravening their will.

They should provide warmth in winter and coolness in summer, settle them at dusk and attend to them at dawn, offering sustenance in every way and serving with tireless diligence, thereby fully exhausting the way of a filial son to offer even a small recompense for the kindness of giving life and raising them. How could it be appropriate to, on the contrary, employ an evil heart?
Out of a mind of hatred, one falsely commits acts of killing and harm. The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states:

"If there are sentient beings who are unfilial toward their parents, or even go so far as to kill them, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Killing one's father or mother is called an obstruction to the precepts (*śīlāvaraṇa*)."

The fourth [offense] is the killing of one’s *upādhyāya* (among the five or six *ānantarya* sins, there is no question regarding this). An *upādhyāya* is here translated as "one who gives birth by power" (*lìshēng*).

This means that the power of the Path of the Three Vehicles and the fivefold *dharmakāya* are all produced through the majestic virtue of this master; he is the fundamental teacher from whom one receives the precepts.
Now, even in the mundane world, parents give birth only to the physical body, yet their kindness is already inexhaustible; how much more so for the supramundane father!
The mother gives birth to one’s physical body, yet the kindness of the one who causes the arising of the essence of the precepts (śīla-ātman) is beyond measure.

This is why the Buddha established the rule for disciples to attend upon their *upādhyāya* (preceptor), with the Vinaya being extremely strict and detailed. This is because the kindness of the *upādhyāya* is profound and vast; one ought to serve him in accordance with the Vinaya.
Yet, if one instead harbors anger or malice and commits murder against him, the Buddha therefore said: "To murder one's *upādhyāya* is called an obstruction to the precepts (*śīlāvaraṇa*)."
Fifth is the killing of an *ācārya*. In Sanskrit, *ācārya* means "preceptor" (*guǐfàn* in Chinese).
According to the regulations of the Vinaya, there are five types, all of whom are capable of serving as models for later students and correcting their practice.

First is the *keśa-apanayana-ācārya*, who can cause one to leave secular life and distance oneself from the dust of the world, leading one to loathe suffering and seek pure bliss. Second is the *karmācārya*, who can...
1. The Preceptor of Ordination (*Upādhyāya*) purifies one as a vessel for the Path, because he causes the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) to arise.
2. The Preceptor of Instruction (*Ācārya*) is able to transform coarse and frivolous behavior, ensuring that one’s deportment is dignified and disciplined. 3.

The Preceptor of Reliance (*Niśraya-ācārya*) is able to bring about mastery of the Vinaya, being skilled in the rules of what is permitted and what is prohibited (this includes even the case of relying on him for a single night). 4. The Preceptor of Scriptural Transmission (*Śāstr-ācārya*) is able to cause one to cultivate Prajñā through hearing the teachings.

Because they enter through reflection, cultivation, and realization (this constitutes one phrase of the *Sūtra on Receiving the Precepts*), these five kinds of ācāryas all possess the aforementioned virtues and graces.
They are truly excellent guides for transcending the world and genuine spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the life of wisdom.

Even if one were to exhaust body and mind in serving them for the remainder of one’s years, the grace of their Dharma-milk would still not have been repaid by even an inch; how much more so, then, to respond with anger and malice and commit regicide?
As for "harming": therefore the Buddha said that killing one's preceptor is called an obstruction to the precepts. (This passage is used [from among the seven heinous offenses];
if clarifying the fourth of the six heinous offenses, the following passage may be used, as the meaning of the matter differs, and thus it is listed as a separate section.)
The fourth is the murder of an *ācārya*. In Sanskrit, *ācārya* means "preceptor" (*guǐfàn* in Chinese).

The one you have questioned here does not refer to the two types of *ācāryas* involved in the ritual (*karmavācanā*) and instruction (*śikṣā*) for receiving the precepts, nor does it refer to the *ācārya* relied upon after having received the precepts.
Rather, it refers to the two types of *ācāryas*: the one who first shaves your hair and the one who bestows the scriptures.

Furthermore, these two kinds of ācāryas are able to cause you to emerge from the deep pit of emotional attachment, to draw near to the Triple Gem, to hear the sublime Dharma of detachment from desire, and to realize the single truth.
For such kindness and virtue, do not fail to harbor a heart of gratitude and seek to repay them.
To instead inflict murder and harm with a mind of anger and malice—for this reason, the Buddha said that murdering one’s preceptor is called an obstruction to the precepts.

Sixth is the schism of the Saṃgha regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma through ritual action (*karmavācanā*). (Among the five heinous acts, this is the fifth; among the six heinous acts, this is the fifth. As for "ritual action" (*karma*): [text follows]
This refers to those pure bhikṣus who dwell together within a single boundary, blending like water and milk, sharing the same poṣadha and the same karmavācanā;

this is called "turning the wheel of the pure precepts. If they gather and transform beings according to their circumstances, engaging with sentient beings as appropriate, proclaiming and expounding the teachings and contemplations, and practicing according to the instructions, this is called "turning the wheel of concentration and wisdom.
These are all companions on the path who have transcended the mundane world, providing salvation through their wisdom.

The person who upholds the three trainings serves as the beam and pillar of the Dharma-gate; they transform and benefit all sentient beings, acting as a vessel and a navigator upon the sea of suffering.
If there were no Jewel of the Sangha in the world, how could the Buddha-dharma be propagated? Who would then be able to succeed to the life of wisdom?
It is because the *vinaya* abides that the True Dharma remains for a long time; thus, it causes the realms of humans and devas to flourish and the evil destinies to be eliminated. Even if...
If one does not know how to return in reverence to seek instruction, but instead destroys [the Sangha] with an evil mind or a mind of anger, for this reason the Buddha said:
"To destroy the Sangha that performs the *karmavācanā* and turns the Wheel of Dharma is called an obstruction to the precepts."

The seventh is the murder of an Arhat (this is the third among the five heinous crimes and the sixth among the six heinous crimes). An Arhat is one who has excellently transcended all realms of existence and realized the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
He preaches the Dharma to open the way for the delusions and ignorance of the myriad beings, and responds to conditions to plant the seeds of merit and wisdom in sentient beings.
It enables one to receive protection and benefit in the present life, while the retribution for such acts is to be experienced in the future.

Yet, instead of giving rise to a heart of reverence and the realization that such beings are difficult to encounter, one instead adds the poison of malice, hatred, and murderous intent. Therefore, the Buddha said: "To murder an Arhat is called an obstruction to the precepts.
This is the definition and meaning of the fifth of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*). (Strike the *chì* once.)

Regarding what are called the ten evil deeds: "evil" refers to that which is unwholesome. Because sentient beings are deluded regarding the truth and pursue the false, their discriminative consciousness and emotions cause them to encounter circumstances with discordance;

thus, in their every movement and stillness, they are bound by fetters. Within the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, they commit the ten sinful offenses. Since the accumulated causes are profound and heavy, they are capable of summoning bitter retributions in the future.
First, regarding the killing of evil through killing: this refers to taking life oneself and also inciting others to kill.

All sentient beings take consciousness (*vijñāna*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and warmth (*uṣman*) as their life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). When these three do not disperse, it is called the preservation of life;
if these three are separated, it is called the severance of life. If, among fellow sentient beings, one commits killing due to the resentment of enmity, or...
Among beings of different species, some may kill for the sake of nourishing themselves by craving their flesh.
To thus inflict injury and raise harm, intentionally severing the life-force of sentient beings, is not in accord with the virtue of the Supreme Sage who saves living beings;
it damages one's own innate compassion. Therefore, this is called the first evil of killing.
The second type of theft, *adattādāna*, refers to the secret taking of another’s property. Indeed, the means by which people sustain their lives are called "external life.
Now, such property differs according to whether it belongs to householders or those who have left the home-life (*pravrajita*). Regarding the property of householders:
Whether they be one's parents, kinsmen, donors, acquaintances, or even those who are neither kin nor acquaintances—whatever belongs to another and has an owner must not be stolen.
As for the property of the monastic community, this includes the property of the Buddha-Dharma or the property of the Sangha.
Regarding the property of the Buddha-Dharma, it refers to carved incense images, as well as paintings and statues of the golden countenance.
Printing the Tripitaka and transcribing the scriptures—these, along with all such articles of adornment, constitute the property of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the property of the Saṃgha, according to the *Nanshan Shichao* (The Record of the Southern Mountain), it is classified into four types: First, permanently fixed permanently fixed property (*zhǒngcháng zhǒngcháng wù*).

This refers to the monastic kitchen, storehouses, temple buildings, all flowers, fruits, trees, gardens, groves, servants, livestock, and so forth. These do not extend beyond the boundaries of the monastery; they may only be...

It is for use; its division or sale is not permitted. Therefore, it is emphatically termed "perpetual property" (*sthavira*). Twenty-first, the property of the perpetual community of the ten directions (*daśadig-sthavira*) is like the constant food provided to the Sangha;
its substance extends throughout the ten directions and is used according to the occasion, yet it is restricted to the specific location where the wood [or the object] resides.

Twenty-second, the property of the present Sangha (*sammukhībhūta-saṃgha*) refers to items obtained as offerings by the Sangha; these are offered specifically to the present assembly at this location and do not extend to the Sangha of the ten directions. Fourth.

Regarding the property of the *saṃgha* present before one from the ten directions—such as the light personal effects of deceased members of the five assemblies, namely bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs—although each has their respective share even when such items are present before the assembly from the ten directions, once the distribution by *karmavācanā* is completed, those who arrive later are deprived of hope.
One must understand that all wealth belonging to the Three Jewels originates from offerings of faith; those [deceased] sought happiness in the future.

Therefore, one plants fields of merit for this present life; yet, when cause and effect are mistaken, the karmic fruit returns to one's own person. How much more so when one steals and claims it as one's own!
For this reason, it is called the second evil of theft.
The third is the evil of sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*). This refers to lewdness, which is the most debased and vulgar of worldly affairs;

yet it serves as the very root of all sentient beings' transmigration through birth and death. Whether one commits impure acts with male or female relatives of the six kin, or with those who are not kin, or violates the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) of others, or even defiles monasteries (*saṃghārāma*), or assails women of integrity—[all these constitute this evil].
It defiles one's pure reputation; by this, one falls of one’s own accord into the Avīci Hell and undergoes all manner of sufferings.

Therefore, this is called the third evil: sexual misconduct. The fourth evil is false speech. False speech refers to the fabrication of empty words with the desire to induce others to believe them. Thus, false speech—
There is a distinction between the great and the small. A great falsehood refers to claiming to have attained what one has not attained, or claiming to have realized what one has not realized;
because one seeks fame and profit to manifest extraordinary qualities and delude the masses, it constitutes a great falsehood.

A small falsehood refers to saying one has seen what one has not seen, saying one has not seen what one has seen, saying one has heard what one has not heard, or saying one has not heard what one has heard; because one employs the habitual arrogance of hypocrisy and deceit, [it constitutes a small falsehood]. Light...

To insult one's predecessors constitutes minor false speech. Thus, deceiving oneself and others through flattery and crookedness rather than straightforwardness is called the fourth evil of false speech.

Fifth is the evil of divisive speech (*paiśunya*). This refers to circulating rumors between others, instigating disputes over right and wrong, or acting out of resentment to seek private revenge, or out of envy to obstruct the superiority of others.
Thus, one acts as a go-between for both sides, praising them openly while slandering them behind their backs, causing superiors and subordinates to fall into conflict and estranging close kin.
When there is no recourse for grievances and one's own virtue is utterly diminished, it is therefore called divisive speech.
The fifth evil is divisive speech.
The sixth evil is harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). Harsh speech refers to uttering words that are coarse and violent, thereby bringing humiliation upon others.

It may arise from the failure to satisfy one's desires, or from the arising of anger due to frivolous jesting. It obscures the fundamental social order and causes the loss of ethical principles, such that the distinction between the honorable and the humble is no longer maintained.
To disparage others at will, causing them distress and taking pleasure in satisfying one’s own mind—this is called the sixth evil, that of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
The seventh evil is frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*): this refers to words that deviate from truth and contradict reason, yet are skillfully adorned with rhetoric, perhaps out of self-conceit.

One’s own talents are flaunted and deluded according to one's whims; or, for the sake of ruining another’s reputation and virtue, one employs the tongue like a drumhead to captivate the sight and hearing of others, increasing their emotional consciousness and corrupting their will. For this reason, it is called the seventh evil: frivolous speech.
The eighth is the evil greed of craving and lustful desire. This refers to being stained by attachment to what is pleasing, such that mindfulness finds no rest.

Those who live as householders seek fame, achievement, wealth, and status through clever schemes and unrestrained pursuit. Those who have left the home life, for their part, take pleasure in gain and reputation, contenting themselves with wrong livelihoods.
They never know satisfaction when encountering objects that accord with their desires; hearing of generous aid, they are stingy even regarding a single hair’s breadth.
Seeing pleasure and attachment, one becomes stuck like glue or lacquer; pursuing all manner of things, one does not fear the suffering of karma. For this reason, it is called the eighth evil:
greed. The ninth evil is anger (*dveṣa*).
Anger means that the object and the mind are at odds; one gives rein to a wicked nature, whether due to one's dwelling...
Regarding one's family, reputation, profit, and property, if one seeks them and does not attain them, various feelings of resentment arise.
Or, regarding the four requisites for those who have left the household life, if they are difficult to obtain as hoped, one immediately gives rise to a mind of anger. As a sutra says:
"When a Bodhisattva gives rise to a single thought of anger, it opens a hundred thousand kinds of doors to obstacles. For this reason, it is called the ninth evil: anger and hatred.

The tenth is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); as for those with evil wrong views, they are characterized by delusion and a lack of right wisdom. Their knowledge and insight are largely biased and one-sided.
Because they do not understand the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—they falsely speculate on the views of nihilism and annihilationism.

They deny the causes and effects of defilement and purity, destroy the roots of mundane and supramundane goodness, and cause right faith to be extinguished like ashes while their deviant minds blaze fiercely. As it is said:

In this land, those who follow the teachings of the White Lotus of the Heavenly Lord, the Unconditioned (wuwei), the Pointing Finger (guanzhi), the Hearing Fragrance (wenxiang), and so forth, are all like the blind leading the blind;
they all fall into pits and ditches. While alive, they receive the retribution of royal punishment; after death, they suffer the fruits of hell.

Even when a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, there is no means for them to repent. Therefore, this is called the tenth evil: wrong view. This is the name and meaning of the ten non-virtuous actions.

(If one examines those who seek the precepts according to the first two types, it is not necessary to inquire about the four lower root offenses; one proceeds directly to the subsequent text, which says: "Good sons and others, since you have now all listened to my words... and so forth.
If one examines those who seek the precepts according to the third and fourth types, one should inquire about the four root offenses. (Strike the wooden gavel).

Regarding what are called the four fundamental precepts: whether you were formerly in the household life and received the five precepts of an upāsaka, as well as the six grave and twenty-eight light precepts of a bodhisattva;

or whether, after shaving your hair, you received the fivefold pure precepts—among these, the four prohibitions consisting of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and great falsehood—[are the four fundamental precepts].
These are the roots of the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras, the full precepts for bhikṣus, and the threefold great precepts of the bodhisattvas.

Once they have been conferred and received, if one does not firmly uphold them and violates even a single precept, one may no longer receive the ten precepts, the full precepts, nor the bodhisattva great precepts.
Furthermore, these offenses of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are more serious than the ten unwholesome paths previously mentioned.

Among these, the karmic retribution for killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying increases and becomes even more severe, because they have violated the Buddha’s pure precepts. (Strike the *shaku* and say:
"O sons of noble family, now that you have all heard my words, each of you should clearly understand:

regarding any of the aforementioned evil karmas that you may have committed, disclose them to me with an open heart; not even the slightest detail must be concealed or hidden. If there is even the slightest flaw..."

Defects remain obstacles to the precepts. For example, when washing old clothes, it is essential that the base material be pure and all stains and grease be completely removed before they can properly receive new dye.
I shall now question you one by one; you should come forward in order and answer each question truthfully. (Strike the ruler once.)
The ritual master says: "All sons of good family, stand up together. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations. [They] divide into two rows and stand facing each other.

(If there are many, let three people at a time confess together; if few, one person at a time in succession. As for those who act as teachers, do not become weary from sitting too long, nor neglect your duties; you must certainly teach others without weariness, out of compassion.

The instructions were repeated with earnestness. As for those who serve as ritual attendants (*yǐnlǐ*), since they assist the Dharma-gate and act on behalf of others, they must not decline the labor. Once the assembly has taken their positions, the three individuals from the lead row first stand facing the Master in a single line.
The ritual master says:
"Virtuous sons, upon hearing the sound of the sounding-stone, perform three prostrations (if there are many, one prostration will suffice). Kneel with long knees and join your palms.
With the utmost sincerity of your three karmas, follow my voice and recite:"
Namo to the Three Jewels, eternally abiding throughout the ten directions (three times). [Each person] recites their own Dharma name.
