Having finished, the Master strikes the sounding block and says: "Good son, I shall now first question you."
The obstacle of the five heinous transgressions against the precepts. Next, ask him about your ten grave karmas of evil (this is the first kind of inquiry).
The obstacle of the six heinous transgressions against the precepts. Next, ask him about your ten grave karmas of evil (this is the second kind of inquiry).

The seven heinous offenses constitute an obstruction to the precepts. Next, inquire regarding your ten grave karmas of evil and the four kinds of root [offenses] (examine these two types, the third and the fourth;
the seven heinous offenses are listed collectively below; if examining the five or six heinous offenses, apply the "round" and "pointed" designations as above).

(○ Among the five *ānantarya* offenses, shedding the blood of a Buddha is fifth; △ among the six *ānantarya* offenses, shedding the blood of a Buddha is first. The ruler is struck: "First, have you ever shed the blood of a Buddha?

(If you have, say "yes"; if not, say "no. No bystander may instruct the answer as to whether it was yes or no. This is because there is concern that one might not know how to respond when the time comes for questioning;
therefore, each point has been previously explained in detail. Now you must speak for yourself; there is no need for instruction. The same applies to all subsequent questions.)

"Good son, you should know that the one thousand years of the True Dharma (Saddharma) of Śākyamuni Tathāgata have already passed, and the one thousand years of the Semblance Dharma (Saddharmapratirūpaka) have also passed.
This is now the time of ten thousand years of the Final Dharma (Paścimadharma), and more than six hundred years of it have already elapsed.

Although there are none who shed the blood of the Buddha’s body, there exist sacred images carved, painted, cast, or modeled, as well as stupas and temples containing the Buddha’s relics. [This is] the Mahāyāna..."

Regarding the Prajñā of the True Mark and the definitive, perfect, and sudden sūtra texts, those who have ever defiled or destroyed them with a mind of anger or malice shall be judged according to the same category as this offense. Have you ever done so? (Answer truthfully whether you have or have not.)
(○Among the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), patricide ranks first. Matricide ranks second. △Among the six heinous crimes, patricide ranks second. Matricide ranks third).
Second, have you ever murdered your father? (Answer truthfully as before. Third, have you ever murdered your mother?
(Answer truthfully as before. [Note: A person has three fathers and eight mothers;

only those who are one's biological parents are designated as objects for the crime of parricide. Although others do not constitute parricide, they are nonetheless included within the category of the evil of killing.]

"Fourth, have you ever murdered your preceptor? (Answer truthfully as before. This question is subsumed only within the seven heinous offenses; it is not included among the five or six heinous offenses.)
(△ Among the six heinous crimes, the murder of an ācārya is the fourth).
Fifth: "Have you ever murdered an ācārya? (Answer truthfully as before).

(Regarding the five types of ācāryas explained above, there is also the ācārya of the five precepts. For example, if one previously received the eightfold fast-precepts while living as a layperson, then there is the ācārya of the eight precepts.
Whichever precepts one has previously received, one asks about that corresponding ācārya.)

(○ Among the five ānantarya offenses, the schism of the saṃgha regarding the formal ritual and the turning of the wheel of Dharma is ranked fourth. △ Among the six ānantarya offenses, the schism of the saṃgha regarding the formal ritual and the turning of the wheel of Dharma is ranked fifth).
"Sixth, have you ever disrupted the *saṃgha* by means of a formal act (*karmavācanā*) or the turning of the wheel of Dharma?

(Answer truthfully as before). Within this single question, there are two types: first, the disruption of the monastic community (*saṃgha*); second, the disruption of the *saṃgha* through formal acts. Some sources speak of "disrupting the harmonious *saṃgha*" (*saṃghasāmagrī*). This term "harmonious *saṃgha*" encompasses both of these types;

for when there is disruption, there is no harmony, and when there is harmony, there is no disruption. What is meant here by "disruption" refers to being in opposition to the path of the sixfold concord (*ṣaḍ-vidhā sāmagrī*). The Buddha said: "There are two ways of disrupting the harmonious *saṃgha*: first, through false speech; second, through equivocal speech. Whether by means of a formal act or by casting voting sticks (*śalākā*), if..."

To destroy the monastic community (*saṃgha*), there must be at least nine persons; one person must claim to be a Buddha, and this can only be accomplished by a man. This applies both within and outside the boundary (*sīmā*). That which is destroyed is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) saṃgha, which is restricted to Jambudvīpa.

One who commits such an act incurs the grave offense of *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression), which is not a *pārājika* (defeat) and cannot be expiated. If it is the destruction of the ritual saṃgha (*karmasaṃgha*), there need be only eight persons, and one need not claim to be a Buddha; women are also capable of doing so. It requires performing a separate ritual (*karma*) and *poṣadha* within the boundary.

That which is destroyed here is also the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) saṃgha, which extends throughout the three continents. One who commits such an act incurs a *sthūlātyaya* that is not a *pārājika* and can be expiated. However, what is called "destroying the monastic community" refers specifically to the case of Devadatta; today, such an offense does not exist. As for the destruction [of the ritual saṃgha]...
As for the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) of the Saṃgha, it may perhaps exist [in such cases].
(In the five *ānantarya* [heinous] acts, the murder of an Arhat is ranked third; in the six *ānantarya* acts, the murder of an Arhat is ranked sixth.)
Seventh, have you ever murdered an Arhat? (Answer truthfully as before.
Since these six or five or seven heinous crimes do not apply to you, there are further ten evil deeds which I shall now question you about. (Strike the ruler once and say:)
First, have you ever taken the lives of members of your own species, such as men or women? (Answer truthfully as before.
Have you ever taken the lives of any animals belonging to other species? (Answer truthfully as before.)

Regarding those who are "careful" (*śikṣā*) in this context: if, while living as a layperson, one has previously taken human life, violated national prohibitions, or been involved in grave matters related to the Dharma gates and so forth, such individuals must be excluded. However, in this inquiry, one must investigate the circumstances in detail; do not be negligent or hasty. Cases involving the gravity of theft and other evils are to be treated by analogy with this.

If one has taken the lives of animals and the like, it is sufficient to perform a sincere and earnest confession; they are not subject to exclusion. If one has already left the household life (*pravrajita*), although one may not yet have received the full precepts, one must absolutely refrain from committing killing.

If one takes human life, one must certainly be expelled. If one takes the lives of animals, one should be made to perform repentance. Whether lay or ordained, if one violates this rule after having received the precepts, it is subsumed under the four root offenses (*mūlāpatti*).

Distinguishing between light and heavy: Question. Since the gravity of killing is already subsumed within the four root [offenses], why is it examined here again in such detail? Answer: It is for the sake of completing the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) and to prevent confusion regarding the enumeration of dharmas.

If one were to subsume it entirely within the four root offenses, the enumeration of the ten unwholesome actions would be deficient; furthermore, for those who have not yet received the precepts, what other questions could be posed to them?
Second: Have you ever stolen any property belonging to others in the secular world? (Answer truthfully: yes or no.
Have you ever stolen the property of the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha? (Answer truthfully: yes or no.)

Regarding those who are "deliberate" (*śikṣā*): if one has not yet left the household life and joins a gang to plunder heavy property from officials or the common people, this is unforgivable by state law and is not admitted by the Buddha’s discipline. If one steals property belonging to the Triple Gem, it should be prohibited according to the *Sujātāsūtra*, among the seven obstacles to the precepts, which states that stealing the property of the *saṃgha* present [at a ceremony] is likewise to be barred.

If one has left the household life but has not yet received the full precepts, and steals heavy property belonging to a secular owner, or any property belonging to the Triple Gem and so forth, such a person does not fear the laws of the king, does not believe in cause and effect, and does not dread the hells;

they are not a true vessel for the Path and should also be barred. If, whether as a layperson or one who has left the household life, one commits such acts after having received the precepts, these are included within the latter four root offenses (*mūlāpatti*).
Third: Have you ever committed sexual misconduct with your own male or female relatives, or with those who are not your relatives? (Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.
Have you ever violated the holy life of another or defiled a pure monastic community? (Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.)

Regarding "careful scrutiny" herein: if one has not yet left the household life, one must refrain from committing sexual misconduct with the six paternal relatives—namely uncles, brothers, sons, and grandsons—or the six maternal relatives—namely paternal aunts, maternal aunts, sisters, daughters, and granddaughters;

or from violating the *śīla* of a *bhikṣuṇī* who maintains pure conduct. According to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, among the seven obstacles to the precepts, these two cases—committing incest with one’s own kin and defiling a *bhikṣuṇī*—must be strictly prohibited. If one has already left the household life, even before receiving full ordination, such acts are absolutely forbidden.

Whether the partners are relatives or non-relatives, whether they are male or female, one must refrain from all forms of impure conduct, including those that defile the *saṃghārāma*. Whether one is a layperson or a renunciant, once the precepts have been received...
Regarding these matters of impurity (which are subsumed within the latter four root precepts):

Fourth, have you ever falsely claimed that you had attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), concentration (*samādhi*), or supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)? (Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.)
"After you have shaved your hair and are living together with the Saṃgha, before you have yet received the precepts, do you falsely claim to be a bhikṣu?

Do you participate with the assembly of monks in the same uposatha, the same karmavācanā, and the same distribution of offerings, and do you receive the respect and prostrations of others? (Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.)"

Regarding "examination" herein: If, prior to leaving the household life, one falsely claimed to have realized the Way, deceiving the worthy and holy ones, and held the śramaṇas in contempt—even though they have now left the household life, they are not true vessels for the Dharma and it is difficult for them to receive the precepts;

logically, they should be barred. If they have already left the household life but have not yet received the categories of precepts, yet falsely claim to be bhikṣus, participating in the community’s *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* rites and sharing equally in offerings, while never having realized the Way, they falsely claim to have realized it.

If this occurs only once, they may perhaps be excused; however, if they constantly deceive everyone, they too should be barred and expelled. If those, whether lay or ordained, commit this offense after having received the precepts, it is subsumed within the latter four root offenses.
Fifth, have you ever acted as a messenger for disputes, inciting discord between parties, sowing dissension among those bound by affection, or destroying another's property?
Have you caused others to suffer grief and distress, depriving them of peace and happiness? (Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.)
"After you have shaved your hair and live together with the community, have you ever engaged in instigating disputes between two parties, causing those above and below to be at odds?
(Answer truthfully whether this has occurred or not.

[In this regard, the examiner should investigate: If, while living as a layperson, you ever spoke words that caused division or incited strife—words that interfered with people's lives, causing them to harbor resentment for a lifetime and remain in a state of injustice without recourse—you ought to refrain from such things. If you can reform your past ways and recognize [your errors]..."

This is not so. One should give rise to great shame and remorse, and with bitter urgency and sincere entreaty, one may also seek forgiveness. Once having left the household life, whether toward those who are monastics or laypeople, one must not engage in such divisive speech that causes discord among others, especially when it concerns the lives or families of others.

"You must also restrain yourself. You must sincerely and earnestly reproach yourself to eliminate these evil habits; only when you resolve never to commit them again may you be permitted to receive [the precepts].
Sixth: Have you ever been insolent toward anyone, disparaged those above or below you, or spoken with such coarseness as to cause others humiliation and distress?
(Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.)"

Regarding those who are obstinate: whether they be laypeople or monastics, whenever one utters such harsh speech toward them, one should employ skillful means to guide and instruct them, and earnestly exhort them with urgency, so that they may recognize their error, reform themselves, and be able to constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and patience.
Furthermore, one must not engage in the karma of harsh speech; only then may the reception of the precepts be permitted.
Seventh: You have previously used words with deceptive intent and skillfully employed literary phrasing to subvert the truth and oppose principle, thereby acting without virtue.

Do you adorn those with virtue, disparage those without virtue, and deceive others by causing them to lose right knowledge and increase their false views? (Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.)

Regarding those who are subject to careful scrutiny herein—whether lay or ordained, whether they have received the precepts or not—if they have committed such acts that ruin their virtue and corrupt social ethics, or which involve state affairs and obstruct the Dharma-gate, they shall not receive the precepts.

This is done to protect them from the censure of worldly truth and to preserve the dignity and honor of the monastic community. However, if they can vow never to commit such acts again and strive with diligent effort toward the Path, it may be permissible to admit them and grant them the precepts.
Eighth: Have you ever, regarding objects of attachment, been variously attached with pleasure, your mind never weary of them nor abandoning them;

desiring only to obtain them for yourself while disregarding harm to others, lacking any compassion or relief, and losing all kindness and benevolence—even to the point of failing to provide for your parents, teachers, elders, juniors, and kinsmen? (Answer truthfully whether this is so or not.)

Regarding "thoroughness" herein: generally, those who have left the household life must first empty themselves of all possessions and extinguish all mental攀緣 (pāraṇa, clinging/seeking). If one is greedy for gain without satiety, being difficult to satisfy and difficult to support, then worldly entanglements will bind them, and they will be utterly severed from the Path.

However, in this present age of the Dharma’s decline, many monks resemble the laity; they fail to attend to their own religious duties and are submerged in worldly conditions. Therefore, one should first cause them to feel shame and practice contentment; only then can the observance of the precepts be maintained. Furthermore, the precepts are the very foundation for correctly conforming to liberation.

If one cannot achieve liberation regarding various sensory objects, how can one proceed toward pure karma? Thus, one must not easily grant others the reception of the precepts; rather, one should cause them to wash away their former inclinations so that they may plant the seeds of the Path.
Ninth, you have frequently given rise to anger and resentment toward objects that oppose your will;

you have harbored malice toward yourself and others, cursed the gods and spirits, provoked heaven and earth with resentment, and reviled your parents, teachers, and elders—answer whether this is true or not.

Among those who deliberate upon this matter, all who have left the household life must necessarily restrain and protect their own minds and cultivate the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) extensively. Even when encountering circumstances that conflict with one’s desires, one should subdue oneself.

If a single adverse condition arises and one immediately stirs up the fire of anger—whether cursing the gods and spirits, resenting Heaven and Earth, or even reviling one’s parents, teachers, and elders—how can such ignorant and vexatious acts be tolerated? For while those in the secular world may still violate laws and prohibitions, how could one who has left the household life to practice the Way permit such things?
Therefore, you must be interrogated.
Tenth: Have you ever associated with false teachers, studied their heterodox teachings, recited scrolls and chanted verses, or practiced "observing fingers" and "smelling incense"?

Mistakenly interpreting the principles of the Truths, they lead others like blind men, acting as masters and disciples; thus they both sink themselves and sink others (whether this is real or not, one must answer). Herein lies the careful examination:

any person who has left the household life must first clearly understand the Four Truths and the Four Fruits, and subsequently practice according to the Eightfold Noble Path. Only then can they distance themselves from deviant, heterodox, and hypocritical teachings. If false views are not eliminated, pure precepts are difficult to receive;

even if one has received them, there is fear that they will break them, becoming either an internal or external heretic. Therefore, before receiving the precepts, one must conduct an even more rigorous examination. If such a person exists, one must certainly employ harsh tongs and hammers to uproot the very source of their deviance, so that—

Only after [the recipient] possesses firm and upright faith should one transmit and receive [the teachings]. If they are as hesitant as those standing between two pillars, their power of faith being unstable, they must still be barred from it; this is done to preserve the weighty Dharma-gate. One must select and clarify those of right faith. Lately, ignorance and heterodoxy have flourished; therefore, one should be especially rigorous and discerning.

"Good son, since the seven heinous offenses and the ten evil deeds are absent, you should inquire about the four fundamental precepts (if one has carefully examined the third and fourth types [of practitioners], only then should one inquire about the four fundamentals, as stated in the text below; if one has carefully examined the first and second types, these are not necessarily required). Furthermore, regarding the four precepts of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, the text concludes by stating:"
"Good son, as for the ten non-virtues that obstruct the precepts which you have just asked about, one who has committed none of them is called a 'pure vessel.
Having paid homage, arise [proceeding with the ritual of bowing once to rise and exit the altar]. Then, call the second group forward."
Regarding the first precept against killing, is there an offense or not? (Answer truthfully: Yes or No.

In this context, if one severs the life of a sentient being of the same class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), it is called a breach of the root [precept]; re-ordination is not permitted. If one kills but the life is not severed, one is to be disciplined according to the Vinaya; it is not called a breach of the root.

If one intentionally severs the life of a sentient being of a different class, one must perform the *taku-gira* (duṣkṛta) repentance for what ought to be confessed. If the life is severed but the victim does not die, it is likewise a *taku-gira* offense. If there was no intent to kill and the injury occurred by sudden accident, one performs the *takushin* (manasā-duṣkṛta) repentance for the *taku-gira*. Hereafter, do not commit such acts again.

If, while living as a layperson, one has received the six grave and twenty-eight light precepts of a Bodhisattva Upāsaka, then regardless of whether the victim is of the same class or not, any act of giving rise to a mind of anger and malice to take their life is termed a "breaking of the root" (mūla-bheda).
This is explained in detail in the *Great Vehicle Twelve Gates Analysis of Profound Meaning* (*Dasheng shiermen fenbie xuanyi*).
Regarding the second precept against stealing, is there an offense or not? (Answer truthfully whether it exists or not):

In this context, if one steals five coins or more, it is called a violation of the root [precept], and re-ordination is not permitted. If one steals less than five coins, down to even a single coin, one must perform the *tūlīya* repentance for a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one steals more than five coins, the crime is determined according to the value of the money;
in all such cases, repentance is difficult to admit. This is explained in detail, as in the *Great Vehicle Twelve Gates Analysis of Profound Meaning*.
Regarding the third precept on sexual misconduct, is there an offense or not?

(The answer is given with factual certainty. Herein, the five groups of the ordained completely sever sexual desire. The two groups of the laity sever only improper sexual conduct; furthermore, regarding their own wives or concubines, they are further restricted by the prohibitions of improper time and improper place. "Improper time" refers to either midday, or the six fast days, or the eight Wang days.

One observes the three-month fast (*traimāsa-upavāsa*) in the third month of the year. Or, [it may be observed] after one's wife has become pregnant or given birth, and so forth. Regarding "inappropriate places," these exclude the pathways for excrement and urine, as well as the mouth. If one perceives the right opportunity, an exception may be permitted; however, this applies only to lay bodhisattvas. For those who have left the household life, such permission is absolutely not granted.

Whenever any member of the seven assemblies receives the precepts and commits such impure acts, they are all said to have violated the root [precepts]. If there was no intentional desire and the act was not completed, one should deal with them according to the Vinaya; this is not called a violation of the root.
This is explained in detail in the *Great Vehicle Twelve Gates Analysis of Profound Meaning* (*Dasheng shiermen fenbie xuanyi*).
Regarding the fourth precept against false speech, whether there is an offense or not (i.e., whether there is a truthful answer or not):

herein, if one claims for oneself, "I have attained the state of a superior person," "I have attained dhyāna," "I have attained samādhi," "I have attained the fruits [of the path]," or "Gods, dragons, ghosts, and spirits all come to provide me with offerings," and speaks these words clearly to another person, it is called a violation of the root [precept].

If one speaks but does not do so clearly, there may be grounds for exemption, as explained at length in the *Great Vehicle Twelve Gates Analysis of the Profound Meaning* (*Dasheng shiermen fenbie xuanyi*).
"Good son, since you have not committed the ten non-virtuous actions that obstruct the precepts, nor the four root transgressions mentioned above, you are called a 'pure vessel. Rise and withdraw."
The ritual master says:

"All rise together. Upon hearing the sound of the *qing*, perform three prostrations (if the assembly is large, one prostration is also acceptable). Exit the hall and ascend to the altar to worship the Buddha.
Wait for the sounding of the *guanzui*, then enter the hall with the assembly to perform repentance and dedication. (After they have departed after performing their prostrations, call out again:)
The second group comes forward from the assembly to confess their transgressions.

(Proceed in this manner for as many groups as there are. Once they have been individually examined in order, strike the *ghanṭī* three times. Then, those seeking the precepts enter the hall slowly and arrange themselves in rows as before.)
The ritual attendant says:
"All together, line up facing upward. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations, then kneel long with palms joined.
The Master strikes the sounding block and says:
"Good sons, you have each already confessed your past transgressions before me at this time.

You should reflect that within this hall of repentance, upon the ground of the monastery, the Three Jewels are present and the myriad deities provide protection; the five eyes see all clearly, and the six supernormal powers know all. Should there be any further transgressions..."
If you have not yet confessed, do not hesitate; open your hearts and reveal your very souls to me and speak further.

Just as when washing old clothes, although the stains may be removed, one must wash them again and again before they are fit to receive dye. Therefore, I now ask you once more; you all shall answer once more.

If there truly is nothing [to confess], then you are true vessels of purity. If there is something, it will be difficult for you to ascend to the ranks of the precepts. (Strike the ruler once. You all—
Has each person finished recounting their offenses? (The response must be truthful. Among them, there may be those who initially forgot but later remembered;
such a person replies, "I have not finished recounting. The Master strikes the *chui* (ruler) and asks: "What matters have you not yet finished recounting? You must now speak directly to me.

According to the three categories—the five heinous acts, the six heinous acts, and the seven heinous acts—he shall examine the case in detail according to the individual's capacity to determine its gravity. The scribe then takes the register recording the names and offenses of the individuals, leaves his position, and approaches the Master’s seat. He offers a single greeting and presents the document. If...

For minor offenses, they are weighed and dismissed on the spot; for serious ones, they are presented to the Upādhyāya, who may provide skillful and opportune relief according to the ritual procedures of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras (though these are not yet known).

"Good sons, although you have finished confessing those deeds and actions committed during this present life, from time immemorial—before you had recognized the Buddha, before you had heard the Dharma, and before you had encountered the Sangha—you have assumed immeasurable physical forms and committed immeasurable karmic offenses.
Your consciousness was clouded and deluded, such that you were neither aware nor conscious of them; only the Buddhas [know them]."
Bodhisattvas, you thoroughly know and thoroughly see the extent of your transgressions, whether they be light or heavy.
Now, facing the Triple Gem of the ten directions, with yearning and diligent devotion, contemplate with a sincere heart and, following my voice, once again extend your repentance.
Each person recites the name of the Dharma (after the assembly has finished reciting the names),
the Master recites the verse (and the assembly bows in unison):
"All evil karma created in the past, Arises entirely from beginningless greed, anger, and delusion."
All karmic obstacles arise from body, speech, and mind; now, before the Buddha, I seek repentance for all roots of sin.

(Throughout all the methods for receiving the precepts, these four lines of verse are universally employed to repent of transgressions and offenses committed since beginningless time; it is not a matter of merely invoking the *heshang* in a perfunctory manner. The master should give rise to a heart of great compassion that seeks to uproot suffering, while the one seeking repentance must possess deep faith and a sense of shame and remorse.

When this single sound is uttered, its resonance reaches Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; when this single thought is activated, one’s form pervades the presence of all Buddhas. Yet, my body does not go there, nor do the Buddhas come here; rather, the Way of response and stimulus intersects.)

Subject and object are both quiescent. Furthermore, I pray that by the merit of this repentance, it may universally cause all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm to together dissolve their karmic obstacles and collectively be liberated from the cycle of suffering. Thus raising the harmony [of the assembly] is called the True Repentance of Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices.
The supreme practice of the merit of repentance— I dedicate all boundless and excellent blessings universally,
Vowing that all sentient beings drowning in suffering May swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, And to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas:
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra has been recited and the confession of transgressions completed above. Each of you should now quiet your minds and prepare your robes and bowls.

You must consult the Vinaya and study the scriptures one by one to seek instruction. We respectfully await the Venerable Master’s ascent to the seat tomorrow morning to request the ordination of a śrāmaṇera.
"Regarding the ten precepts, can each of you practice them according to the teachings? (They answer: "We shall practice according to the teachings.

(During this interval, the teacher should interrogate them. If there are no serious obstacles, they descend from their seats as usual. However, if there are those who have committed transgressions or possess serious obstacles, the teacher should address the assembly, saying:)
Now, among this assembly, there is one named [Name] who has committed a grave obstruction. This most serious obstacle of sin is strictly regulated by the Buddha in the Vinaya;
I dare not handle it arbitrarily. Tomorrow morning, I shall inform the Upādhyāya and convene with the teachers, monks, and Sthaviras.
If he is fit for upliftment, the Upādhyāya will have his own skillful means to act according to the teachings and the individual's capacity. If he is unfit for upliftment, even if...

The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is likewise difficult to encounter for the sake of deliverance; you must give rise to profound and great shame and remorse, and must not treat this with casual indifference.
For now, follow the assembly and withdraw for a while.
The ritual attendant says:
"All rise together. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, they perform three prostrations in gratitude and then divide into ranks.
Those who escorted the Master shall see him back to his quarters.

(Once the Master has been escorted back to his quarters, the assembly returns to the Karmadāna Hall. The newly ordained candidate bows three times to all the ritual masters, the recorders, and the masters of ceremonies to express gratitude for their assistance in performing the rites and accomplishing the merit of the repentance.

The master of ceremonies leads the assembly up to the hall and instructs them to perform prostrations to the Buddha throughout the night, each maintaining sincere devotion and remaining free from weariness.)

Chapter Six: Weighing Confessions (If, during the interrogation, there are those who have committed grave offenses, the following morning the various ushers shall, together with the secretary, first ascertain the number of individuals in each hall.
They shall be summoned to one place, where they shall perform a single prostration toward the ushers and the secretary master, then stand to one side.)
The ritual master says:
"Last night in the Karmadāna Hall, we interrogated you and have already recorded what you have confessed upon the register.
However, this matter is extremely grave; I shall now first lead you to the quarters of the Karma Master to beg for his compassionate consideration."
Together they proceeded to the abbot’s quarters and presented themselves before the Master, saying: "Venerable Sir, you may follow me. (As for those who have confessed their transgressions:

they are led by the ritual master and the secretary to the Karmadāna Hall, where they perform the customary prostrations and personally submit their request, earnestly entreating that the rites be performed to deliver them.)

The Karmadāna said: "You yourselves have confessed your transgressions; you may truly be called those who possess a sense of shame and remorse. Now, good and evil arise from the mind, and one receives retribution for sins and blessings according to oneself.
It is fortunate that you have recognized your faults; perhaps they may be remedied through skillful means. Moreover, since you have entreated us with such earnestness..."
Truly, how could I bear to sit idly by and watch? You should follow me at once to the Abbot’s quarters; whether it be appropriate or not, we shall await the Master’s instructions.

Having heard this, he prostrates once and rises, immediately following the master and others to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*). The ritual attendant leads those with business to stand and wait outside the door. First, he informs the attendant to announce the matter to the Abbot. The Abbot emerges from the quarters and ascends the seat.

The *karmadāna* master performs a single prostration toward the upper direction. Next, the ritual attendant and the secretary perform three prostrations together. They present the record of offenses (*zuice*), which the Abbot unfolds and examines. He then dispatches an attendant to invite the various *kalyāṇamitras* and the heads of the various halls to the quarters.

Once they have arrived, they all perform three prostrations to the Abbot and arrange themselves into the two ranks (*liuxu*). The ritual attendant calls those with business outside to enter; they proceed before the seat and perform a full prostration as usual, then remain kneeling with palms joined.
The Master struck the sounding block and said:
"Although you have given rise to a good heart and requested the Dharma of the precepts, alas, you have committed grave offenses and defiled the vessel of the Way."
The regulations of the Vinaya are strict and stern; human sentiments find it difficult to be fully accommodated.

However, if you are indeed able to possess great shame and remorse and resolve to give rise to the Great Bodhicitta, I shall now join with the Vinaya Master Zhi and others to follow the Mahayana Vaipulya Repentance Method and provide extraordinary salvation for you.
According to the *Sūtra of the Names of the Three Thousand Buddhas*, the Buddha said: "If there are sentient beings who wish to eliminate the four kinds of prohibitive sins,
who wish to repent for the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, and who wish to eradicate the extremely grave sin of groundless slander against the Dharma,
they should diligently pay homage to the names of the fifty-three Buddhas, as well as the magnificent names of the myriad virtues of the three thousand Buddhas."
It is truly because the Buddhas are called the Great Masters of the three realms and the Compassionate Fathers of the four modes of birth;

there is no suffering they do not rescue from, and no happiness they do not bestow. If sentient beings possess even a hair’s breadth of goodness, the Buddhas immediately extend their hands to lift them up.

When performing rites of repentance, one must necessarily wash one's body and clothes and reverently prepare incense and candles, whether for a seven-day period or even seven weeks, seeking to behold auspicious signs.

If one beholds auspicious signs, such as the manifestation of radiant light and portents, then one may know without doubt that one's transgressions have been extinguished and that one remains a pure vessel for the Way.
However, if during the time of performing prostrations and repentance, the mind is not single-minded, the ritual is not reverent, or one does not believe in the laws of karma regarding sin and merit—
Regarding those who do not fear the hells: although the Buddha’s compassion is universal, it is difficult to encounter when one’s karmic resonance is obstructed.

It is like the bright moon in the midst of the sky; it does not appear in turbid water. There is nothing that can be done [for such a person] (one strike of the *chime*). Can you thus follow the teachings and practice accordingly?

[The candidate] replies: "I can follow the teachings and practice accordingly. [The Preceptor addresses the two orders: "Virtuous ones, now, in accordance with the teachings of the Vaipulya Sūtras, we shall perform the repentance for him."

"Is it acceptable? (The assembly answers in unison: "It is so. (The Abbot says: "Since all you virtuous ones have deliberated with one mind and all say it is acceptable, the ritual master of the Main Hall shall select a location for him to settle.
This will facilitate his sincere concentration of mind and the performance of repentance rites.
Once the repentance rites are completed, he shall return to report again."

(The ritual master conducts the ceremony as usual, instructing them to perform prostrations and have them stand fixed by the side of the door. After the various *kalyāṇamitras* and teachers have finished bowing toward the upper [seat], they wait for the *upādhyāya* to enter the room, after which they each disperse. The ritual master then leads them to offer thanks at their respective locations.)

He shall then settle himself before a certain Buddha image to perform the ritual of repentance (*li-ch'an*). When the repentance and prostrations are completed, he first informs the Master of Ceremonies (*yin-li shi*) of the main hall, stating whether he has seen auspicious signs (*hao-xiang*) or not.

Next, the Master of Ceremonies leads him to the quarters of the Karma Master (*ge-mo shi*), informing him in the same manner. Thereupon, he is led to each of the halls to invite the assembly; once they have all gathered at the Abbot’s quarters (*fang-zhang*), the one who performed the repentance stands outside the door. He waits until the Venerable Master (*ho-shang*) emerges from his room and ascends the seat, after which the assembly performs three prostrations.

The ritual master calls for the candidate to advance. As usual, he performs three prostrations with the head to the ground and joins his palms. He then kneels long-legged. The *upādhyāya* questions him in detail before the assembly: "During your repentance, have you seen any auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*)?

If he replies that he has seen them, the *upādhyāya* must examine whether they are authentic based on the scriptural accounts of how such signs appear. If they are verified as genuine, he grants permission for the candidate to receive the precepts. If the account is merely similar to the descriptions or if he says he saw no auspicious signs, the *upādhyāya* washes his hands, burns incense, and personally writes three lots:

one saying "Permission to Receive," one saying "Repent Again," and one saying "Not Permitted. The *upādhyāya* leads the assembly to the hall and places the three lots before the Buddha. The *upādhyāya* offers incense, prostrates, and prays silently, saying: (Insert prayer here)
I look up and address the Great Awakened World-Honored One and all Bodhisattvas throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
Now, [Name], of [Province] [District], has resolved his mind to seek the reception of the pure precepts from me, the Bhikṣu [Name].

However, he has committed extremely evil deeds in this present life (having transgressed certain heavy prohibitions and violated certain forbidden precepts). I, the Bhikṣu [Name], dare not willfully contravene the Vinaya regulations by acting on my own authority.

I grant permission for them to receive the precepts. Having previously followed the Mahāyāna Vaipulya teachings, I have had them prostrate before the majestic names of the Buddhas and recite the holy titles that extol their myriad virtues, seeking a vision of auspicious signs.
Although they have completed their prostrations, no such signs have yet been seen; perhaps this is due to obstacles, shallow faith, or a lack of reverence in the three karmas.
I now, before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, offer this earnest prayer on their behalf: I pray only that you will not forsake them.

Sentient beings are embraced by compassion, which purifies their capacity for the Path and eliminates their karmic offenses, enabling them to receive the precepts and practice according to the Vinaya.

Even those sentient beings who have violated all prohibitions and committed various evil deeds shall together enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Vinaya, becoming fully endowed with the virtue of abandonment and perfecting the Dharmakāya. Now, three lots shall be used as the standard.
The Holy Mirror is impartial. We entreat you most earnestly with compassion; we pray that you will bestow your compassionate protection.

(The Preceptor shall thus direct his thoughts and offer silent prayers, performing three prostrations. Next, the assembly shall likewise give rise to the mind of great compassion to extract suffering, silently performing three prostrations. This is the ritual procedure for the practice-gate of Samantabhadra; do not harbor thoughts of merely following the crowd.

When the assembly has finished their prostrations and stands in two rows, the Ritual Master calls the practitioner of repentance forward, instructing them to sincerely make vows, perform visualization, and direct the mind to universally prostrate before the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the Dharma-realm. [They] perform three prostrations, then kneel before the Buddha.)

Draw a lot from the bowl at random so that the assembly may see it clearly. If the lot drawn permits one to receive the precepts, then have them receive the precepts together with the assembly. If the lot drawn requires further repentance, they must go and perform repentance according to the Dharma; once the repentance is complete, they shall be given the precepts, and there is no need to draw the lot again.

If the lot drawn does not permit it, they must continue to perform repentance, increasing their efforts with earnest sincerity without limit as to the number of times, until they certainly draw a lot permitting them to receive the precepts.

Thus, whether it be for the first time, the second time, or even up to dozens of times, the procedure for gathering the assembly and performing the ritual is exactly as described above. For the Buddha’s regulations are absolute and do not follow personal sentiment; if one’s initial repentance were merely perfunctory, how could one possibly maintain firm resolve after receiving the precepts? Therefore, in this present ritual, the procedures are performed repeatedly; do not grow weary of this.

Its intricacies are nothing other than means to ensure that the teacher and disciple remain pure, so that both self and others may obtain benefit, and thereby to clarify the ocean of the Vinaya-dharma by raising the banner of the light-precepts upon its branches.
The Authentic Model for the Transmission of Precepts at the Three Altars, Volume One;
The Authentic Model for the Transmission of Precepts at the Three Altars, Volume Two.
Composed by the Vinaya Master Śramaṇa Duti of Baohua Mountain in Jinling.
First, regarding the ritual for requesting the precepts and repenting prior to the bestowal of the bhikṣu precepts at the two altars, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"The bhikṣu precepts are subsumed under the fourfold meaning: first, the reception of full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*); second, the subsequent fulfillment of that ordination (*anuśaṃsā*)."
Third, the perfection of protecting the minds of others; fourth, the perfection of maintaining [the precepts].

Regarding what is called "the perfection of protecting the minds of others," it means that a bhikṣu possesses a portion of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) because he is able to protect and increase the pure faith of others.

This is because it causes them to feel joy and reverence, thereby drawing them back to the Buddha-dharma. For those who are sons of the Śākya, if one’s deportment is incomplete, then one’s movements and stillness will violate the prohibitions, and one’s coming and going will invite censure.
The *Jingxun* (Warnings and Instructions) for the Black-Robed Gate states: "When the World-Honored One dwelt in the world, he deeply understood the capacities of sentient beings;
in all his actions, he invariably took deportment as primary. This was because the Great Sage’s vast compassion was manifest in every detail."
He guides and disciplines sentient beings; internally, he serves as a model for the monastic community, and externally, he benefits the donors and patrons.
All the more so in this degenerate age, when we are far removed from the Buddha; it is essential to rely entirely upon the Vinaya discipline to establish the Three Jewels.

Therefore, once a śrāmaṇera has reached the required age, he attains the status of a man, yet prior to ascending the altar to receive full ordination, he ought to practice the formal rituals and decorum.

If there are many fully ordained monks and *śrāmaṇeras*, one should use tally sticks (*śalākā*) to record their names, with three persons forming a single altar (*maṇḍala*). One tally stick shall list three altars; within this, one person is moved forward to serve as the head, presiding over the remaining eight. If those seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*) are few, one may simply follow the order of the altars without the need for tally sticks.

Three days prior to the ordination, the Master of Ceremonies (*pravartaka-ācārya*) shall instruct the lay attendants (*karmadāna*) to sweep and clean the Dharma Hall (*dharmasabhā*), arranging a single seat in its center. At the appointed time, the *gandī* drum shall be struck. Once all those seeking ordination have assembled and taken their places in rows, the two Masters of Ceremonies shall lead five persons to invite the Preceptor (*śikṣācārya*).

Upon receiving the invitation, the Preceptor shall emerge from his quarters, followed by an attendant holding the tally sticks. They enter the hall, and the Preceptor takes his seat. The attendant then places the tally sticks upon the table.
The Ritual Attendant says:
"Offer incense. Return to your positions. All line up facing upward. Spread your ritual implements.
Upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations. (After the prostrations) lift your robes, kneel long, and join your palms.
The Master struck the sounding block and said, "O śrāmaṇeras:

you who now wish to receive full ordination and enter the ranks of the Saṅgha-ratna must know that among the four meanings of 'fullness' (saṃpanna), there is the 'fullness of dignified deportment' (īryāpatha-saṃpanna).
'Dignity' (wei) means being pure, solemn, and awe-inspiring; 'deportment' (yi) refers to physical form."
Their deportment may serve as a model, for the Sangha Jewel is most venerable and their office is no light matter.

By strictly purifying the *vinaya* and upholding the True Dharma, they can eliminate famine and act as a field of merit for the world of men. They guide and transform sentient beings toward the wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa*, such that those who see or hear them increase their own faith and reverence.
This is like the noble and composed conduct of Aśvajit, which moved the man gathering beans to develop faith.
He delighted in leaving the household life. Śāriputra begged for food with composed dignity, gathering in non-Buddhists and leading them from error back to the right path.
The dignified deportment of śramaṇas throughout antiquity and the present—those who gather beings and benefit living creatures—is truly difficult to enumerate exhaustively.

Generally speaking, the myriad minor practices of the thirty thousand and eight thousand rules do not transcend the four modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; within each of these, there are skillful means for careful protection.
Through the pure faith of others, one is able to accomplish the path and practice of one's own person. Therefore, I now comply with the compassionate command of the Upādhyāya:
first, you shall practice the ritual observances for three days; subsequently, you shall receive the precepts through repentance and ascend the altar for transmission.

This is intended so that when the time arrives, your dignified deportment will have its proper rules. Whether among you there are those who have long dwelt in the forest hermitages and been in close proximity to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), your character and disposition are surely...

Having already undergone transformation, your conduct naturally accords with the established standards. Were there those who have newly entered the monastery and have not yet been refined, how could their dispositions be melted away?
Their movements and stillness would surely deviate from the guiding rules. Thus, gold that has not been smelted remains nothing more than stubborn ore;
jade must be polished and ground before it becomes a fine vessel. I shall now include the names of you all in the register.
The sequence of the tally-sticks (*zhān*) is arranged for the convenience of practicing the ritual procedures. Regarding the numbering of these tallies:

since three persons receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) at one altar, each single tally lists three altars. Within each tally, one person is designated as the leader to oversee the remaining eight;

thus, nine persons mutually practice humility and observe the rites, their movements like a string of pearls. For all ritual matters that they do not yet understand, they rely on the collective authority of the assembly.

The Ritual Master, out of compassion, provides these kind instructions: do not shrink from toil or hardship. As the Confucians say, "If one does not guard against minor lapses in conduct, they will eventually bring ruin to great virtue.
How much more so for those who are disciples of the Buddha—should they not be careful? (Strike the *chī* once. Can you all follow these teachings and put them into practice?

(The assembly replies in unison: We shall follow the teachings and put them into practice. (The Master says: Since you can follow the teachings and put them into practice, you may be said to be acting in accordance with the Dharma. Upādhyāya.
Furthermore, within the hall of repentance, various positions of virtuous elders were appointed:
one inspector of lot-drawings (*zhēnqiān shī*), one collector of lot-drawings (*jiǎoqiān shī*), one scribe (*shūjì shī*), and several patrol officers (*xúnsì shī*).

As for the inspector of lot-drawings, during the time of confession, he was to prevent laypeople or non-Buddhists from intruding to eavesdrop; therefore, [he] requested Master [Name] to serve as the one who examines the lot-drawings for you all.

[The Master] Ming instructed them one by one to proceed forward. Regarding those who had submitted their slips: having already confessed their transgressions, he feared that some crafty, unprincipled, or unworthy individuals might surreptitiously watch for the faults of others;
therefore, he requested that Master [Name] withdraw the original slips and, according to the names, have them come forth. Regarding the scribe:
during the process of confession, he still feared that the names and offenses might coincide with errors in recording; therefore, he requested that Scribe [Name] ascend [to verify].
A record of names has been kept to ensure no one is overlooked. As for those on patrol, they must maintain strict solemnity due to the requirements of the *caṇḍamā* (confession/repentance).

Fearing that people might easily become lax, and further apprehending that they might sleep privately during the stillness of night or engage in idle chatter while seated in rows, we request that the various masters [named] below inspect and exhort the assembly to prevent drowsiness and distraction.
All the masters appointed as above shall provide assistance and support in bringing this to completion.
of his merit. You all should pay him respectful homage; do not harbor arrogance or a sense of superiority, lest you fail the instructions he has bestowed.
The ritual master says:
"All the śrāmaṇeras, having bowed once and risen, shall divide into ranks and stand in order to the left and right."

(When the distribution of the lots has been completed in sequence, the *kāśyapa* invites the Preceptor to return to his quarters. He then returns to the place where the lots were distributed and bows once to the assembly as a gesture of thanks to the Master of Ceremonies.

The Master of Ceremonies then instructs a *śrāmaṇera* to invite the various masters who received their assignments to the hall, teaching them to perform three prostrations to the assembly in general. Once the masters have dispersed, the Master of Ceremonies leads the *śrāmaṇeras* back to their respective halls. The Master of Ceremonies then posts the notice for the *upasaṃpadā* ordination platform so that each person knows the number of platforms upon which they will receive full ordination, ensuring that the order of precedence for the precepts is not confused).

Regarding the second point on the exhortation to receive the precepts, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one generates an inferior state of mind, one receives an inferior grade of precept; if one generates a middling state of mind, one receives a middling grade of precept;
if one generates a superior state of mind, one receives a superior grade of precept. Thus, we know that the essence of the precepts is fundamentally [determined by the state of mind].
First, there is no distinction of superior or inferior; it is through the conditions and responses of the mind that differences arise.

If one were to wait until ascending the altar and performing the ritual before being taught to generate the superior grade of mind and receive the superior grade of precepts, those individuals would be utterly ignorant and would not know what constitutes the superior grade of mind.
It is like the sound of thunder from the peak of a wondrous mountain, followed by sweet rain.
When one is stranded in a land of molten gold, it is difficult to awaken to understanding and there is no capacity for receptivity;

therefore, before receiving the precepts, I first address the Upādhyāya to provide preliminary guidance, so that upon reaching the altar, they may attain a state of vigorous alertness and give rise to the mind of the highest grade,
whereby their essential nature becomes perfectly complete— what then would not be a supreme precept?

On the morning of the invitation for ordination, first purify the Dharma Hall and arrange the Dharma seat. When the time arrives, strike the wooden mallet to assemble the śrāmaṇeras seeking full ordination. From among the assembly, the four senior novices at the head of the row go to invite the officiating masters;
once they have reached the hall, all the śrāmaṇeras perform three prostrations toward the officiating masters, then stand up, and the leader joins his palms and says:

We, the śrāmaṇeras [Name], are but individuals of dull wit and stubbornness; how could we possibly understand the principles and models of the Vinaya? Relying on our teachers as excellent guides, we have gained a slight knowledge of the monastic conduct and dignified deportment.
As our gradual cultivation has given rise to a heart of aspiration, we further hope that our earnest desire to receive and uphold the precepts may be fulfilled.
Therefore, we now once again entreat the various masters to petition the Upādhyāya on our behalf once more.
(Having thus made this announcement, they join their palms and inquire after one another’s welfare).
The ritual master says:
"O śrāmaṇeras, I observe that your intention to receive full ordination is most sincere, and your words of earnest entreaty are most profound. I believe..."
By such power, your aspirations shall surely be fulfilled. Nine persons from among the assembly who are leaders shall step forward from their ranks;

one person shall hold incense and accompany me to the Abbot’s quarters to pay respects and invite the Venerable Master. The others shall remain standing in their places, maintaining solemn and dignified deportment, awaiting his instructions.

(They proceed to the Abbot’s quarters and perform their customary prostrations. The Abbot accepts the invitation and ascends the seat in the hall. Those who invited him each return to their respective positions. The four ritual masters perform three prostrations with full prostration gear before the seat, then kneel long with palms joined. The former generation makes the formal announcement.)

I respectfully address the Venerable Master. May your great compassion grant me leave to speak. Those śrāmaṇeras [Name], etc., have gained a basic familiarity with the monastic deportment and now seek ordination with earnest resolve.
They aspire to enter the ranks of the Saṃgha and desire to ascend to the realm of the sages; therefore, they have now first come before your seat to prostrate themselves and submit this request.

"I only pray that the Venerable Master’s wisdom will discern and weigh whether this is appropriate. If my capacity is such that I may be uplifted and saved, please grant me a measure of compassion and provide me with preliminary instruction.
(Having spoken thus, he performs three prostrations, rises, arranges his robes, stands to the left and right, and calls out:)
Offer incense. Stand once more. All the śrāmaṇeras line up facing upward in unison.
Unfurling their formal robes (*mahāparyañka*), they prostrate three times upon hearing the sound of the *qing* gong. After bowing, they adjust their robes, kneel long, and join their palms.
The words for requesting the precepts shall be recited by you yourself (the leader recites them aloud):
A human body is difficult to obtain; birth in a central land is difficult to achieve; the Buddha-way is difficult to encounter; and the precepts of the Dharma are difficult to receive.
We, [Name], have fortunately met the Great Upādhyāya, who plants the banner of radiant light and spreads the pure Brahma-net, guiding ordinary beings and gathering them into the Jewel of the Sangha.
We pray that you will bestow upon us, [Name], the full ordination, so that we may practice according to the Vinaya, realize the Way, and benefit all living beings.
To repay his kindness and virtue.
(After the announcement, all the śrāmaṇeras bow their heads in unison, join their palms, and kneel attentively to listen.
The Upādhyāya strikes the sounding-block and says:
Now, one who seeks the wish-fulfilling jewel enters the ocean, proceeding from the shallow to the deep; one who receives the full precepts ascends the altar, advancing from the small to the great.
The treasure of the precepts cannot be sought by leaping over stages; the Buddha’s regulation requires that they be conferred only when one is truly prepared.
There has never been anyone who bypassed the stage of a śrāmaṇera and proceeded directly to the rank of a bhikṣu. Now that you all have already...
If you maintain the precepts of *śikṣamāṇā* and further seek to receive the *bhikṣu* vows, then you will not overstep the stages of practice;
it is logical that you should cultivate them further. How much more so when your request is made with such earnest sincerity—how could I begrudge you the granting of them?

However, these full precepts are most venerable and their responsibility is no light matter; they are the root source for the long endurance of the True Dharma and the means by which the Saṃgha flourishes.
The life-vein [of the Sangha]: were it not for full ordination, the monastic order would have no means to be established; were it not for the Sangha Jewel, how could the Buddha-Dharma be propagated?
Therefore, among the assemblies of devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, non-Buddhists, and Brahmins, the community of bhikṣus is foremost.

For this reason, one who desires to perfect the complete precepts must not rely on an improper place, but must necessarily depend upon the formal ritual of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to establish the boundary (*sīmā*).
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "In a place that is not a *karmabhūmi* (a site for formal ritual action), one must not remain inside to receive the *chanda* (consent) and perform monastic affairs.

Since the location is in accordance with the Dharma, an altar is established therein; the number of the ten masters (*ācāryas*) must be complete, and they must be carefully selected according to the Dharma with strict integrity.
Thus, the Vinaya-śāstra says: "The *upādhyāya* and the two *ācāryas* must all be in accordance with the Dharma; the seven monks who serve as witnesses must all be pure and enlightened."

"Xiao! If there is no *upādhyāya*, or if the number of monks is less than ten, [the ordination] will not be accomplished in either case. Although the Master is thus, it is further necessary that your persons be free from obstacles and hindrances.

Therefore, the Vinaya states: 'Those whose physical characteristics are incomplete, those subject to the hundred types of prohibitions, those who have themselves broken their pure conduct, or those who have defiled the Brahma-conduct of others—none of these may receive full ordination. Even if you possess the vessel for the Path, this is precisely for your sake."

When proclaiming the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the time for establishing the essence of the fourfold formal act (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), one must strictly adhere to the wording without adding, subtracting, or omitting anything;

all who perform the *jñapti-karman* must respect the disciplinary regulations (*vinaya*). Thus, one shall not fall into what is contrary to the Dharma, even if external conditions are otherwise fully met.
Furthermore, your resolve to seek the precepts is of three grades: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
According to the mind you have generated, you shall accordingly receive precepts of superior, middling, or inferior grade.

Nevertheless, when compared with the precepts, the essence of the precepts, the practice of the precepts, and the characteristics of the precepts of the full ordination (upasampadā), those received by a śrāmaṇera cannot be compared to them even by a hundredfold or a thousandfold.

As an analogy: if one does not recognize such profound meanings, then even though one has ascended the altar to receive the precepts, having received them, it is as if they had never been received at all.
Such a person resembles a monk but is not a true monk; living together with the assembly, they are called a "mute sheep" bhikṣu.

When participating in the communal monastic rites, they are labeled as belonging to the ranks of the *māhala* (ignorant). If one wishes to sustain and flourish the Triple Gem and benefit all sentient beings, this [lack of understanding] is a failure in that merit.

Virtue—by what means can it be mastered? Therefore, before you ascend the altar today, I shall provide clear instruction so that when you formally receive the precepts, you may understand them with unclouded clarity.

As for what is called "receiving the superior grade of precepts with a superior grade of mind," this refers to your ability, upon ascending the altar tomorrow morning, to generate firm power of faith and universally [regard] all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm as...
In terms of the situational context: one gives rise to a heart of vast compassion and protection; eliminates thoughts of unwholesomeness and harm;
vows to sever all evil; vows to cultivate all goodness; and vows to deliver all sentient beings. Within this, one is neither terrified nor regressive, maintaining a firm and profound resolve.
This is called generating the superior grade of mind and receiving the superior grade of precepts; it is truly what is meant by "concealing within."
The Bodhisattva practice: outwardly manifesting as a śrāvaka, one is able to abide in the True Dharma and establish the ranks of the Saṃgha.

If, despite possessing a compassionate and protective mind, one’s protection is not universal; or if, while taking the realm of the dharmadhātu as an object, one’s contemplation is not all-encompassing;

or if, regarding the task of delivering sentient beings, one appears to have fear and retreat, such that one’s vows are not yet profoundly firm—this is called the middling or lower grade of mind. This mind...
That which is narrow and inferior is not supreme; the precepts thus obtained are merely of middling or lower grade. These precepts can only benefit oneself and allow one to dwell in a thatched hut;
since they lack the capacity to benefit others, how can the lineage of the Buddhas be sustained?

Therefore, I now desire for you to give rise to the superior mind and receive the superior precepts, rather than desiring you to give rise to a base and inferior mind and receive precepts of middling or lower grade.

Furthermore, as for what is called the "Dharma of Precepts," it refers to the two hundred and fifty pure precepts and one hundred and eighty-four types of *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) ordained by the golden mouth of the World-Honored One during the twelve years following his attainment of enlightenment.
These were established after he observed the arising of matters concerning the causes and conditions of outflows (*sāsrava*),

in order to restrain the three poisons for those monks who were free from worldly affairs and to subdue the seven branches [of bodily and vocal conduct], extending even to the three thousand eight [rules].
This refers to the ten thousand immeasurable codes of discipline (*vinaya*). As for what is called the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-bhāva*):

it is precisely at the moment when one approaches the seats of the ten masters on the following morning and formally performs the *karmavācanā*, the power of the mental karma of your superior resolve (*adhimukti-citta*) mobilizes the visualization of the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), universally taking all sensory objects as its focus.
While these objects appear from the mind, the objects so manifested do not possess manifest form (*vijñapti*).
Form is the very substance of all objective realms within the dharma-realm; it is also the cause for attaining the precepts.
Prior to the moment one forms a mental perception and accepts it, this substance of the objective realm has no connection to you.

However, once you have given rise to a thought, formed a perception, and accepted it, this substance of the objective realm within the dharma-realm will forever rely upon your own minds, never being forgotten from moment to moment.
At that time, one maintains protection; thus, the precepts serve as the support, while the mind is that which is supported.
The harmonious integration of the mind and its mental factors is termed the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-svabhāva*). This can be understood by analogy with the metaphor of a medicinal pill.

As for what is called "precept-practice," it refers to relying upon the essence of the precepts originally received, whether through daily activities, recitation, meditative concentration, the practice of incense-offering and repentance rituals, or other forms of cultivation.
Purifying one's karma—even down to such acts as putting on robes and receiving food—all must not transgress the *vinaya*.
Therefore, all practices are collectively termed "preceptual conduct" (*śīla-caryā*); it is not that there is a separate preceptual conduct apart from all other practices.

All supramundane activities take pure precepts as their foundation. As for what is called the "characteristics of the precepts," they refer to the two hundred and fifty rules established by the Buddha.

The complete precepts; the one hundred and eighty-four types of *karmavācanā*; within each of these individual precept-characteristics, the clarification of what is light or heavy, and what is permitted or prohibited;
and within each *karmavācanā*, the two conditions of accomplishment and failure—this is the characteristic of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the matters constantly practiced during the four modes of daily conduct, whether they pertain to timely or untimely occasions—this is the characteristic of practice (*pratipattilakṣaṇa*). Its...
The Dharma is established based on circumstances, and circumstances are accomplished in accordance with the Dharma.

If all matters such as wholesome karmas are in accord with the Dharma, yet one fails to perform what ought to be performed, this is called "cessation-offense" (*sthāpana-āpatti*). If one performs immediately that which ought to be performed, this is called "active-upholding" (*kriyā-samvara*).

If all matters such as unwholesome karmas are contrary to the Dharma, yet one performs what ought not to be performed, this is called "active-offense" (*kriyā-āpatti*). If [one does not perform] what ought not to be...
To act while not acting is what is called "stopping and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*). If one lacks knowledge of stopping, one commits offenses while performing acts that should be maintained;

thus, when stopping is an offense and acting is maintenance, the distinctions between what is permitted and what is prohibited become entirely obscured, and the nature of accomplishment and failure remains utterly bewildered. For this reason, the Vinaya regulations require that a bhikṣu devote himself exclusively to the study of the precepts before five years of ordination (*pañca-varṣa*).

Only after five years may he be permitted to receive formal instruction and engage in Chan meditation. This is intended to ensure that he recognizes the characteristics of the rules and maintains them.
In essence, I hope that you will give rise to concentration and wisdom; only then will there be a basis for the path of world-transcending practice.

If you all can have such faith and understanding, and maintain this in such a way, you will likely accord with the sacred virtue of the sages and truly be children of the Dharma who have left the household life.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "To offer this profound mind to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. You all are able to...
"Will you practice according to the instructions? (He replied: "I shall practice according to the instructions. (The Upādhyāya said:
"Since you can practice according to the instructions, tonight you must invite a Karmācārya. First, I shall examine your ten branches of prohibitions as śrāmaṇeras.
If you maintain them without defilement, you may be called true and pure vessels for the Way. If there is even the slightest transgression, your body and mind will still be defiled and impure."
"You must undergo severe and painful reprimand and repent according to the Vinaya. Furthermore, there are thirteen grave obstacles and sixteen minor impediments.

At the time of entering the ordination platform, these shall be separately interrogated by the Preceptor in a secluded place. Upon reaching the formal performance of the *karmavācanā*, they shall again be sternly interrogated before the assembly.
I now command the Master of Ceremonies to lead you, Venerable Ones, to the quarters of the two masters to inform them."
Regarding your request for the full ordination (*upasampadā*), guidance, and so forth, please wait until the ritual procedures and the examination of the confession have been completed.
If it is indeed found that you have not committed a grave offense and have not destroyed the root [of the precepts], only then may the great *saṃgha* of this realm be assembled.

Within that assembly, ten masters shall be respectfully invited to ascend the platform to bestow the Great Bhikṣu Precepts upon you all. The virtuous master who leads the assembly shall act as previously described by me.
"We shall immediately carry out these instructions. (The attendants lead the way. The assembly bows deeply with palms joined and responds in unison: "As the Preceptor has commanded.
(The four attendants turn toward the upper direction, unfold their ritual implements, and perform three prostrations. They then resume their positions on the left and right and call out:)
All the śrāmaṇeras rise together; hearing the sound of the chime, they perform three prostrations in thanks. (After the prostrations), they adjust their robes, rise, and form ranks.
Those who escorted the Master shall see him back to his quarters.

(As usual, having escorted the Abbot back to his quarters, he returns to the Dharma Hall. The assembly of śrāmaṇeras together prostrate three times to thank the Master of Ceremonies. Rising, they divide into two groups and stand.)

In the third stage of the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for bestowing the full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is essential that the three preceptors (*tri-upādhyāya*) be as harmonious as water and milk, that they share a single boundary (*ekasīmā*), and that the six points of concord (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) be present;

only when the Vinaya rules are thus in accord may the transmission take place. Although these śrāmaṇeras have now requested their *upādhyāya* to provide guidance and instruction on repentance, [the formal rite must proceed accordingly].
Admonition: Since the responsibility rests with the two masters, the procedure is further ordered so that they perform prostrations to notify them.

(The notification to the two masters occurs immediately after the invitation for the *śīla* has concluded. The ritual master leads the *śrāmaṇeras* to remove the Dharma seat, and they then stand in their respective ranks. One ritual master first leads the two *śrāmaṇeras* to the hall.

The ritual master performs a single prostration with touching heads toward the master, stands up, and calls the *śrāmaṇeras* to unfold their ritual implements and perform three prostrations. They then kneel long with palms joined. The ritual master, with hands folded, speaks on behalf of the assembly as follows):
The śrāmaṇeras [Name], etc., have recently requested their Upādhyāya to receive the full precepts (upasampadā).

Having already received his compassionate consent and been granted preliminary instruction, they are yet unaware of the fundamental precepts for those who exert themselves in discipline, nor do they know how to maintain or what constitutes an offense.
Therefore, the Upādhyāya has dispatched me, [Name], etc., to lead the śrāmaṇeras first to inform the Karmācārya regarding the formal ritual (jñapti-karman). This is done now...
During the night, the seats were spread and the assembly was respectfully invited, hoping that they would deign to attend the hall. According to the ritual procedures of the Vinaya, it was said:
"Out of compassion. (After the ceremonial attendant had finished his announcement, he called for the śrāmaṇeras and others to perform one prostration.)
The *karmavācanā* master says: "Excellent, śrāmaṇeras!
It is well that I shall perform the ritual for you here in the hall. Each of you should quiet your thoughts and reflect upon your observance or violation of the precepts.
Assemble and wait until the appointed time; then confess according to the facts. (The assembly replies: "We shall follow and practice according to the instructions."

(The ritual master calls for the śrāmaṇeras and others. After they have performed three prostrations and risen to their formal posture, the one who previously invited [the preceptor] escorts the teacher back to his quarters. The ritual master then leads two śrāmaṇeras to invite the Teaching Master to the hall. As before, they perform the prostrations, kneel long with palms joined.
The ritual master speaks on behalf of the assembly, saying:)
Those śrāmaṇeras (so-and-so), having just now prostrated before their preceptors and requested full ordination, have fortunately been granted compassion and guided according to the Vinaya.
They have already been instructed to invite a karmavācanā master to perform the confession tonight; yet, they still fear that their deportment may be deficient.
Since it is not in accordance with the Dharma to take [the assembly] as an object of focus, we have again appointed [Name] and others to oversee the śrāmaṇeras.

We respectfully inform the Preceptor Ācārya: we humbly pray that you will once more admonish those who are unacquainted [with the rites], and bestow upon us again your compassionate voice out of your great mercy. (After the ceremonial attendant has finished speaking, the śrāmaṇeras prostrate once.)
The preceptor said: "Excellent, śrāmaṇera!
It is truly a cause for great rejoicing that you have spoken as you did. I hope further that you will receive instruction on the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*);

I trust you have already practiced them according to the Dharma. As for the great bhikṣus, they shall follow the regulations of the Vinaya; only after your full ordination (*upasampadā*) may they attend to each matter one by one."
The instruction is given. (The assembly replies: "We shall follow and practice according to the instructions.

(As before, they escort the Master back to his quarters. Then they return to the Dharma Hall to offer general thanks to the assembly and the Master of Ceremonies, after which each returns to their respective hall in order.)
Section Four: On the Teaching Concerning the Robe and Alms Bowl.

Regarding the preliminary inspection of the robe and alms bowl before receiving the śrāmaṇera precepts on the first altar: this is done out of fear that there may be deficiencies or borrowings among them, or that they might be used for improper purposes.
