One must certainly ensure they are replaced and properly prepared. Now, as you are about to ascend the precious altar, because you are advancing [to receive the precepts], [the inspection is performed].
Regarding the observance of the precepts and all ordinary practices, there is nothing that does not accord with those of the Great Sangha.

However, if one does not know the origins of the names and characteristics of the robes and bowl, nor their underlying significance, then every application will be erroneous and one will repeatedly commit transgressions.

Therefore, the preceptor should first provide instruction so that the candidate understands each point thoroughly; this should be done during the period of questioning while at the secluded location on the day of ascending the platform.
I shall briefly describe the ritual implements to avoid further delay.

(After the two masters have been informed, after a short while, they order a lay attendant to go to the Dharma Hall and strike the *ghanṭā*. The preceptor leads the novice who is to receive full ordination to enter; each one wears the seven robes, carries the five major and two minor garments, hangs the bowl, and brings their requisites.

They enter the hall in succession, take their places in order, and place the garments they carry upon the tables. Following the usual protocol, they invite the Preceptor of Instruction (*śikṣācārya*) to enter the hall.)
The ritual attendant announces:

"Incense offering. [The assembly] returns to their positions. The śrāmaṇeras line up facing upward, spread their ritual implements, and upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations.
[After the prostrations,] they adjust their robes, kneel with their right knees on the ground, and join their palms.
These śrāmaṇeras (so-and-so), being about to ascend the platform to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*),
may find it difficult to maintain the proper practice if they do not understand the origins and reasons for the regulations concerning their robes and alms bowls. Therefore,
we now respectfully invite the Preceptor (*ācārya*) to provide clear instruction, so that they may act in accordance with the Vinaya and thereby accord with the holy intention of the Buddhas.
(After the master of ceremonies has announced this, the śrāmaṇeras prostrate once, join their palms, and kneel to listen.
The Preceptor says: (This is excerpted from the ancient *Jiè tán wén*).

The tailoring of the three robes was personally proclaimed by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata; the single alms bowl for acceptance and maintenance is the noble vessel for sustaining the body of a Śākya son.
Its dyed color stands far beyond secular attire, and its prescribed dimensions distinguish it from ordinary people.
Those who wear them find their patience redoubled; those who uphold them possess complete merit. Its value exceeds that of the seven precious jewels, making it difficult to fathom.

One may stay two or three nights with the bhikṣus;
however, if a lustful mind arises and one stops before consummation, it constitutes an offense of intermediate gravity that admits of repentance, and is termed *āpatti*.

Confessing the *duṣkṛta* offense: if, with a lustful mind, one touches the body of a woman, sits with a woman in a secluded place, or speaks with her in a secluded place, all constitute an intermediate offense that admits of repentance; this is called the *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
The fourth precept against false speech: if one has not yet awakened to the Way, yet falsely claims to have awakened;
if one has not attained dhyāna or samādhi, yet falsely claims to have attained them; if one has not realized the four fruits of the path, yet falsely claims to have realized them;

or even if one falsely claims that devas, nāgas, spirits, ghosts, and so forth have come—such falsehoods that are empty and unreal, which deceive and delude the people of the world, are all termed "great false speech. You...

Within this precept, has there ever been an offense? (If you have previously told someone that you committed a certain false speech, you should truthfully answer that you committed such a false speech.
If indeed there is none, then answer: "No."
Furthermore, there are false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech; all of these are termed minor false speech.

Regarding this precept, have you ever committed any violation? (If you have committed a particular instance of false speech, answer truthfully that you have committed such-and-such false speech; if you have not, say: "No."
Regarding the offenses herein: if one speaks a great falsehood to another person and they understand the words clearly, it constitutes a grave offense.
This is a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural transgression) that destroys the root; one loses the śrāmaṇera precepts and is subject to the *parivāsa* (exclusion) for the *duṣkṛta* offense.
It does not admit of repentance. One may not share a lodging or engage in communal activities with other śrāmaṇeras, nor may one be treated like other śrāmaṇeras.
If one stays with other bhikṣus for two or three nights,
and if the original intention was to speak a great falsehood, or if one spoke unclearly and the person before did not understand, or if one stopped speaking in the midst of the discourse—
in all such cases, one commits a middle offense that allows for repentance; this is called a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) requiring confession.

Regarding offenses: if one speaks a minor falsehood that is not clearly understood, one must perform a *tṛkṣāla* (confession) for a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) to purify the mind, and thereafter must not do it again. (The above four precepts are the foundation of all precepts.)
The fifth precept is the abstention from intoxicants. Regarding all things that can cause intoxication, not even a single drop may enter the mouth.
Among these, have you ever committed an offense? (If you have committed one, answer truthfully that you have; if not, say: "No."

Regarding the offenses herein: if one takes five grains, flowers, fruits, or the like that have already been processed into liquor—even including the yeast or dregs—provided it possesses the aroma and taste of alcohol;
and if, perceiving it as alcohol, one places it in the mouth and swallows it such that it can cause intoxication, one commits a *śikṣāpada* offense.
This is permitted to be remedied through repentance and is termed a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) requiring confession. However, if one suffers from a grave illness and the physician...
Regarding those who treat illness by boiling medicine with alcohol: one must first inform one’s teacher; only when the teacher grants permission may one take it.

It is permissible provided there is no scent of alcohol and no taste of alcohol, such that upon entering the mouth, no thought of alcohol arises. If the offense is grave, one must cease [the practice] entirely to avoid transgression.
If, due to illness, one boils medicine with alcohol, yet continues to drink and use it after the illness has been cured, one still incurs the original offense.
The sixth is the precept against using perfumes, flower garlands, or scented oils to anoint the body. Have any of you committed an offense regarding this?
(If you have committed a particular offense, answer truthfully that you have committed it; if you have indeed not committed one, answer: "No."

Regarding the transgressions herein: if in this land one uses silk, wool, or precious gems to fashion and adorn turbans and crowns, it is analogous to the wearing of flower garlands in the Western Regions.
If in this land one uses incense to fumigate robes and canopies, or secretly wears fragrant sachets, this is likewise analogous to the smearing of perfumes upon the body in the Western Regions.
According to the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Buddha permitted [the adoption of] local customs according to the country.

This teaching is not without basis. Therefore, we know that although the customs of dress and adornment in the various regional styles (*gāndī*) differ, the heart that delights in fine ornaments is one and the same.
If anyone performs such acts, they violate a prohibitory precept (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*), yet repentance is permitted.
This is called the offense of *duṣkṛta* that should be confessed.
Seventh is the precept against intentionally going to see or hear singing, dancing, or theatrical performances. Among these, have any of you ever committed an offense?
(If you have committed a certain matter, answer truthfully that you have committed such-and-such; if indeed there is none, say: "No."
Regarding the offenses herein: if one sings songs or chants lyrics, it is called "singing. If one swings the arms or stamps the feet, it is called "dancing.

If one blows the flute or plays the lute, or engages in games such as *shuanglu*, *weiqi*, dice-rolling, gambling with money, *touhu*, archery, or even galloping horses and polishing swords—all these are termed "performances.
Whether one performs them oneself, or sees or hears them and feels joy, it constitutes an offense.

"Delightful. If one intentionally goes to view or listen to such things, each instance constitutes a violation of a prohibitory precept (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*). Repentance is permitted; this is called a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.

The eighth is the precept against sitting on high, wide, or large beds. Among these, have any of you ever committed a transgression? (If there is an answer that "I have committed a transgression," then...)

The one who said "no" replied: "In this present age of the Final Dharma (mofa), the monastic seats everywhere fail to meet the prescribed measurements. Yet, when a teacher is questioned on such matters as they arise, he ought to feel deep shame and remorse. Only if he recognizes that he has violated the Buddha’s regulations might it be permissible;
otherwise, he treats the Vinaya with childlike frivolity, which is why I asked specifically."

Regarding the offenses herein: The Vinaya regulations for monastic beds permit only a height of one chi and six cun (if measured by the Zhou chi standard, one chi is equivalent to eight cun of a modern carpenter’s measure;
thus, one chi and six cun corresponds to one chi and two cun eight fen on the carpenter’s scale). When sitting, the feet must not hang in the air. If it exceeds this measurement, it is termed "high.
As for "broad," it refers to excessive length and width for reclining; since it is both high and broad, it is so named.

Regarding large beds: using one constitutes a violation of a prohibitory precept (*pratikṣepaṇīya-śikṣāpada*), for which repentance is permitted; this is termed a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If one obtains one that is already made, it is not an offense provided one cuts it down to the proper measurements.
The ninth precept: abstaining from eating at improper times. Among these, have you ever committed an offense? (If you have committed one, answer "I have committed one.
If you have not committed one, answer: "No."
Regarding the offenses herein, they are regulated by time. "Time" refers to the period from when the first light of dawn appears in the east until midday at the zenith.
"Non-time" refers to the period from when the sun begins to decline until the next day's first light of dawn has not yet appeared.
If one eats or chews any solid food at an improper time, it is called breaking the fast and violating a prohibitory precept (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*);
this is permitted to be remedied through repentance and is termed a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.

For those who are ill or hungry, it is permitted to take all grains, beans, or wheat—boiling them until the husks are broken and straining the liquid; such may be drunk at improper times, as well as various kinds of syrups.
Once the water has been purified, it may be used.
Tenth is the precept against grasping or holding raw gold, silver, or precious objects. Among these, have any of you committed an offense?
(If one has committed such-and-such, one should truthfully answer that one has committed such-and-such an offense. If, indeed, there is no [offense], one should say: "None.
Regarding those who have committed offenses herein, they are "born," meaning born with innate endowments, such as gold, silver, pearls, jade, coral, and agate.
These include crystal, conch shell, lapis lazuli, amber, glass, tortoise shell, rhinoceros horn, ivory, and all manner of rare and precious objects.

Regarding "images" (xiàng): this refers to the creation of images, such as coins and paper currency, or any kind of vessel fashioned from gold, silver, and the seven treasures, produced in various shapes and forms. All of these are long-lasting things.

A covetous mind contradicts the noble resolve; therefore, the Buddha did not permit its possession. If one possesses such a thing, it constitutes a violation of a prohibitory precept (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*).
Repentance is permitted; this is called a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession. However, if it is for the sake of the Triple Gem...
Furthermore, if one is held by a teacher, an elder, or one's parents, and does not harbor the thought that the items belong to oneself, then there is no offense.

(Having thus examined each of these nine cases in detail, if among them anyone has committed one of the four root offenses of a grave nature, this shall be recorded in writing and entered into the register; on the following day, it shall be presented to the Upādhyāya.
If anyone has committed one of the six subsequent minor offenses, the Karmadāna shall immediately weigh the case according to the Vinaya on the spot and instruct them to perform repentance.)
The ritual attendant says:
"Prostrate once and rise. The first lot is cast from the right side and brought to the station of the official who collects the lots.
One by one, they exit the hall in successive order (waiting for the first lot—nine people in total—to turn and descend from the right side; then, he calls out again).
The second lot is at the top left. Proceeding to the place where the divination master is located, enter the hall one by one according to the names on the lots.

(In this manner, call out each number in sequence, responding as they enter, until the very last lot. For this final lot, there is no need to leave the hall; simply stand up on the right side. Then, strike the wooden mallet to assemble those who previously made their confessions. Each shall enter the hall according to their rank and stand in two rows.

Those appointed to verify the lots, submit them, and patrol the assembly shall exit the group and, facing their seats, join their palms together in a gesture of greeting. The divination master then speaks:)
We, [Name] and others, having completed the duties assigned by our Upādhyāya, have maintained our ranks without diminution and proceeded according to the Dharma.
We have conducted the inspection of Miṃyán with composed and dignified movements, ensuring that none of us violated the rules of decorum.
The *karmadāna* says:
"You have rendered meritorious assistance. As the night grows deep and you are weary, each of you should take your rest.

(The assembly takes their leave and withdraws; each returns to his own place. The *shuji* emerges from the assembly, presents the register at the seat, joins his palms upward, bows in greeting, and speaks:)
I, [Name], having received the commission of the Upādhyāya, have recorded the characteristics of the offenses as questioned. Now, these śrāmaṇeras have fundamentally committed no transgressions;
they are all entirely pure. I inform the Karmavācanā-ācārya, who shall in turn inform the Upādhyāya.
Regarding those who have committed one of the four pārājika offenses within this context, the text is modified as follows:

"Now, among these śrāmaṇeras making their confession, only so-and-so has violated a chapter of the Vinaya; all others are pure. Having informed the *karmavācanā* master, he then informs the *upādhyāya*.
(Once the Karmadāna has offered the consolation as before, the scribe again joins his palms in greeting, takes his leave, and exits the hall to return to his quarters).
The Ritual Master says:

All the śrāmaṇeras simultaneously spread their sitting cloths; upon hearing the sound of the chime, they perform three prostrations with full obeisance, then lift their robes (after the prostrations), kneel long, and join their palms.
The Master strikes the sounding block and says:
"O śrāmaṇeras, I have now followed the Vinaya in questioning you all in detail. Each of you has understood my words and answered them one by one;
I trust there are no further obscurities remaining. It is hoped that your physical vessels are pure, so that you may ascend the platform and receive the full ordination.
Nevertheless, on the day of ascending the platform, I shall still question you regarding the four pārājika offenses, both in private and within the assembly of monks."
Fundamentally, you all are now before my seat this very night; answer with truth and sincerity.
At this moment, I shall further offer incense on your behalf and pray with earnest devotion.
May all Buddhas grant their protection and all sages bear witness. May the transgressions accumulated throughout many lifetimes be utterly extinguished from this day forward;
may the wholesome deeds unperformed since beginningless time be diligently cultivated from now on.

You, the assembly, each visualize the Buddhas of the ten directions and, following my voice, perform sincere repentance. Each shall recite the names of the Dharma (having finished reciting, the Master rises, offers incense, and then returns to his seat).
[The gesture of the "Meaningful Hand" (Arthahasta). With utmost sincerity, perform the Brahma-gesture and recite:
"All evil karma created in the past, Arising entirely from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion— May all karmic obstructions and transgressions..."
Arising from body, speech, and mind, I now seek repentance before the Buddha.
May all roots of transgression be purified through this supreme practice of repentance; may all boundless and victorious merit be dedicated.
May all sentient beings submerged in suffering Swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha.
All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, And all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
The Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā).
The ceremonial attendant says:

"All the śrāmaṇeras shall rise together; upon hearing the sound of the chime, they shall perform three prostrations in gratitude. After the prostrations, they shall lift their robes, rise to their full height, and divide into ranks."

(The ritual master leads the head novice as before to escort the teacher back to his quarters. He then returns to the Dharma Hall and instructs all the novices to ascend to the hall together. Each must maintain profound reverence and perform prostrations to the Buddha throughout the night. After the novices have thanked the ritual master, they proceed immediately to the Great Hall.

Lighting candles and burning incense, with the utmost sincerity of body, speech, and mind, they realize that both subject and object are empty, and thus perform their prostrations according to reality.)
Regarding the aforementioned cases where a śrāmaṇera commits a grave offense (*guru-apatti*), the disciplinary regulations (*vinaya*) do not permit repentance.

However, if one observes that although the śrāmaṇera has indeed broken a grave precept, he possesses genuine shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) and seeks to reform his errors and start anew, one may employ Mahāyāna skillful means to rescue and uplift him.
One should cause him to develop a profound dread of the hells and to forever cease worldly attachments; then, having selected a suitable location, one should establish a ritual altar (*maṇḍala*).
With a heart of intense grief and suffering, one may seek a favorable sign for one or two weeks; only when the transgressions are thus extinguished can the precepts be received.
If no such sign appears, one must wait for months or years, making the appearance of a sign the prerequisite for receiving the precepts.

This is because one fears that obstacles to the necessary conditions might prevent the ritual altar from being established according to the Dharma; even if the altar could be established, should a favorable sign fail to manifest, [the precepts cannot be conferred].
Then it will be difficult to remedy one's regrets later; it is better to be cautious from the very beginning. One must earnestly maintain the practice of doing good.
*The Authentic Model for the Transmission of Precepts at the Three Altars*, Fascicle Three. *The Authentic Model for the Transmission of Precepts at the Three Altars*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Vinaya Master and Śramaṇa Duti of Mount Baohua in Jinling.
The General Preface for the Ritual of Invoking the Precepts and Repenting Prior to the Three Altars for Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts.
Part One: Invocation of the Two Masters.

According to the *Bodhisattva-śīla-karman-sūtra*: "When any bodhisattvas wish to receive the bodhisattva precepts, they should first be taught the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the *mātṛkā* of bodhisattva training rules, and the characteristics of the points of transgression."

One should cause them to listen and receive [the precepts], observing with wisdom. Having the capacity through one's own inclination and having deliberated upon it, one should accept the bodhisattva precepts—not because of being exhorted by others, nor for the sake of surpassing others.
Know that such a person is called a firm bodhisattva, capable of receiving the pure bodhisattva precepts.
According to what is clarified in the sūtras, one should know that whenever one receives the bodhisattva precepts, one must first request the precepts.
He reveals [the Dharma]. Next, he performs a careful confession and addresses questions and challenges. The transmission is conferred according to the Dharma;

for without relying on guidance, there would be no means to initiate the request. Therefore, one must first inform the two masters who assist in the transformation, and only then petition the Upādhyāya.

Regarding the method for requesting the precepts and receiving instruction: it must take place two or three days prior to the formal bestowal of the precepts. In the afternoon, one should have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) sweep and clean the Dharma Hall and arrange a high seat within it. If no *karmadāna* is available, a newly ordained *bhikṣu* may do so as well.

When the time arrives, strike the wooden mallet to assemble the assembly. However, those gathered here are not restricted solely to *bhikṣus*; all *bhikṣuṇīs*, *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, *śrāmaṇerīs*, *upāsakas*, and *upāsikās* who wish to seek the Bodhisattva precepts should likewise assemble together.

If the number is large, ten *bhikṣus* should go to invite the Master of Ceremonies. If there are fewer than four, or even if there are only a very small number of *bhikṣus*, they may go together. Upon arrival, perform a single prostration with touching the ground.
They were led into the Dharma Hall, where they all performed three prostrations together, then stood up. The leader among them joined his palms and said:
"We bhikṣus, [Name], and the rest, now wish to advance in our quest for the Bodhisattva Great Precepts. Regarding the various ritual protocols, we are entirely ignorant of their regulations.
We therefore entreat you, O Teachers, to kindly provide us with instruction and guidance."
The ritual master says:

"O bhikṣus (if there are members of the group of six among you, address them according to their status), since you have been able to increase your resolve and increase your precepts, benefiting both yourselves and others."
The Dharma-gate is flourishing; its merits are inconceivable. I shall now first inform both masters on your behalf and request that you go together to the Abbot’s quarters.

(After they have replied, everyone performs a single prostration with touching heads. Rising, they divide into two groups. At that time, the two ushers each lead two bhikṣus and separately invite the two masters. Once they have been invited to the Dharma Hall, the ushers call the assembly as usual to perform three prostrations with full-length bows.)
Kneel with palms joined. Second, the ritual master leads the assembly toward the two masters; perform a single prostration by touching the ground, then stand and join the hands.
On behalf of the assembly, speak as follows: "The bhikṣu [Name] (and others, including the six groups of disciples as applicable), now wish to request the full Bodhisattva precepts.
Therefore, we first announce this to the two ācārya masters. We pray that you will not withhold your compassionate heart for the benefit of others, but encourage these new learners."
In accordance with this supreme aspiration, we joyfully follow the traces of the Dharma to the Abbot’s quarters together.

We request that the Venerable Master deign to enter the hall and graciously bestow an exposition, so that these members of the assembly may hear, understand, and uphold it, ensuring their correct practice remains unclouded. Out of compassion, [recite the foregoing]. (Having finished the recitation, call the assembly to perform one prostration.)
The Preceptor said:

"O Bhikṣus (including the six groups of followers who were added later), if you now wish to petition your Upādhyāya to seek the perfect and wondrously good Bodhisattva precepts, you may truly be called disciples of the Buddha;
this is what it means to be a person of the Great Bodhicitta. After a short while, the Upādhyāya...
Furthermore, when the Venerable Ci-yun presides over the hall and provides instruction, you should each listen attentively and reflect deeply upon whether you are capable of receiving these precepts.
This is because the vows of a Bodhisattva are profound and vast, and the gates of practice are immeasurable; they are not at all like those previously cultivated by a Bhikṣu.
Should there be even the slightest trace of cowardice or fear, or if one's faculties are inferior, it will be difficult to perfect the Great Precepts. As it is said:
"Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one's head, one shall never retreat or lose the bodhicitta.
Only when one’s practice and vows are thus firm can one be called a holder of the Bodhisattva precepts. Therefore, my two teachers have previously instructed you:
each of you, harboring reverence and diligence, proceed together to the Abbot’s quarters to welcome and invite the Upādhyāya."

(The usher calls the assembly to perform three prostrations with raised hands. Rising, they divide to the left and right. The leader follows the two masters to the abbot’s quarters; the others remain standing in their places.)
Inviting the Preceptor for Instruction, Part Two:

When inviting the *upādhyāya*, nine persons may be appointed. One person shall hold incense and walk in front; next, the ritual master shall strike the *qing* gong and lead the way; the two masters follow, with the remaining assembly bringing up the rear. Upon reaching the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), the ceremonial protocol is as usual. When the *upādhyāya* enters the hall and ascends the seat, the two masters first perform their prostrations and return to their positions.
The ritual master then proceeds toward the high seat, performs three prostrations with the *daju* (ceremonial robe) spread out, kneels long, joins his palms, and speaks as follows:

I address the Venerable Master with reverence. May Your Great Compassion grant me leave to speak. This bhikṣu [Name] (and others, as many as may be added) now wish to seek the perfect Bodhisattva pure precepts.
For this reason, we have first respectfully come before your seat to prostrate and submit this request:

we pray that you will open the Dharma-gate of ambrosial liberation and transmit the Vajra Radiant Jewel Precepts. Without forsaking your compassion, we beseech you to graciously provide us with guidance. (Having finished the announcement:)
After three prostrations, rise, adjust your robes, and return to your positions.
Call out: "Incense for the High [Honored Ones]. Return to your positions. All the bhikṣus (insert names as above) shall line up together facing upward. Spread the large ritual implements.
Upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations with full prostration. After the prostrations, lift your robes, kneel long, and join your palms.
The Preceptor said: "O Bhikṣus,

regarding all the words of those who have requested the precepts, let the leader of the assembly act on behalf of the multitude with utmost sincerity to make the formal announcement (the leader announces as follows)."

We, the bhikṣus (so-and-so), have long since altered our appearance and departed from the secular world; yet we have always harbored the aspiration to advance upon the Path, finding no means to do so.

Fortunately, we have encountered the Great Upādhyāya, whose mountain of preceptual virtue is lofty and whose ocean of Vinaya is profound. By this grace, we have been able to ascend the altar and receive full ordination, finally entering the ranks of the Saṃgha.
Now, wishing to still our thoughts and offer our sincere devotion, we seek to further increase our great precepts. Therefore, we now prostrate before your seat with utmost earnestness.
I respectfully entreat you: may you deign to behold our single-minded devotion and bestow your compassionate pity upon all sentient beings.
May you equally grant us the wondrous, virtuous, and pure precepts of a Bodhisattva, enabling [Name] and others to study and practice the Mahāyāna and realize the Mind-Ground.

We shall then employ the merit of guiding and transforming through the Four Great Vows to repay the virtue of the milk of the Dharma bestowed by the gift of the precepts. Our humble hearts are overcome with earnest supplication.
[Having finished the announcement, the ritual master leads the assembly in prostrating once, joining their palms, and kneeling with the mind focused on listening attentively].
The Abbot strikes the sounding block and says:

O bhikṣus (or other assemblies as appropriate), you who now earnestly and with utmost sincerity seek the sublime and virtuous precepts of a bodhisattva must first, by means of three kinds of firm, deep, and great faith, give rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*) and seek them.
If your faith is not firm, you will be unable to sever the net of doubt; if your mind is not deep and firm, then...

Because they are unable to practice with courageous diligence, those who cause the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to dwell securely in the Mahāyāna—remaining as immovable and unshakable as a mountain or the ocean—all do so by virtue of possessing the power of this one faith and perpetual confidence.
What are these three? First, the firm and deep conviction that all sentient beings are endowed with the Tathāgata-nature.
The marks and characteristics of wisdom and virtue are not realized solely because of deluded thoughts and attachments;

therefore, one now diligently cultivates supreme practices, vowing to attain the path of enlightenment and wishing to deliver all sentient beings so that they may all ascend to the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "You are one who shall become a Buddha;
I am one who has already become a Buddha. Constantly maintaining such faith, the categories of precepts are already fulfilled. Second, the determination...
One must firmly believe that the *prātimokṣa* precepts are the fundamental cause for the cultivation and realization of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa.
If one lacks the precepts as the fundamental cause for cultivation, it is like steaming sand to make rice; even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be accomplished.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed Bodhi; one should fully maintain the pure precepts. If one can...
To persevere in the pure precepts is that which is praised by the Tathāgata. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those who wish to see the Buddha-nature and realize great nirvāṇa must cultivate and maintain the pure precepts with a profound mind.

Third, one must have firm and deep faith that all Buddhas—the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-body—possess pure radiance and boundless marks and signs, all of which are attained by relying upon the observance of the precepts.
Thus, the perfection of adornment is achieved. Therefore, the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states: "The body of merit of the Tathāgata has precepts as its foundation.

From this, we know that in seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above, one must fully equip oneself with the two types of adornment; and in transforming sentient beings below, one must bring the myriad practices to completion.
If one possesses the precepts, cultivation and realization will not be in vain; if one lacks the precepts, all toil is merely laborious and of no benefit.

If you all possess these three kinds of power of faith, you may then invoke and seek Śākyamuni Buddha, the Teacher of this Sahā world, as your Precept Master (Upādhyāya), and the Great Wisdom Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva as your Karmācārya. [In this way,] in a single lifetime...
The Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is to succeed [the Buddha], serves as my preceptor; all the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions serve as my venerable witnesses;
and all the Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions serve as my fellow students. Although I have accepted the invitation to ascend this seat, [I do so with such support].
However, you who instruct the Dharma masters are called the Precept-Grasping Upādhyāyas, because you uphold and proclaim the Buddha’s regulations to instruct future students.
When you enter the altar tomorrow to formally receive the precepts, each of you must focus the mind on a single object and immediately cease all external conditions.
Although this body remains before the teacher, the mind must necessarily visualize the various [deities].
In this ocean-like assembly of Buddhas, one must know that the pure precepts of a bodhisattva cannot be received with shallow or superficial faith or a distracted mind.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "When the threefold declaration and the *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts are completed, immediately thereafter, before all the Buddhas and great bodhisattvas currently dwelling throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, it occurs by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*)."
Signs appear. From these indications, it is known that this bodhisattva has already received the pure precepts undertaken by bodhisattvas.
At that time, all Buddhas and bodhisattvas observe these natural signs of the bodhisattva and know: "In such-and-such a world, there is a bodhisattva of such-and-such a name."
At the abode of such-and-such a bodhisattva, one correctly receives the pure precepts undertaken by bodhisattvas.
All [beings] regard this bodhisattva who has received the precepts as a son or a younger brother, giving rise to feelings of kinship and goodwill, cherishing and feeling compassion for them.

Through the cherishing and compassion of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, this bodhisattva is caused to seek the wholesome Dharma with even greater increase, without any decline or diminution. Thus, the bodhi...
The pure ethical discipline undertaken by a Bodhisattva is the most excellent and unsurpassed among all other forms of pure ethical discipline;

it is accompanied by an immeasurable and boundless treasury of great merit, is initiated by the foremost and supreme virtuous mental disposition, and is universally capable of eliminating every kind of misconduct toward all sentient beings.
It is the ethical discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*).
It does not even approach a fraction—whether by calculation, by enumeration, by analogy, or even by the slightest degree (*upaniṣad*)—because it encompasses all great merits.

Having received these precepts, even if one changes bodies and wanders throughout the worlds of the ten directions, in every place of birth one does not abandon the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline. By means of this, the bodhisattva does not forsake unsurpassed enlightenment.
One with great vows does not commit an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) through bonds of even the highest degree.

If, upon transitioning to another life, one forgets the original mindfulness [of the precepts], but then encounters a virtuous friend who seeks to awaken the mindfulness of the bodhisattva precepts, although one receives them repeatedly, they are not newly acquired.
According to this scriptural passage, it is known that upholding the bhikṣu precepts is called the "Saṃgha-precepts" (*saṃgha-śīla*), and they should be maintained within the Saṃgha.

One requests the ten masters according to ritual and receives [the precepts] through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. One merely vows to uphold the Bodhisattva precepts for the remainder of this life and its duration, which are called the "Buddha-precepts.
One should make an announcement before the masters to all Buddhas, and receive them through three rounds of *karman*, continuing until the final body of ultimate enlightenment.
Therefore, Śākyamuni Buddha, Mañjuśrī, and Maitreya serve as the [masters] for the Bodhisattva precepts.
Regarding the three masters: although the Buddhas serve as their witnesses, neither the Buddhas nor the Bodhisattvas have departed from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Yet, those who seek the precepts truly abide in this world. That they are able to grant and receive them so as to obtain benefit is due to the resonance between the faculties of sentient beings and the path of the Buddhas.

It is like a child whose filial piety increases and whose mother’s compassion increases in response; it is like water that becomes clearer and the moon that becomes more manifest. To receive the Great...
Those who uphold both the precepts and the vehicle are true children of the Buddha; the compassionate protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas toward them is likewise so.
Tomorrow, for your sake, I shall honor and follow the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya by establishing a ritual altar, arranging seats, assembling the assembly, and invoking the holy ones.
We shall change the names of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
With a mind of benefit, they take upon themselves the vast resolve of a bodhisattva to adorn the buddha-fields and benefit sentient beings,
and they turn away from the prātimokṣa precepts of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerikās, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

Thus, for the sake of bodhisattvas, one maintains the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*) for liberation (in this text, the seven classes of practitioners are mentioned in general; each should be added according to who is present).

Now, the essence of these wondrous three clusters of precepts is non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Its magnitude is equal to the sands of the Ganges, manifested through conventional forms (*rūpa*).

Although it is said that one "receives," this is the non-duality of duality wherein the entirety of nature gives rise to cultivation; although it is said that one "upholds," this is the non-duality of duality wherein the entirety of cultivation resides in nature.
This is because the seeds of Buddhahood arise from conditions, and nature and cultivation mutually complete one another. Having attained this essence, [one realizes it].
Spontaneously ceasing evil and practicing good; spontaneously benefiting others and saving sentient beings.

Amidst this spontaneous cessation, practice, and benefiting of others, there is in truth no "benefiting of others" or "cessation and practice" to be found, because all phenomena are unborn and the single path is truly pure. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is undefiled, one practices the *śīla-pāramitā* in accordance with it. And this...
The nature of the precepts of intrinsic virtue (*prakṛti-śīla*) is that which all Buddhas possess in common from birth; it is not absent even in the wriggling insects of the world.
Where there is this nature, there is mind; where there is mind, all shall attain Buddhahood. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"The Vajra Radiant Jewel Precept is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. All consciousnesses..."
Form and mind—whether sentient beings or the mind—all enter into the precepts of Buddha-nature.

However, I fear that if you are unable to give rise to the great vow for supreme bodhi, or if there are among your present bodies those who have committed the seven grave offenses, then although the principle-substance of Buddha-nature is inherently possessed by every person without ever lacking anything, it will ultimately be difficult to give rise to the actual substance of the precepts. (From the *Sutra*)
The Vinaya clarifies the articles: you should interrogate one another. For a short while, follow the assembly to pay respects to the Venerable One.
Tonight, enter the Sāṃghāṭī-hall before the Karmavācanā master; first, each person shall present the specific precepts they have received and uphold.
In the interim, one must confess each instance, whether defiled or pure. Next, one should carefully examine and clarify the seven heinous offenses prohibited by the Mahāyāna.

Only when the fundamental heavy precepts remain unbroken and the seven evil heinous crimes have not been committed may the transmission be performed according to the Vinaya and the Dharma, in a state of purity.
This is what the Buddhas praise as virtuous, and what the dragons and devas protect; it is that which is called "the Vinaya abiding in the world."

The True Dharma shall thus endure for a long time. Are you able to rely upon the teachings and practice them accordingly? (The assembly answers in unison: We are able to rely upon the teachings and practice them accordingly.
The Ritual Master says:
The bhikṣus all rise together; upon hearing the sound of the chime, they perform three prostrations of gratitude.
Having adjusted their robes after the prostrations, they rise and form ranks. The one who invited the master steps forward from the ranks to escort the Venerable Master back to his quarters.

(The ritual procedures are as usual. After the [deceased] has been escorted out, one proceeds to the hall to pay respects and escort the two masters, followed by expressing gratitude to the master who guided the ceremony. Once these are completed, each person returns to their respective quarters in order to await the inquiry for confession at the beginning of the first watch of the night.)

Regarding the examination of precepts, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (Fanwang jing) states that when bestowing the precepts upon others, one must not engage in discrimination. This applies to all kings, princes, ministers, and officials;
bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; laymen and laywomen who have faith; as well as men and women of licentious conduct—the eighteen [categories].
Brahmā, the devas of the six heavens of desire, those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, eunuchs, slaves, and all spirits and ghosts—all may receive the precepts.
Furthermore, it is said that when one wishes to receive the precepts, the master should ask: "In this present life, have you not committed the seven heinous offenses?
A Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not confer the precepts upon one who has committed these seven heinous offenses. Thus, we know the principle of the nature [of reality].
There is no distinction; those who possess the mind are all encompassed within this. One must guard against obstacles to the practice, for only those who are free from transgressions may be admitted.

Since one distinguishes within what is not itself a distinction, yet within the process of careful interrogation there further exists the difference between the direct and expedient, the sudden and the gradual, they are now compiled into four categories.
This serves as a clear mirror suspended before the altar, for the purpose of discerning.
Regarding the appropriate capacities of those who receive [the precepts]: if one has not previously mastered them, one will be unable to discern what is improper when the occasion arises.
First, as for male and female renunciants who receive and uphold the śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī precepts.

Whether it be one whose years of training in the precepts are complete and without deficiency, or one whose physical vessel is perfect and free from impediments, who has already ascended the ordination platform and undergone the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and who has previously perfected the vows of a Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī, now further arouses the Great Mind and requests the Three Collections of Precepts (*triskandha*).
Because their practice is neither scattered nor excessive, they do not neglect the sustenance of the Sangha Jewel, acting in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. That is to say:
Having received this formal acceptance, they are called Bodhisattva Bhikṣus or Bodhisattva Bhikṣuṇīs.
Second, there are those who are Śikṣamāṇās, Śrāmaṇeras, or Śrāmaṇerīs, or those training in the precepts whose age has not yet reached the required number of years.

Even if one’s sense faculties are incomplete, if they are capable of giving rise to the bodhicitta and are fit to practice the bodhisattva path, although they may not be included among the ranks of the Saṃgha due to such deficiencies, they can still be gathered within the impartial Buddha-nature.

Because they do not undergo the full ordination (upasampadā) but instead seek the three clusters of precepts (triskandhaka), their violation of the graduated stages of discipline is temporarily opened by the Buddha’s compassion; this is called "provisional reception" (kuan-shou). Once received, it is termed [the Bodhisattva Precepts].
Bodhisattva-śikṣamāṇās, bodhisattva-śrāmaṇeras, and bodhisattva-śrāmaṇerīs; thirdly,
laymen and laywomen who revere and have faith in the Triple Gem, delight in cultivating the ten wholesome paths of action,

who may have received the five precepts and guarded them carefully for many years, or observed the eightfold fast-precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) strictly for a single day, and now for the first time [undertake...]
Having generated the supreme resolve, they seek to receive the great bodhisattva precepts. Because they progress from the small toward the great, their faith and wisdom increase accordingly;
this is called "gradual reception. Once received, they are termed *bodhisattvopāsaka* (male lay bodhisattvas) or *bodhisattvopāsikā* (female lay bodhisattvas).
Fourth, as for worldly men and women who have planted profound roots of goodness over many kalpas, yet in this life remain deluded and attached, failing to quickly awaken;

if they suddenly attain awakening and illumination, standing on the spot with a mixture of sorrow and joy, and in a single thought take refuge in the Triple Gem and earnestly seek the Mahāyāna precepts and teachings—
then because their vows are vast and deep, one should employ the means of "commonality" (*samānārthatā*) to gather and transform them, even though they have not long maintained [the precepts].
Regarding the category of precepts for laypeople: if one suddenly receives the bodhisattva training rules (śikṣāpada), it is called "receiving them all at once" (*tun-shou*).

Having received them, one is termed a "bodhisattva upāsaka" or a "bodhisattva upāsikā. These four types, when carefully examined during the time of confession, are still distinguished into four separate categories.
Regarding the examination of the first type of person: if it is a bhikṣu, one must strictly inquire about the two hundred and fifty precepts he maintains;
if it is a bhikṣuṇī, one must minutely examine her three hundred and forty-eight fundamental precepts. As for the seven prohibitions (*saptāvaraṇa*), both orders must cross-examine them together.
If the root has been violated, one should perform the *karmavācanā* to expel the offender. This applies even if the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) have been committed.
There is an offense; it shall be dealt with according to the prohibitions established by the Vinaya. Even if one violates other minor rules, repentance may restore purity.
As for examining the second type of person: if she is a *śikṣamāṇā*—here translated as "a woman training in the precepts"—the Buddha ordained that she must train in three dharmas.
When examining her during the confession, one should question her on each point individually: first, the training in the roots [of the precepts]. (4)

The heavy precepts are these: the two trainings in the six rules, namely—touching with a defiled mind, stealing less than five coins, taking the life of an animal, minor false speech, eating at improper times, and intentionally drinking alcohol.
The third is the training in conduct, which refers to the rules of deportment among the various precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs*.
If one is a *śrāmaṇera* or *śrāmaṇerī*, one should simply examine the ten chapters of the fundamental precepts. Its...

Regarding the seven grave offenses of concealment (*saptānantarya*), all three groups [of nuns] must be interrogated. If, among these three groups, there is one who has committed a fundamental offense of concealment, she shall be expelled according to the Vinaya for each instance.
If a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*) is impure regarding the six rules, she must undergo the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for another two years;
since she has already received the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, she is no longer part of the community of female novices (*śrāmaṇerī*).

They are subsumed [within the category of those who have fallen]. Furthermore, regarding a śikṣamāṇā who has failed in her training, or a woman whose training in the precepts is not truly pure—since she has no refuge in either case and lacks the foundation of the three aggregates, she cannot proceed to receive the bodhisattva precepts.
As for the three minor groups [of female practitioners], they are governed solely by these rules of training; this is because they are twice as strictly regulated as the śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs.

Regarding the examination of the third type of person: if they are male or female lay followers (*upāsaka* or *upāsikā*) who have received the five precepts, there are differences in whether their observance is complete, more than half, less than half, or a single portion. One should inquire in detail about each precept according to what has been received;

one must not ask about many portions of those who have received only a small portion, nor ask about half-portions of those who have received them in full. If they are those who have received the eight precepts...

Regarding those who serve as male or female attendants: since what they undertake differs from the five precepts for lifelong householders, when they are examined, one asks only about their observance or violation during a single day and night.
Furthermore, the eight precepts prohibit sexual misconduct entirely for that period of one day and night without exception;
this is not the same as the five precepts, which merely forbid illicit sexual conduct. As for the examination of the seven heinous offenses and the four...
There is no distinction among these classes. Among them, if anyone has committed even one of the four grave offenses or the seven heinous crimes, they must be barred;
for all other cases, repentance and removal are permitted, and they are still allowed to proceed with receiving the precepts.
Regarding the examination of the fourth type of person: those who have never previously received the *śīla* (precepts) now, for the first time, resolve to seek their reception.
One should follow the *Sujāta-sūtra* in questioning them regarding the seven obstacles to the precepts.
If these virtuous laymen or laywomen are not hindered by the seven obstacles, one should first confer upon them the five precepts of an *upāsaka* or *upāsikā*.
Regarding the precepts: these five prohibitions of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) constitute the fundamental basis for the precepts of a lay bodhisattva.

On that very day, he further reverently examined the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and once again scrutinized the seven grave offenses (*saptānantarya*). Only if he was found to have committed none of them would he proceed to the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣāpada*).

Although one has only just received the five precepts now, how could one possibly have committed the seven heinous offenses? Since the Buddha’s teachings contain prohibitions, one must still follow the prescribed inquiries.

(When performing the ritual, it should take place during the afternoon. The arrangement of seats in the purification hall, the preparation of decorations, the drawing of lots for the assembly, and all other ceremonies are identical to those for full ordination without distinction. When the time arrives, strike the wooden mallet to assemble the community and lead the procession.)

First, they proceed to the Dharma Hall. The assembly performs three prostrations toward them. Then, those headed by the four [officers] go to invite the *shoucha* (examiner), the *jiaoji* (verifier), the *shuji* (scribe), and the *xunshi* (inspector). Their ritual etiquette is no different from what was previously described. The Master of Ceremonies then leads the five men in succession.

One person holding incense goes to invite the *karmadāna* (ceremonial master) to the hall. He prostrates before the Buddha, takes his seat, and offers incense. After the assembly has finished chanting the incense hymn (*xiangzan*), the ritual master says:
Incense is offered. Return to one’s position. Those who are to perform the invitation form a line facing upward.

They unfold their ritual implements. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, they prostrate three times. Having finished the prostrations, they adjust their robes, rise from their seats, and each returns to his own place.
(The rituals for the various masters receiving their assignments, including the formal leave-taking, are all explained in detail within the *Er-tan-yi*; they are not repeated here.)
The Ritual Master says:

"May all the bhikṣus, each with sincere devotion, follow my voice and recite the Great Compassion Divine Mantra in unison, seeking protection to purify this Dharma assembly and relying upon its majestic power to dispel demonic obstacles. (Having recited this divine mantra three times, he raises his voice and says:)
*Namo Amṛtarāja Bodhisattva Mahāsattva* (three times).
All the bhikṣus and others line up facing upward, unfold their half-sets of robes, and upon hearing the sound of the *qing*, perform three prostrations.
Having finished bowing, they lift their robes, kneel with both knees on the ground, and join their palms.
Now, though those who are vessels of the Dharma have long since attained their goal, one still fears that their polishing has not yet reached perfection;

and though they wish to ascend the stages of sainthood, they first seek the initial cultivation of their conduct. Now that you have all received full ordination, your holy minds are once again sharpened.

Therefore, for your sake, I shall burn incense and arrange the seats to respectfully invite the Vinaya Master [Name] (Upādhyāya) and [Name] (Ācārya) to serve as the Preceptor for the Examination of Precepts, the Inquiry into Obstacles, and the Confession of Transgressions.
Lei: "I request the Master's words. You ought to speak for yourself, but fearing you may not yet be able to do so, I shall now instruct you.
Each of you shall state your dharma-name (the assembly each states their name), and all other words shall follow my lead."

"Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name] (or add the names of other members of the assembly), now request the Venerable One to serve as my Preceptor for Examining the Precepts, Inquiring into Obstacles, and Confession.
May the Venerable One act as my Preceptor for Examining the Precepts, Inquiring into Obstacles, and Confession.
By relying upon the Venerable One, I shall enter the pure stage of a Bodhisattva. Out of compassion, [please grant this]. (Request three times, prostrating three times.)"
The *karmavācanā* master strikes the sounding block and says:

"O Bhikṣus (and any other assembly present), since you have already made your earnest triple request, I shall now act as your *ācārya* for the examination of precepts (*śīla-parīkṣā*), the inquiry into impediments (*antarāyika-dharma-prcchā*), and the confession (*deśanā*).
You must each listen attentively to all my instructions; for the teaching is adapted to the capacity of the recipient."

[The Master] said: "First is the gradual [approach], followed by the sudden. The Vinaya is established based on specific circumstances, extending from the body to the mind. If the body is not pure, how can the precepts of the mind arise?

Now that the five categories of offenses are firmly maintained and the three clusters of pure precepts are further augmented, one aspires to the Four Great Vows, no longer focusing solely on self-benefit.

This is to give rise to the causal mind of magnanimity and head directly toward the Precious Abode; it is to hope for the resultant virtues of the Tathāgata and not remain stagnant in transformation."
To possess such superior resolve may indeed be called "supreme goodness. However, I fear that the life-preserving bag (*uḍupa*) may be damaged and the broken vessel difficult to fill.

Since the holy regulations (*ārya-vinaya*) are thus transgressed, how can the holy life (*brahmacarya*) be established? With past transgressions yet unexpiated, there is no way to achieve cultivation and realization. Therefore, the *Vinayapiṭaka* states:
Those who commit the four grave offenses (pārājika) fall away from the fruits of the Path. This is illustrated by the following analogies: one whose head has been severed cannot live again;
a tree whose heartwood is cut cannot grow back; a nose that is pierced with a needle cannot be restored to its former state; and a stone that is split apart cannot be rejoined.
These are matters that are not permitted by the Dharma within the precepts you originally received. Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* of the Mahāyāna states:

If the person currently manifesting their body has committed any of the seven obstructive offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*), the teacher should not confer the precepts upon them. If they are free from these seven obstructions, one may confer the precepts.

Judging by this, while those who have committed grave offenses among the seven classes of followers in the Hīnayāna are ineligible for further advancement and reception [of the Mahāyāna], if a Mahāyāna practitioner commits the seven obstructions, there is a clear basis for excluding them entirely.
Although it is said that offenses have no inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the principle remains fully present.
One must always ensure that essential matters do not cause the mind to be corrupted; only then will the Way accord with its proper measure.

Therefore, we first rely upon the Vinaya-piṭaka to examine, within each individual aspect of the bhikṣu precepts one has received, matters such as observance and violation, completeness and deficiency (this refers specifically to the bhikṣu;

if there are members of the other six groups who likewise request examination and repentance, the text may be modified to read: "examine, within each individual aspect of the bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, upāsaka, or upāsikā precepts one has received...").

Regarding internal matters such as the observance or violation of precepts and their completeness or deficiencies, we now list the names of the seven classes of practitioners for convenience, so that they may be selected and applied as the occasion requires.

Next, in accordance with the Mahāyāna teachings, we shall exclude those who have committed the seven grave offenses of exclusion (*saptātyaya*). I shall now question you one by one; you must each answer truthfully.

If you do not cast aside your defenses and reveal your hearts to answer according to the facts, then past evils will remain concealed and new goodness will be difficult to produce, even if you subsequently perform repentance in accordance with the assembly.
Repentance! From what cause can this offense be removed? Having received the precepts, you will certainly not obtain them; furthermore, you incur the offense of intentional lying.

You should reflect that the Bodhisattva’s Great Precepts originate in the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*). If the mind-ground is defiled and mixed, one is not a vessel for the precepts. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"If you now wish to investigate unsurpassed Bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind. (Strike the ruler.)
"Are you able to follow and practice according to these instructions? (The assembly answers in unison: "We shall follow and practice according to the instructions.
As for those who are being interrogated, if there are only ten or so persons, one may proceed with the examination of the precepts directly without requiring them to rise.
Having exited, they re-entered. If there were six groups of bhikṣuṇīs or others inside, they should be ordered to exit immediately;

they should be summoned separately for examination, as their disciplinary characteristics (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) differ [from those of the monks]. If the number of bhikṣus is large, they may be ordered to leave the hall and enter according to the order of their lot-draw tickets (*śalākā*).
This is because there is a fear that they might not hear the questions and answers, or that their voices would be difficult to understand.
Therefore, the *Lǐjì* (Record of Rites) states:
"The bhikṣus all rise together; upon hearing the sound of the chime, they perform three prostrations with their robes adjusted. (After the prostrations.)
Procedures for Commencement: Those acting as leaders must lead the assembly out of the hall to assemble in waiting; they must not be disorganized or distracted.
Awaiting the call, each person shall proceed according to their rank from the left side door to the station of the divination master, entering the hall one by one in successive order.

Upon reaching the master’s seat, once the formal responses have been completed, they proceed from the right cheek-gate to the place of the official who collects the slips, exiting the hall one by one in order.
The first group remains in the hall to wait; the others withdraw for a time (once the remaining assembly has exited the hall, he calls out).
The first group approaches and lines up facing upward (if the hall is narrow, divide into two rows; if the hall is wide, line up as one group).

Unfolding their half-set of ritual implements, they perform three prostrations upon hearing the signal bell. Having finished bowing, they lift their robes and kneel long. With palms joined, each person performs the visualization and directs the mind, reciting three times.
Homage to the Three Jewels, eternally abiding throughout the ten directions (recite three times). Each shall state their own Dharma-name (having stated it).
The Preceptor strikes the sounding-block and says:
"O Bhikṣus, I now question you regarding the four *pārājika* dharmas which you have originally received and upheld. You should..."
Answer truthfully. First:
Regarding the precept against committing impure conduct—the practice of sexual intercourse—have you committed any offense therein?
(Answer truthfully whether you have or have not.)

(However, the specific characteristics of the precepts asked about herein cannot be recorded in their entirety due to the extensive text; fearing that it would cause undue delay for the assembly, I have merely extracted the essential outlines to inquire about them.)
Second: The precept against taking what belongs to another without it being given with a thieving mind. Have you committed any offense regarding this?
(Answer truthfully whether there is or is not.
Third: The precept against intentionally taking human life, praising death, or encouraging others toward death (as before).
Fourth: [A monk] who has no realization at all, yet claims, "I have attained the state of a superior person" (as previously described).

If a bhikṣu commits any of these four offenses, he may not participate in the *poṣadha* or formal acts (*karmavācanā*) with the other bhikṣus, nor may he dwell with them; this is called a "root violation.

He must be expelled according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s instructions, by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). He shall be removed.
One loses the portion of the fruits of the Path and cannot advance to receive the Bodhisattva Great Precepts.
According to the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one who commits a *pārājika* offense shall fall into the Saṃjīva (Blazing Heat) Hell.
The Master struck the sounding-block and said:
"O Bhikṣus, I now ask you concerning the thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas that you have received and upheld.
You should answer with truth and sincerity."
First: Intentionally emitting semen from the urethra, with the exception of [emission] during dreams. Regarding this, have you committed an offense?
(Answer truthfully: yes or no. Second:
With a lustful mind, making physical contact with the body of a woman. (As before.)
Third: The precept against speaking coarse and lewd words of sexual desire to a woman (as before).
Fourth: The precept against instructing a woman to provide me with offerings through sexual methods (as before).
Fifth: The precept against acting as a matchmaker for men and women to come and go between them (as before).

Sixth: The precept against building a house in a dangerous location, a place that obstructs others, or one without an owner, doing so oneself without having the bhikṣus designate the site, or building it in excess of the prescribed dimensions (as before).

Seventh: The training rule concerning a large dwelling built for oneself on difficult ground, obstructed ground, or land belonging to another, without having had the site designated by other bhikṣus (as previously described).
Eighth: Because he was overcome by ill will, a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense slandered him with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense (as previously described).

Third: Having previously performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding a family under training (*śikṣamāṇa-kula*), one does not accept food with one’s own hands from that family unless invited, provided one is not ill (as before).
Fourth: While staying in an *āraṇyaka* dwelling in a place where there is suspicion or fear, one does not accept food outside the monastery grounds unless first informed by the donor;
within the monastery grounds, one does not accept food with one’s own hands unless one is ill (as before).
If a bhikṣu commits any of these four dharmas, he should confess his transgression before other bhikṣus, saying: "I have committed a censurable dharma that ought not to have been done.
This is called the dharma of confession. If one does not confess before other bhikṣus in accordance with the Vinaya, one shall, according to the Sūtras, fall into the Black Rope Hell.

The Master struck the sounding-block and said:

First: You should be granted the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence). When the *saṃmukhavinaya* discipline is to be granted, one asks:
"Do you have any offense in this matter? If there is an offense, answer "Yes"; if there is none, answer "No."

These seven methods can extinguish the four kinds of disputes. If one fails to apply the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) when it is appropriate, and instead applies another method to extinguish the dispute, one commits an offense against the Dharma and Vinaya called *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); this constitutes applying what should not be applied.

If one asks now, one should answer immediately that there is an offense. Even if a dispute has arisen, if at that time it was consistent with the Dharma and did not contravene the Buddha’s regulations, only when asked now may one answer that there is none. Furthermore, if the dispute never originally existed and this rule was not practiced, one may likewise answer that there is none when asked now.

Because the answers differ from those given for other precepts, this is briefly explained here as an appendix. Should one wish to explain this extensively, one ought to examine the complete Vinaya in detail. (So it may be.)
Second: One should grant the *smṛtivinaya*; the rules for granting the *smṛtivinaya* are as [stated] before.

If a monk should encounter the arising of any of the four kinds of disputes, he must weigh the case and extinguish it by applying whichever of these seven methods is appropriate.
If that which is appropriate is not applied, or that which is inappropriate is applied, the dispute will not be extinguished;
this is called an offense.

If one does not burn one’s body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, one is not a renunciant bodhisattva.
This clarifies that by burning one’s body for the sake of the Dharma to make offerings to the Buddhas, one shares the same compassionate yearning as all sentient beings;
thus, the aspiration to seek the Buddha-way above reaches its ultimate limit. Furthermore, it says that one should even relinquish [one’s body] to hungry tigers, wolves, lions, and all hungry ghosts.

He offered his own flesh, hands, and feet as an act of worship. This clarifies that by sacrificing his body to relieve the suffering of ghosts and animals, he shared the same power of compassion as all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
thus, his aspiration to transform sentient beings through downward-reaching grace reached its ultimate limit.

If one wishes to cause others to burn their bodies as an offering to the Buddha, [one must consider that] the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are endowed with hundreds of thousands of marks and signs, and are adorned with myriad virtues.
It is naturally worthy of reverence and a place of refuge; furthermore, when one seeks the Dharma with a sincere mind, this is something that people are capable of practicing and are willing to do.
However, if one wishes to cause others to sacrifice their bodies to save various ghosts and beasts, consider that these ghosts and beasts possess immeasurable ugliness and wickedness.
The appearance is strange and extraordinary; it is neither something one can approach nor draw near to, and moreover, it inspires feelings of fear and dread.
