Regarding the correct model for receiving the Bhikṣu precepts through the two altars:

those who ascend the altar to receive full ordination must understand the origins of this practice in both lands, as well as the principles regarding the similarities and differences in the construction of the altars.

According to the *Yao-lan* (Essential Compendium): When the World-Honored One was at Jetavana, the bhikṣu Lohitya requested the Buddha to establish an ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) for the purpose of conferring the precepts upon bhikṣus.

The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to establish a single ordination platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*) outside the eastern gate of the monastery’s outer enclosure as a public place for the Saṃgha to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Once this legal decree had been issued, [the news spread] throughout all the monasteries in the sixteen great kingdoms.

He followed this in establishing [the tradition]. Thereafter, those ascending the platform to receive full ordination have adhered to the three categories of the monastic boundary and the Dharma exactly as prescribed by the regulations.

Should there be even the slightest deviation, the recipient does not obtain the precepts. The words of the monks presiding at the platform are spoken from the golden mouth; the Dharma is recorded in the Dragon Treasury (Nāga-kośa).
From ordinary beings to sages, they follow the same track without any divergent paths. In this land, the tradition first began with Master Xuan of Nanshan.
In the second year of the Linde era during the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, a stone ordination platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*) was constructed at Jingye Temple.

Therein, the precepts were conferred and received according to the Vinaya. At that time, among all the Vinaya masters, there were none who did not look up to these noble regulations, honoring and practicing them.
Thus, the Nanshan Vinaya School attained great renown, and its successive transmission through the generations has indeed a profound cause. Today, this is evident at Zhaokong and Xianlin in Lin’an.

In monasteries such as Kaigen-ji in Gusu, ancient remains still exist. Furthermore, in the first year of the Baoli era and the second year of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) ordination platforms were extensively established.
In the second year of the Xiangfu era of the Song dynasty, seventy-two sites for the Ganlu (Amṛta) ordination platforms were established.
"Fangdeng" is a term signifying vastness, equality, and universal pervasiveness. "Ganlu" [refers to nectar].
This [term] is used as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*, meaning that because the precepts serve as the means of entry into *nirvāṇa*, the name is designated based on the fruit [of the practice].
However, while the ritual platform (*maṇḍala*) resembles that of a *bhikṣu*, the precepts conferred are exclusively those of the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, upon the central part of the platform, one makes offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the five ranks of holy masters. When circumambulating the platform, the Precept-Conferring Master (*śīla-upādhyāya*) and the two *ācāryas*...

The *ācārya* [the ordination master] proceeds from the lower seat to the middle, and from the middle to the upper. Once those three masters have finished prostrating to the Buddha and Bodhisattvas, they enter behind the Buddha from the west.
They then exit to the south of the Buddha and arrange their seats to one side. The *śīla-upādhyāya* (preceptor for the precepts) sits, while the two *ācāryas* stand to his left and right.
This ritual is quite different from that for a *bhikṣu* receiving full ordination. When the number of ten monks is complete, it is difficult [to proceed otherwise].

This excludes those who are heavy with transgressions or light in merit. In the Mahāyāna, one is not restricted by physical disabilities or differences in conditions; provided one generates the great mind and accepts the precepts, they are obtained.

Therefore, the altar is named "Vaipulya" (Universal Equality), or as some say, "Amṛta" (Nectar). Alas! The study of the Vinaya has declined and the consecration of altars has been severed for a long time.

Now, at Mount Hua in Jinling, an altar has been established according to the regulations to serve as a model for future practice, thereby reviving the lineage of the school that upholds and maintains the precepts in the South.
This is not like the superficial and empty talk found in the *Dacheng zanyi* (Rituals of the Mahāyāna), which lacks substance.

Therefore, I have first clarified the similarities and differences regarding the ordination platform (*śīlakaṇḍa*) and placed it at the beginning, so that one may know that the reception of full ordination within the monastic community must have a platform as its basis.
The location of the *śīlakaṇḍa* (precept platform) does not share the same substance as the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), because it is a separate boundary. The Vinaya states:
"At one time, various bhikṣus encountered matters requiring a formal act (*karmavācanā*) by a quorum of four bhikṣus, or matters requiring a quorum of five, ten, or twenty bhikṣus.
The assemblies therein became exhausted. The Buddha then established a rule permitting [the use of the śīlakaṇḍa]."

Regarding the demarcation of the *sīmā* (boundary): The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states that one may not establish a *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) externally and then directly establish a *kṣudrasīmā* (small boundary);
in such a case, one cannot receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and other vinayas are likewise.

Therefore, wherever there are bhikṣus who maintain the precepts according to the teachings, they must first demarcate the *sīmā-kṣetra* (boundary field), followed by the *mahāsīmā*. Within this *sīmā-kṣetra*, one should establish a single *śīla* (precept).

Upon the altar, seats for the ten masters are arranged; when there is no ritual activity, they are enclosed by a railing, but during the performance of rites, they are opened according to the occasion.
Indeed, this altar is a place where no one may enter except the masters. On the day of receiving full ordination, it is swept and made pure and beautiful.
Banners, canopies, and jeweled necklaces are suspended all around the perimeter of the altar. Directly beneath the center of the altar, a single incense table is set.

Those who have not yet received full ordination must not be allowed to listen indiscriminately while candles are lit and flowers are offered as offerings. Furthermore, a seat for questioning and debate should be established in a secluded place.
First, the method for requesting a preceptor from among the Saṃgha is explained.
The Vinaya states: "Because disciples lacked the instruction of a teacher, they committed unrighteous acts. The Buddha said: "One should establish a *upādhyāya* (preceptor).

A disciple should regard the *upādhyāya* as one would think of one's own parents, honoring and attending to them with reverence. Furthermore, because a sick bhikṣu had no one to care for him, he met an untimely death.
The Buddha said: "One should establish a *śrāmaṇera* (disciple); they should mutually honor and attend to one another with reverence."
Thus, the True Dharma will be able to abide for a long time, increasing and expanding. The *Upādhyāya* (Preceptor) should regard the disciple as one would a son. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"Because [the candidate] did not request [ordination] at the outset, they subsequently violate the instructions; therefore, the Buddha established the rule that one must request it.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* state: "The person receiving ordination shall first enter the Saṃgha, and the Preceptor shall instruct them to proceed in due order."

First, having prostrated with one's head at the feet of the Sangha, one then requests ordination. The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: The Buddha said, "First, the preceptor must act according to the Dharma;
second, the two teachers must act according to the Dharma; third, the seven monks must be pure; fourth, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) must be accomplished;
fifth, the assembly of monks must be harmonious and grant their consent (*chanda*). This is called the fulfillment of receiving full ordination."

Now, according to the various Vinayas and synthesizing their principles, the following ritual protocol is established: At the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), first strike the *ghanṭī* (wooden gong).
Assemble the community of resident *bhikṣu* monks within the same boundary (*sīmā*). The assembly’s master of ceremonies shall lead the novices seeking full ordination;

each shall hang his alms bowl, don the two robes—the five-piece and the seven-piece—and hold his implements while supporting the *saṃghāṭī*. Proceeding in single file like a string of fish, they shall arrive at the Dharma Hall.
Having done so, the various masters of ceremony take the robes held in their hands by those [candidates] and place them upon the side tables to the left and right.
First, they perform three prostrations before the assembled Sangha present within the boundary (*sīmā*).
After rising and dividing into groups, one master of ceremony leads two candidates for ordination to invite the seven preceptors to the hall. Then, all the candidates for ordination...

They perform three prostrations with their heads to the ground. Rising, they divide into two groups and stand. Next, the two ritual masters each lead two postulants who possess the requisite requisites to invite the two masters.
Once they have arrived and the nine masters have met and completed their mutual salutations, the postulants perform three prostrations with their heads to the ground before the two masters.
Rising, they form two ranks. The two ritual masters ring the *yin-磬* (guiding stone chime) in unison and proceed forward, leading the eight new postulants.
When all are assembled, the attendant goes to the Abbot’s quarters to invite the first-ranking *vinaya* master to the hall.

The nine *vinaya* masters previously invited then move down from their positions to sit above him. They perform three prostrations with their heads to the floor (*sanbai*). (If the ten masters are of equal rank, they should perform a level bow.

If the nine masters are junior to the first-ranking master, or if they are his disciples, the first-ranking master should receive their prostrations; one must not confuse the order of seniority based on ordination age or status, thereby violating the sacred regulations. Once the ten masters have finished their prostrations, each takes their seat.
Having assumed the full lotus posture, the novices seek their ritual implements. They then prostrate toward the first-ranking Vinaya Master.
The ritual master says:
"All novices, line up together facing upward; unfold your great implements and, upon hearing the sound of the chime, pay homage with utmost sincerity."
Prostrate three times. Adjust the robes. Protect the alms bowl (after prostrating). Kneel with the right knee on the ground and join the palms.
The ritual master of the left row says:

"Now, as a bright mirror set upon its stand reflects whatever form it encounters, and a great bell hung upon its frame resounds when struck, so too is the Perfectly Accomplished [Threefold Nature]..."
The assembly must rely upon three masters; the examination of the seven non-transgressions depends entirely upon seven witnesses.
Now, from among this great community of monks, we shall respectfully invite ten masters for you to ascend the platform and receive full ordination.
Each of you must individually take note of the appearance and names of the preceptor and all the masters present before you, so that you do not forget them.
The first-ranking [upper] Master [lower] So-and-so shall serve as the Upādhyāya for your full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The attendant of the right-hand row announces:
"The second-ranking Master So-and-so shall serve as the Karmācārya for you."
The attendant of the left row says:
"The third seat, Master [Name], shall serve as your preceptor (ācārya).
The attendant of the right row says:
The fourth [person], Master [Name], shall serve as the venerable witness-ācārya for you.

Continue in this manner up to the tenth person; likewise, announce the names and indicate the characteristics of the attendants on both sides, so that all who seek the full ordination may clearly recognize each one.
All the śrāmaṇeras rise together. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, they prostrate three times, adjust their robes, and protect their alms bowls.
(Having finished bowing,) they kneel long with palms joined.
Second, the Ritual for Formally Requesting the Preceptor. The ritual master of the left row says:
"All *śrāmaṇeras*, I shall now respectfully request the Venerable Master [Name], the Vinaya Master of the Hall above, to serve as your *upādhyāya* for the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
As for the words of this request, it is appropriate that you state them yourselves; however, fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, I [shall speak on your behalf]."
I now instruct you: each of you shall recite your own Dharma-name. (Having recited it,) all other words shall follow my lead.
Venerable Sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind; I, the śrāmaṇera [Name], now request the Venerable Sir to serve as my Preceptor for the attainment of the precepts.
"I pray that the Venerable One will act as my Upādhyāya for the attainment of the precepts. Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall receive full ordination.
Out of compassion, please grant this.
Thus one should make this request with utmost sincerity three times, bowing the head three times—though a single bow may also suffice.
The first preceptor said:
"O śrāmaṇeras, since you have so earnestly requested me three times, I shall serve as your preceptor for the attainment of full ordination.
Be pure and do not be negligent. [They replied: "We receive this with reverence and shall carry it out accordingly."
All the śrāmaṇeras rise together. Hearing the sound of the chime, they prostrate three times. They lift their robes and protect their bowls (having finished the prostrations).
Kneeling long with palms joined, the ritual master from the right side leads the ceremony, saying:
"O śrāmaṇeras, we now respectfully request the masters present here to serve as your *karmācārya* and provide instruction."
Regarding the conferral of the Ācārya [initiation]: the words for requesting the Master to serve as the Venerable Witness-Ācārya should properly be spoken by you yourself.
Fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, I shall now instruct you. Each of you should state your Dharma-name (having stated it), and for all other phrases, follow my lead.
Venerable sir, please attend to me, the śrāmaṇera [Name]. We now request the Venerable one to serve as our *karmavācanā*-instructor and *sākṣin-ācārya*.
May the Venerable one act for us as our *karmavācanā*-instructor and *sākṣin-ācārya*.
"I rely upon the Venerable One; therefore, out of compassion, may I receive full ordination" (as before).
The second *karmavācanā* master says:
"O śrāmaṇeras, since you have earnestly extended this request to me and the masters present here, I shall perform the *karmavācanā* for you."
"Upādhyāya, ācārya, and kalyāṇamitra-ācārya: so be it. You are pure; do not be negligent.
(He replies: "I shall receive and uphold this with the highest reverence."

All the śrāmaṇeras rise together. Upon hearing the sound of the *qing*, they perform three prostrations with full reverence. They adjust their robes, secure their alms bowls, and prepare for departure.
The assembly divides into ranks.
The various marshals then distribute the *dàyī* (outer robes) to each individual in order, instructing them to receive them with their own hands. The ten masters [then lead the procession].
Rising from their seats, the First Master leads the chant:
"Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
As soon as the Buddha’s name is raised, the Dharma drum is struck loudly; the entire assembly joins in one voice, chanting together in clear resonance. Second, the Ritual Leader leads.
The pair of sounding bells lead the way from the front, followed by the assembly of bhikṣus, and then the newly ordained śrāmaṇeras who seek full ordination.
Three of these seeking-ordination śrāmaṇeras hold incense; one stands before the tenth preceptor, one before the third preceptor, and one before the first preceptor.
These two leading guides perform the ritual prostrations and first arrive at the left and right sides of the ordination platform.

They stand in rows. The remaining attendants, having arrived one after another, each take their place according to the order of the ranks, surrounding the left and right sides of the altar as well as its three rear sides.
Three incense-bearers stand in a single row beside the front of the altar. When the nine masters arrive, they form two rows before the incense table;
the first master arrives and stands in the center facing upward. At that moment, the Dharma drum and the Buddha’s voice [resound].
Cease. According to the ritual protocols of the ancient altar, at the commencement of ascending the altar, there is a section for offering prayers for longevity.

This is because the propagation of the Buddha-Dharma by the Sangha necessarily relies upon external protection; thus, on the assembly at Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One once issued an entrustment.

If one were to contravene the Buddha’s words and fail the grace of the state, it is feared that the flourishing of the teaching would be difficult to achieve. Now, we shall again follow the ritual models of the ancient altar. The *Weishi*...
The ritual master performs the *brahman-udgītha* to offer incense and praise; the assembly joins in harmony:
Precious censers burn famous incense, pervading the ten directions. With utmost sincerity, we offer it to the King of Dharma.

Solely for the sake of the Emperor, we pray for his sacred longevity—may earth endure and heaven last forever. Solely for the sake of the Emperor, we pray for his sacred longevity—may earth endure and heaven last forever.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Fragrant Cloud Canopy (three times).
The First Master respectfully offers incense, performs three prostrations, and silently offers prayers to the Holy Ones. Having completed this, the nine masters descend in succession.
Standing shoulder-to-shoulder with the First Master, they unfold their large ritual implements and offer praise and prostrations to the Triple Gem.
The First Master leads the chant, and the nine masters join in the praise:
*Homage to all Buddhas,* *And to the Dharma and the noble Sangha.* (Ten masters perform one prostration together, and the assembly joins in harmony.)

Now expounding the Vinaya Dharma, continuing the life-vein of the Saṃgha (as before), may the True Dharma abide for a long time, and the fruits of the Three Vehicles never cease. (The assembly joins in harmony; the Master rises from his seat with the ritual implements.
About to ascend the pure altar, I pray that you bear witness to what is being said. (The assembly joins in harmony; the ten masters join their palms and inquire after one another’s well-being.)
After the ten masters have completed three prostrations of praise, the Rector (Vina) intones the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī, which the entire assembly recites in unison.
The tenth master first turns around and circumambulates the altar from the southeast toward the west; next the ninth master, and then the eighth master.
Proceeding in this manner until reaching the end of the first master’s row, he circumambulates three times.
Having removed his shoes, he ascends the second tier from the west, turns toward the northwest, and circumambulates once. Arriving at the south, he ascends the third tier;

the first master stands facing south, while the nine masters stand facing north. The nine masters perform three prostrations toward the first master (the response of the greeting may be understood according to the preceding rules). The first master...
The lead teacher sounds the first note; the nine teachers harmonize together. The rest of the assembly remains silent.
With precepts held pure like the full moon, body and speech bright and stainless without blemish, and the great assembly in harmony without dispute—only then may the precepts be conferred together.
When the ten preceptors have assembled, performed the three prostrations, and finished reciting the verses, the primary preceptor sits in the central seat;

the *karman* master sits at the head seat on the left; the instructor sits at the head seat on the right; and the seven witnessing preceptors take their seats in order, to the left and right respectively.
The Third Altar Master’s Petition to the Dharma (the Altar Master is none other than the First Master, the Abbot; he petitions on behalf of the nine masters upon the altar):

"The sound of the Dharma is rarely encountered, and his preceptual virtue is inconceivable. He is able to transcend the vulgar and defiled stream of the mundane world and may enter the precious station of the sages and worthies."
To be a teacher and a master is truly easy and truly difficult. When the furnace and bellows are opened wide, the faculties of people must be refined.

One should maintain the prohibitive precepts and keep one's robes and bowl strictly pure. If one lacks robes and a bowl, one must not allow oneself to borrow them. The preceding section lists the grave obstacles; the following section enumerates the minor hindrances.

Question: If one does not understand or know [the truth], then diligent effort is established in vain. One must believe their actual words and receive an actual answer; through such guidance and transformation, one may attain the proper method to give rise to the highest grade of sincerity.
One should make a solemn vow regarding the sensory realms, intending to cause the wholesome dharmas of the ten directions to flow into and permeate the body and mind.
The five parts are established as the foundation; the three bodies are fully endowed. One must share the same aspiration; I pray that you do not allow divergent conditions.
(Name) respectfully informs. The ritual master says:
The śrāmaṇeras each take their respective positions according to rank and form a procession in order.
With the head śrāmaṇera at the front on either side, they proceed from top to bottom, while the others follow in a single file like a flight of geese.
Upon reaching the front of the altar, they divide into groups and stand in their proper sequence. The attendants then temporarily receive the great robes held by them.
Receive and hold [the incense] to facilitate prostration.

Offer incense (three persons holding the incense turn together toward the upper direction, lift once, perform the full ritual, and then kneel long while inserting it into the burner). Return to position; line up facing upward. Inquire after one another’s well-being. Unfold the large mat (*daigu*).
Upon hearing the sound of the *qing* gong, prostrate three times. Adjust the robes and protect the bowl (after the prostrations are completed). Lengthen...
Kneel and join your palms.
The Master of the Altar strikes the sounding block and says:
"O assembly of śrāmaṇeras, you have now gathered as a saṃgha to ascend this altar. According to the ritual procedures of the Vinaya, it is proper that we first offer prayers."

The Three Jewels: may their compassionate light gather and illuminate us. Next, may the myriad spirits be humbled, and their majestic power provide steadfast protection. Each shall invoke the Dharma-name [of the deity].
(Having invoked them,) all shall rise together and, following my voice, perform the visualization and offer the three requests.

The ten masters rise from their seats simultaneously. With utmost sincerity, they direct their thoughts to perform the *brahma*-chanting. The presiding master offers incense, making three successive requests for each of the Buddhas and devas.
The novice candidate, according to these requests, performs three prostrations for each. One must understand that both subject and object are empty and quiescent;
thus, the path of resonance and response is mutually attained.
Welcoming with incense and flowers. Inviting with incense and flowers.

We, the śrāmaṇeras [Name] and others, with single-minded devotion, respectfully invite the Teacher of the Sahā World, our Original Master Śākyamuni Buddha; Amitābha Buddha, who receives us from the West;
Maitreya, the Honored Buddha, who shall descend in the future; and all Buddhas throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm. We pray only that you...
Having violated their original vows, they are gathered and illuminated by the light of compassion; thus they request the witness and reception of the precepts.
Having made this request, the assembly bows together once, then rises again, joins their palms, and stands while performing visualization.

Welcoming with incense and flowers; inviting with incense and flowers: We, the śrāmaṇeras [Name], and others, with single-minded devotion, respectfully invite the Vinaya Piṭaka of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, the five sections and three clusters, the liberation of the Prātimokṣa, and the twelve divisions of the sūtras.

The scriptures of provisional and ultimate teachings, the true purity that is free from desire, the most profound jewel of the Dharma—may we, with single-minded devotion, take refuge in and pay homage to them (as before).
Welcoming with incense and flowers;
inviting with incense and flowers. The śrāmaṇeras [Name], etc., with single-minded devotion, respectfully invite you.
Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the assembly of the Pure Ocean; all the great Bodhisattvas;
the Venerable Upāli from the assembly of the Vinaya Piṭaka; the successive patriarchs of India and China who transmitted the Nanshan school;

the great Vinaya masters; and the Grand Master Huiyun Xing, the Patriarch who revived the Vinaya tradition (hereafter follow the names of the preceptor and the ordination master of the presiding teacher).
I only pray that you will not violate your original vows, but will gather us in with your compassionate light to bear witness to and empower our reception of the precepts (as before).

With incense and flowers, we welcome; with incense and flowers, we invite: the śrāmaṇeras [Name] and others, with single-minded devotion, respectfully invite the various devas who occupy their stations within the Assembly of Radiance—the Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings; the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and so forth; and the local deities of the monastery grounds.

The King-Spirits who protect the precepts, the Vajra-wielding Māhasattvas, and all numinous deities of the hidden and manifest realms: we pray that you do not violate your original vows, but remain to guard the altar and protect the precepts.
Having thus completed this petition, the ten masters resumed their seats and sat in the lotus posture, while the śrāmaṇeras likewise took their places.
Each again knelt with palms joined.
Fourth, regarding the location where one receives the precepts, the Buddha said:
"The person receiving the precepts must not be in an empty or hidden place, nor in a location beyond the range of sight or hearing, nor outside the boundary (*sīmā*). The *Upādhyāya*...

It is likewise for those who complete the required number (the nine masters on the altar). One should place the candidate for ordination in a location where they can be seen with the eyes but cannot be heard with the ears.
The Master of the Altar strikes the sounding block and says:

"The formal invocation to the Triple Gem has been completed. The various ritual attendants shall now escort those seeking the full precepts, such as the śrāmaṇeras, and place them where they are within sight but not within earshot."
Stand at the place where you heard [the summons]. The ritual attendant says:

"All śrāmaṇeras, prostrate once, rise, and prepare your equipment; divide into ranks" (the ritual attendants shall then distribute the *kaṣāya* robes back to each person, instructing them to hold them individually). You all follow.
With the sound of my voice, everyone recites the Buddha’s name in unison and exits the altar.
The bhikṣus below the altar exit first. Two ritual masters lead the way, ringing the *qianqing* bells in tandem as they proceed, chanting the Buddha’s name aloud.
The śrāmaṇeras hold up their great robes (*saṃghāṭī*) in their hands and chant together in a single voice, following behind while facing each other on the left and right.
[The preceptor] proceeds. Having exited the altar area, he places [the robe] where it belongs.
Fifth, regarding the time for appointing the instructor (*śikṣācārya*):

if there is a candidate receiving the precepts who is taken outside the boundary to have their clothes removed and examined, it causes a delay in the matter of receiving the precepts. The Buddha said:
This should not be done. From this day forward, one must first inquire about the thirteen grounds of disqualification before conferring the precepts.
The presiding master strikes the sounding-block and asks:

"Is the Saṃgha assembled? (The Karmadāna replies: "The Saṃgha is assembled. (He asks: "Is it in harmony? (He replies: "It is in harmony. (He asks: "Are there any bhikṣus who have not yet received the precepts?"

[Question: "The precepts exclude what? [Answer: "They have already excluded it. [Question: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony. What shall we perform? [Answer: "The *karmavācanā* for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
(The presiding master strikes the wooden gavel and says: "Since the full ordination has been received, who among this assembly is able to act as the instructor (*śikṣācārya*)?
Go to a secluded place and engage the śrāmaṇeras in questioning. (The third teacher, with palms joined at his seat, replies: "I, [Name], am capable."

(The Master of the Altar says: "Elder, since you are capable, let the *karmavācanā* master among the assembly perform the *jñapti-karman* to appoint a teacher of instruction to descend to the altar for the interrogation.
The *karmavācanā* master remains in his seat and, with palms joined, speaks as follows:"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These śrāmaṇeras (so-and-so), etc., seek to receive full ordination from their preceptor (so-and-so).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. [I] shall act as the instructor. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). [Question: "Is the formal motion established?
[The seven witnesses, remaining in their seats, join their palms and respond in unison: "It is established."

The seven teachers answered in unison that [the act] was accomplished; this refers to the three factors of person, dharma, and matter, all of which were in accordance with the Vinaya, in accordance with the Dharma, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions.

This is called "weighing and finding what is appropriate," whereby the task is successfully completed. If even one factor is not in accordance with the Vinaya, then even if they answer that it is accomplished, the matter will not be brought to fruition.
Regarding the offense of the seven witnesses, the office of a single character is no small responsibility; it must be based on reality. Now...

Once the *karmavācanā* has been completed, the preceptor shall immediately rise from his seat, prostrate three times to the presiding master (*maṇḍalīśvara*), turn toward the south, and descend the second tier.
Turning toward the southwest, he circles around until reaching the northeast, where he descends the third tier.
Putting on his sandals, he circles again until reaching due south. Facing the altar, he joins his palms in a single salutation and exits by way of the southwest, proceeding to—
The Master of Dharma goes to a private location, takes his seat,
and sits down. Upon the first strike of the wooden gavel, one attendant monk leads three virtuous monks [into the assembly].
The ordained śrāmaṇera approaches the preceptor, receives the great robe (saṃghāṭī) held out by him, performs three prostrations, and kneels for a long time.
He then returns the robe to him, and the preceptor leads him away to a place beyond the range of sight and hearing.
The Master struck the sounding block and said:
"O śrāmaṇeras! The masters upon the altar are performing the ritual; they have dispatched me down here to inquire of you three regarding the obstacles to ordination.
Do not be afraid. In a brief moment, I shall cause you three to ascend the precious altar and receive the full precepts."
A great bhikṣu enters the ranks of the Triple Gem; this is no small matter, and you should feel profound joy.

Now, the precepts are the very root of Bodhi and the foundation for the Noble Path. In the Buddha’s era, when conditions were favorable, a single accordant movement would immediately evoke a response.

In this degenerate age of impurity, the Sage’s regulations follow conditions. When conditions assemble, the ritual is performed and merit is accomplished; when conditions disperse, [the practice ceases].
The virtue of the precepts has no fixed location; its unconditioned merit cannot be seen. One must rely on conditions to determine its presence or absence.

These three robes and one bowl are the primary conditions for the three of you to obtain the precepts. Before I inquire about the prohibitions and obstacles, I shall first explain to you the names and characteristics of the robes and bowls.
(The Master points to the five, seven, and two robes worn on his body and the large robe held in his hands, saying: "This is the *antaravāsaka*..."
I understand. This is the *uttarāsaṅga*, this is the *saṃghāṭī*, and this is the *pātra*.
Indeed, these robes and bowl are the insignia of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and the standard practice of the noble and holy *śramaṇas*.
Even among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths in the Western Heavens, they do not even know their names; only the Buddha alone has revealed this unprecedented teaching.
Now that you have obtained and received this, you must cherish, respect, and protect it. Is this robe and bowl now your own?
(He replies: Yes. (The Master says: Since they are yours, that is excellent. You should receive, maintain, and wear them.

In the various Vinayas, the formal acceptance (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is likewise added. Regarding the five, seven, and two robes, those were previously permitted to be worn provisionally at the time of receiving the śrāmaṇera precepts;
now, only the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) remains to be accepted. First, one assistant calls out to the three persons [involved];
they prostrate and stand to the side. Then, one śrāmaṇera steps forward, holds up the robe before the preceptor, and speaks as follows:
"Say: 'Venerable sir, attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, [Name], receive this twenty-five-fold saṃghāṭī robe; it has four long pieces and one short piece;
it is a robe of cut-and-sewn cloth, and I shall maintain it. (Recite three times. The teacher replies: 'Excellent' (for the nine-grade great robe, receive it according to its grade)."
Those who have already received [the precepts] stand to one side and recite the verses and mantras from memory. They adjust their robes properly.

Those who have not yet received them likewise receive them one by one before the teacher. Once they have finished adjusting their robes, they all bow once before the teacher, kneel with their right knees on the ground, and join their palms.
The teacher strikes the sounding board and says:

"Listen attentively, all you śrāmaṇeras. Since beginningless time, you have given rise to deluded and false minds to deceive the worthy and the holy, sinking into the cycle of birth and death with no prospect of liberation.

Now that you have surrendered yourselves to the Buddha and left the household life to become his disciples, receiving the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts and crossing the ford to transcend birth and death, you must strive to sever the root of falsehood and practice the path of reality. This very moment is precisely the time for utmost sincerity."
At this time, when speaking the truth, I ask you all about grave offenses and light prohibitions. You should examine this body with careful scrutiny:
if it exists, say it exists; if it does not exist, say it does not exist. "Have you three of you not committed a pārājika offense? (They answer: "No. (The Master should say:
"Considering that you three have only recently entered the gate of the Way, you may not have known the names of these offenses. However, having already received the Buddha's precepts..."
Among the four grave precepts of sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying, the transgression of even one such precept causes one to be cast adrift outside the ocean of the Buddha;
therefore, they are called "offenses of the limit" (*ānantarya*). Do you not have any? [Answer: No.

In all inquiries regarding existence or non-existence, the intent lies in mutual understanding. Therefore, if the Middle and the Extremes are not mutually understood, one cannot even be said to have relinquished the precepts.
Now, if one asks but does not understand, it is no different from not asking at all. As the Vinaya states, "The reception of the precepts is not accomplished.
Thus, all subsequent cases should be understood by analogy with this.
"When you were a layperson or a śrāmaṇera, did you defile a bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct? [He] answers, "No.
"When you were not a layperson nor a śrāmaṇera, did you eavesdrop on the Saṃgha reciting the precepts and falsely claim to be a bhikṣu, receiving from others respect, offerings, and prostrations?
This is called 'living as a thief' (caura-vāsa). A person living as a thief is not permitted by the Buddha to be ordained. Were you not such a person?"
"Is this person [a true disciple]? (Answer: "No. You were not originally a non-Buddhist;

you entered the monastic life by taking refuge in the Buddha. Having received the Buddha’s precepts, you returned to the non-Buddhists. Now you have come once more to receive the precepts. This person’s disposition is unstable;
he is called one who has 'broken' both internal and external paths. He is not a vessel for the Buddha-dharma; the Buddha does not [ordain him]."
"Permission is granted for your ordination. Are you not one of these persons? [He answers: "No.

"Are you not one who is 'castrated by birth' (meaning a person who has been male from birth but lacks the male organ; this is called *jāti-paṇḍaka*)? One who is 'castrated by surgery' (meaning a person who has had the male organ removed with a knife; this is called *kṛta-paṇḍaka*)?

One who is 'jealous' (meaning the male organ seems absent, yet upon seeing another engage in sexual intercourse, jealousy arises and subsequently causes the organ to appear; this is called *īrṣyā-paṇḍaka*)? One who is 'transformable' (meaning one capable of changing form: encountering a man, he transforms into a woman; encountering a woman, he transforms into a man; this is called *pakkha-paṇḍaka*)?"
"Is it not the case that there are five kinds of 'half-impotent' persons—namely, those who are impotent for half the month and potent for the other half? [Answer: No."
"Have you not killed your father? (He answers: "No. "Have you not killed your mother? (He answers: "No. "Have you not killed an Arhat?
(He answers: "No. "Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha? (He answers: "No. "Have you not, with malicious intent, shed the blood of a Buddha? (He answers: "No."
"Are you not a deva, a ghost, or some such being who has transformed themselves into human form to receive the precepts? (Answer: "No.
"Are you not a nāga, an animal, or some other capable of transformation who has manifested as human form to receive the precepts? (Answer: "No."
Within the bodies of you three, none possess both male and female sexual organs. This is precisely contrary to the vessel for the Way.
Do you now possess them? (Answer: No.
"O śrāmaṇeras, since these thirteen grave obstacles do not exist for you, I shall now further question you regarding the sixteen minor prohibitions;
answer each one truthfully, just as before."
"O śrāmaṇeras, since you three have gone forth, each of you has been instructed. What are the names of these dharmas? (After each has answered their name:
These are the dharma names by which you three shall be known upon entering the Path; they are your appellations for the duration of this life.

From now on, after receiving the precepts, whenever you see your Upādhyāya, Ācārya, fellow practitioners who are witnesses of the same altar, those of the superior, middle, or inferior seats, as well as government officials or elders—"
In the presence of friends, acquaintances, parents, teachers, and elders, one must always address them by these two characters of their Dharma-name;
one must not use such terms as "you," "I," "so-and-so," or the designation "little monk."

"Who is the Preceptor for Ordination (*upasampadā-ācārya*) upon whom you three have received the precepts today? [They] answer, "The Great Monk [Name] of the Upper [Monastery] and [Name] of the Lower [Monastery].

The Master says, "This is the Vinaya Master [Name] of [Name] Monastery; he is the Preceptor for Ordination for you three. In the Sanskrit language, *upādhyāya* means 'one who gives birth by power' (*balotpādaka*).
The powers of the Path of the Three Vehicles and the fivefold Dharma-body all depend upon the majestic power of this master."
Therefore, it is called "born of power. It is also called "relying on training," meaning that by following this master, one trains in the supramundane Dharma;
hence, it is called "relying on training. If this master did not exist today, the precepts would have no source from which to arise.
You must commit your Preceptor’s honorable name to memory and recognize his compassionate countenance. If you fail to remember his name and appearance, you shall not receive the precepts.

Regarding the precepts: from this day forward, whenever you encounter the seasonal festivals, the closing of the retreat, or the opening of the retreat, you must respectfully offer incense and prostrate before your Preceptor of Ordination (*jiejie heshang*).
If the distance is too great for you to travel there in person, you should burn incense, face the open sky, call out his name, and pay your respects;
you must not harbor thoughts of disrespect.
"Are you three of full twenty years of age? (They answer: "We have reached it.
"Are your robes and bowl complete? (They answer: "They are complete.
"Have your parents given you permission to leave the household life? (They answer: "They have."
"Do you not owe money or debts to others? Have you come to receive the precepts with the intention of not repaying them?
(He answers: "No. "Are you not a servant in another's household? (He answers: "No."
"Are you not an official of the current dynasty, one who possesses both fame and emolument? (He answers: "No.
"Are you a man of integrity? (He answers: "I am a man of integrity."

The Fundamental Vinaya states: "One who has reached the age of twenty is able to endure cold and heat, wind and rain, hunger and thirst, the observance of the one-meal-a-day precept, and the endurance of harsh speech and venomous insects; such is the station of a man."
Since you are a man, you must also be free from disease. First, scabies; second, carbuncles; third, leprosy; fourth, consumption; fifth, insanity.
Do you truly have none of these five ailments? [He] replied: "I do not."
At that time, there were these five kinds of sick people who sought Jīvaka for treatment. Jīvaka said, "I am a physician only for kings and the disciples of the Buddha.

Having reflected on this, they immediately left the household life and received full ordination. He then treated them, and once their illnesses were cured, they abandoned the path and returned home. On the road, they encountered Jīvaka;
having learned of the situation, they informed the Buddha, who consequently established a prohibition, not permitting it. According to the Vinaya, as for the body in general—

Regarding those who do not possess the proper marks and thus bring disgrace upon the Great Sangha, none are permitted [to ordain]. Now, I shall merely inquire concerning the final regulation to encompass the broad prohibitions.
As for the śrāmaṇeras and others, I now ask you this; shortly, before the assembly of masters on the altar, it shall be the same.
He asked, "When you answer me thus now, you shall likewise answer before the assembly of masters upon the altar after a short while.

Follow me; wait until I first go before the Saṃgha and make the formal announcement. If the Saṃgha remains silent and grants permission, I will beckon you with my hand, at which time you must all proceed onto the altar."
The attendant calls for the three śrāmaṇeras; they perform one prostration and stand to the side. The preceptor rises from his seat, leaves his position, and walks forward.
The three śrāmaṇeras follow behind the preceptor in succession. Upon approaching the ordination platform, he instructs the śrāmaṇeras to stop and stand, so that they may gaze upon the altar above.
Seventh, the ritual for the white invitation to enter the assembly:
The preceptor arrives before the mandala, stands in the center with palms joined, bows toward the upper direction, and makes the following declaration:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These śrāmaṇeras (so-and-so), following their preceptors (so-and-so), seek to receive full ordination.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants its consent, I, (so-and-so), having already completed the questioning, request that they be brought forward. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
(After the teacher has made this motion, he turns toward the śrāmaṇeras and beckons them with his hand, saying: 'All you śrāmaṇeras, come here.'"
Upon hearing the summons, the śrāmaṇeras proceed with full decorum to the altar. The Master steps forward to the left of the incense table and stands there. He says:
"All of you, approach the incense table together. (Having arrived), they perform a bow of inquiry (*praṇāma*), kneel for a long time, and the one in the center picks up the incense.

One incense offering to the masters upon the altar. (Having offered the incense) he performs one prostration and rises. Following me, he ascends the altar to request the precepts. Eighth, the procedure for requesting the precepts:
the Preceptor-in-charge goes first, with the śrāmaṇera following behind. They circumambulate until they reach the west side of the altar; there, they remove their shoes and ascend the second tier.
Circling from the northwest to due south, he ascends the third step. The Master returns to his seat and stands with palms joined.
The śrāmaṇera stands at a distance from the Master such that their hands can reach one another. The assembly stands facing north in a single row. The Master instructs them, saying:
Unfurl the great ritual implements. Prostrate three times. (Having prostrated,) kneel upright with palms joined.
Good sons, with earnest sincerity, rely upon the pure assembly to seek compassion and request the precepts. As for the words of requesting the precepts, you ought to speak them yourselves;
however, fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, I shall now instruct you. Each of you state your Dharma-name. (Having stated it,) the remaining phrases are as follows:
All follow my path.
Venerable Sangha, listen. I, [Name], seek to receive full ordination from the preceptor [Name].
I, [Name], now request the Sangha for the conferral of full ordination, with [Name] as my preceptor. May the Sangha, out of compassion, grant it. Pull me up.
"Save me. Thus he begs three times. Having performed one prostration, the preceptor takes his seat on the original seat.
The Ninth Karmavācanā Master performs the single-announcement rite (*ekajñapti*).
The *karmavācaka* (preceptor of the ritual), standing at his original seat with palms joined, first performs the *jñapti-karman* (motion) alone, and subsequently proceeds with the interrogation.
He makes the following declaration:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! These [persons], such-and-such, seek to receive full ordination from their preceptor, such-and-such. These [persons], such-and-such..."

Now [Candidate] requests from the Saṃgha to receive full ordination, with [Preceptor Name] acting as the Upādhyāya. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience as I inquire regarding the various obstacles.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Is the motion established? (The seven witnessing masters, remaining in their seats, join their palms and reply: It is established.
Tenth, the formal ritual procedure for posing the correct inquiry:
The *karmavācanā* master says, "Do these three—this *antarvāsaka*, *uttarāsaṅga*, and *saṃghāṭī*—and this *pātra* belong to you three? (They reply: "They do."
"Good son, listen attentively. Now is the time for sincerity; now is the time for truthful speech. Regarding what you are about to ask, you should answer in accordance with the truth.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: 'If one does not answer truthfully, one deceives the devas, māras, and brahmās, as well as śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and worldly people, and the Tathāgata and the Saṃgha. One will thereby incur a great transgression.'"
"Have you three not committed a pārājika offense? (Answer: No.
While you were laypeople or śrāmaṇeras, did you defile a bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct? (Answer: No."

"When you were not yet a layperson, nor a *śrāmaṇera*, did you not eavesdrop on the *bhikṣu* saṃgha reciting the precepts and falsely claim to be a *bhikṣu* to receive the respect, offerings, and prostrations of others?
This is called 'living as a thief. The Buddha does not permit the ordination of those who live as thieves.
Are you not such a person? [He] replied, "No."
"You were not a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). Having gone forth under the Buddha and received the Buddha’s precepts, you returned to the non-Buddhists.
Now you have come again to receive the precepts. This person is of unstable character; they are called one who 'breaks' both internal and external paths.
They are not a vessel for the Buddha-dharma, and the Buddha does not permit their ordination. Are you not such a person? [He] replied, "No."
"Are you not one of the five kinds of non-men, such as a *jāti-ṣaṇḍha*, a *paṇḍaka*, a *vikaṭa*, a *pārāyaṇika*, or a *pañcama*?
[He answers: "No. "Have you not killed your father? [He answers: "No. "Have you not killed your mother?
[He answers: "No. "Have you not killed an Arhat? [He answers: "No. "Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha? [He answers: "No. "Have you not, with an evil mind..."
"Have you shed the blood of a Buddha? (Answer: "No.
"Are you not a deva, a ghost, a spirit, or the like, who has transformed into human form to receive the precepts? (Answer: "No."
"Are you not a transformed being such as a dragon or an animal who has taken the form of a human to receive the precepts? [He] replied, "No.
"Do you not each possess within your three bodies the two sexual organs of male and female? This would truly be contrary to the vessel for the Path. Do you have them now? [He] replied, "No."
"Good son, since these thirteen grave obstacles do not exist, I shall now further question you regarding the sixteen minor prohibitions.
Since each of you three has gone forth, what is the name of the Dharma by which you have been instructed? (Having stated the names:
Who are the preceptors for the full ordination whom you three have received today? [They reply: "The Great Preceptor named So-and-so, Upper [Name] and Lower [Name]."
"Are you three of full twenty years of age? (Answer: "We have reached it.
"Are your robes and bowl complete? (Answer: "They are complete.
"Have your parents given you permission to go forth? (Answer: "They have."
"Do you not owe money or debts to others? Have you come to receive the precepts with the intention of not repaying them?
[Answer: "No. "Are you not a servant or laborer in another's household? [Answer: "No."
"Are you not an official of the current dynasty, one who possesses both fame and emolument? (He answers: "No.
"Are you not a man of honor? (He answers: "I am a man of honor."
Since you are a man, you must also be free from disease. First, scabies; second, carbuncles; third, leprosy; fourth, consumption; fifth, insanity.
Are you indeed free from these five ailments? (He replies: "I am not."
Eleventh, the Method for Bestowing the Substance of the Precepts: The Preceptor strikes the sounding-block and says:
"Good son, you have no grave obstacles before you and no minor hindrances behind you; you are a most pure vessel. The Sangha rejoices together that they shall bestow the precepts upon you.
These precepts are supremely good, extensively encompassing the Dharma-realm, and equal in measure to empty space. Now you wish to proceed and receive them."
It is necessary to give rise to the resolve by taking an object as its condition; only when the mind and its object are mutually compatible does one produce non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first be instructed with the Dharma to guide and enlighten them:

'You three have, since beginningless time, committed various evil karmas across all objects; these evils pervade the entire dharma-realm. Now, wishing to receive the precepts, you must overturn those previous evil objects.'"
Simultaneously giving rise to wholesome minds, the source of the precepts thus pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Therefore, I, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, have created boundless karma and established boundless precepts. Since the precepts follow what has been established, they must take objects as their conditions.
Although the extent of these objects is vast, to state the essentials, they do not exceed two kinds: first, the realm of sentient beings; second, the realm of non-sentient things.

Regarding "objects" (*viṣaya*): as for what is termed the "sentient object," from the Buddhas above down to sentient beings below—the primary retributions (*pratyātmabhāva*) of the ten realms, as well as sentient beings in the intermediate state—anyone possessing a mind is called a "sentient object.
As for the "non-sentient object," this refers to the environmental retributions (*bhājanaloka*) of the ten realms:

all worlds such as mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, thickets, forests, boats, carts, houses, dwellings, precious treasures, fields, gardens, and the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
From wind up to empty space, the Buddha’s holy teachings, the texts of the Confucian tradition, and physical images, stupas, and temples—all these are termed non-sentient objects (*asattva-vastu*).
Good son, since you know that the scope of such objects is so vast, you must generate the resolve for enlightenment based upon these objects.
The mind has three grades. The middle and lower grades of mind are inferior and weak, not superior; they can only deliver oneself, but cannot deliver others.
I now instruct you to give rise to the superior grade of mind and seek the superior grade of precepts. What is the superior grade of mind?
It is to now stand before me and my teachers and make three vows: first, to vow to sever all evils, such that there is no evil that is not severed.

Second, he vowed to cultivate all that is wholesome, such that there is no wholesome deed he would not practice. Third, he vowed to deliver all sentient beings, such that there is not a single sentient being who would not be delivered.
Having made these three great vows, he proceeded to receive the full bhikṣu precepts during the formal ritual of the white fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
This was not for the sake of merely seeking the minor fruits of a śrāvaka, but because he directly desired to achieve the [three]... [bodhisattva precepts].

Because they gather pure precepts; because they proceed toward the three gates of liberation; because they rightly seek the fruit of Buddhahood and seek great *nirvāṇa* so that the Dharma may long abide;
they give rise to such superior-grade minds and receive superior-grade precepts.

As for the subsequent instruction to "further expand your resolve," it is because the essence of the dharma of the precepts is all-pervasive throughout the *dharmadhātu*, its measure equaling the sands of the Ganges; it is certainly not because of you three individuals alone.
The physical body and mind born of one's parents from previous lives are naturally narrow and inferior, yet they are able to receive and contain [the precepts].
One must become a body with the vast capacity of empty space before being able to fully receive the *sands-of-the-Ganges* number of dharmas of the precepts. Therefore, the Treatise says:

"If these dharmas of the precepts possessed form and color, when they entered your body, they would produce a sound like the collapsing of heavens and the cracking of the earth. It is because they are non-material (*arūpa*) dharmas."

I shall cause you to give rise to a sense of alertness that you have not yet perceived or known, so that you may develop a mind of the highest degree of reverence and receive the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous precepts (strike the *chī* once).
Now, for your sake, we shall perform the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to confer the great Bhikṣu precepts.
You should observe the altar rites with your eyes, listen to the *karman* with your ears, and receive it with single-minded attention; do not let your thoughts wander elsewhere.

Contemplate other points of awareness. The *karmavācanā* master first performs one formal announcement (*jñapti*) to inform the assembly; next, he conducts three formal acts (*karmavācanā*). He then weighs the propriety of the matter.

This is the extensive text of the ancient ritual manual. Below the section on the sounding of the ruler, I have supplemented one or two items. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "The *karmavācanā*..."
When receiving the precepts, you should listen with a single-minded focus; do not harbor other thoughts or reflections.

You should only maintain reverence, practice right reflection, and keep it in mind at every moment of consciousness. You must discern this clearly. To violate these instructions constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the number of those receiving the precepts at the ordination platform is large, one may use the abbreviated text from the *Jīkènmó* (Karmavācanā). These extensive and abbreviated texts both originate from [the Vinaya].
From the Southern Mountain: When providing a brief guidance, you should say to them:
"Sentient beings in the six realms mostly possess obstacles to the precepts. Even among humans who may receive them, they still contain prohibitions and difficulties;

it is not necessarily the case that all are capable. You, however, being free from prohibitions and difficulties, will certainly receive the precepts. You should rely on the treatises and generate a superior resolve. Regarding what follows...

This means to rescue and gather in all sentient beings, delivering them through the Dharma. Furthermore, the precepts are the root of all virtues and can serve as the direct cause for the Three Vehicles.
Moreover, the precepts are a treasure within the Buddha-dharma that is not found in other paths. They can also protect and maintain the Buddha’s True Dharma so that it endures for a long time.
Furthermore, by relying on the majestic power of the *karma* (ritual action) and the great strength of the Sangha, one is able to uphold the Dharma.

I place the supreme dharmas of the realms within your body and mind. You should observe the ritual of the maṇḍala with your eyes and listen to the *karmavācanā* with your ears (and so forth), as may be known from the detailed account previously given.
The twelfth procedure for receiving the essence of the precepts: The *karmācārya* joins his palms and says:

"I pray that the Upādhyāya and the Great Assembly will not withhold their compassion, but bestow these precepts upon us. May we act with one mind and together uphold them; be careful not to allow divergent conditions to arise.
Let these three persons be moved to generate the essence of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) precepts. As we are about to perform the *karmavācanā*, please listen as I announce the formal motion."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These [persons], such-and-such, seek to receive full ordination from the preceptor, such-and-such.
These [persons], such-and-such, now request the Saṃgha to grant them full ordination. Such-and-such is their preceptor. They themselves declare that they are pure and free from all obstacles;
they are twenty years of age, and their three robes and alms bowl are complete. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent. May the Saṃgha...
"I confer the full ordination upon [Name] and others; [Name] shall serve as the preceptor. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). "Has the announcement been completed?
(The seven witnessing masters respond in unison with palms joined: "It is completed."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These [persons], such-and-such, seek to receive full ordination from the preceptor, such-and-such. These [persons], such-and-such...

Now, [so-and-so] requests from the community of monks to receive full ordination (upasaṃpadā). [So-and-so] acts as the preceptor (upādhyāya). [So-and-so] and the others have declared themselves pure and free from all obstacles;
they are twenty years of age and possess the three robes and alms bowl. The Saṃgha now confers full ordination upon [so-and-so] and the others.
"Let such-and-such be the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). Which elders consent? The Saṃgha grants full ordination (*upasampadā*) to such-and-such, with such-and-such as the preceptor;
those who consent remain silent. Those who do not consent speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*. Is it accomplished? (Answer as before: "It is accomplished."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These individuals (so-and-so), having sought the full ordination from their preceptor (so-and-so), now request the full ordination from the Saṃgha.
With so-and-so as their preceptor, they have declared themselves pure and free from all obstacles;
they are twenty years of age and possess the three robes and the alms bowl. The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon these individuals (so-and-so).
"Let the Sangha grant full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as preceptor. Those elders who consent to the Sangha granting full ordination to [Name] with [Name] as preceptor, let them remain silent.
Whoever does not consent, let them speak. This constitutes the second *karmavācanā*. Is it accomplished? (Answer as before: It is accomplished."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These [persons], such-and-such, have requested the full ordination from the preceptor, such-and-such.
These [persons], such-and-such, now petition the Saṃgha for the full ordination. Such-and-such is their preceptor. They themselves declare that they are pure and free from all obstacles;
they are twenty years of age; they possess the three robes and the alms bowl. The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon these [persons], such-and-such.
"Let [so-and-so] be the preceptor. Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha conferring full ordination upon [so-and-so], with [so-and-so] as the preceptor, remain silent.
Whoever does not consent, please speak. This is the third *karmavācanā*. Is it accomplished? (Answer as before: "It is accomplished.")
The Sangha has consented. The full ordination (upasampadā) has been conferred upon [Name] and others; [Name] serves as the preceptor (upādhyāya).
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and various Vinayas all state: Once the full ordination (*upasampadā*) has been received, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the instructor (*ācārya*), and others must record the seasonal period—whether spring, summer, or winter—and the specific month and day, down to the measurement of the shadow and so forth, at which time the full ordination was received.

If these details are not recorded and explained, the master presiding over the ordination platform incurs an offense. This clarifies the calculation of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-varṣa*) according to the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

[The Buddha] established the counting [of seats] so that those who come and go, sit and rise, would know the distinctions of superior, middle, and inferior seats, as well as the etiquette of honor and humility.

On the thirteenth occasion, when the four *pārājika* rules were being recited, there was a bhikṣu who, having received full ordination, had the community of monks depart; since he did not recognize what constituted an offense, he immediately committed a grave one.
[This constitutes] an offense. The Buddha said: "From this day forward, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one must first confer the four *pārājika* dharmas.
The preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the instructor (*ācārya*) shall strike the sounding-block and say:"
"Listen, son of good family. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has proclaimed the four pārājika dharmas.
If a bhikṣu commits even one of these dharmas, he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya."

"You must all refrain from committing sexual misconduct and engaging in impure practices. If a bhikṣu commits an impure act and engages in the practice of sexual desire—even with an animal—he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a parable: "It is just as if someone were to have their head cut off; they could never return to life. So it is with a bhikṣu:
once he has committed an offense of pārājika, he cannot again fulfill the conduct of a bhikṣu.
You must not do this for as long as you live. Can you uphold this? [He] replied, "I can uphold it."
Under no circumstances may one steal, even down to a blade of grass or a leaf. If a bhikṣu steals five coins or more from another person—whether he takes it himself or causes another to take it;
whether he breaks it himself or causes another to break it; whether he cuts it himself or causes another to cut it; whether he burns it himself or causes another to burn it;
or whether he buries it or destroys its color—he is no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya. He is, for example, like one who has severed...
The heartwood of a *tāla* tree never grows again. It is the same for a bhikṣu who has committed a *pārājika* offense:
he can never again fulfill the conduct of a bhikṣu. You must not do this for as long as you live. Can you uphold this? (He replies: I can uphold it.
Under no circumstances may one intentionally take the life of a living being, even down to an ant.

If a bhikṣu intentionally takes a human life with his own hand, provides a weapon to another, instructs someone to die, praises death, gives another a non-medicinal substance, causes an abortion, or kills through incantations or curses—whether acting as the primary agent or instructing another to do so—he is neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya. As the Parables (Avadāna) state:
It is just as when the point of a needle is broken; it can no longer be used. So it is with a bhikṣu:
having committed a pārājika offense, he no longer constitutes a bhikṣu in his practice. You must not do this for as long as life lasts. Can you maintain this? (He answers: I can maintain it.

No one shall speak falsely, even in jest (in jest refers to practicing "verbal Zen" by rehearsing kōans and turning-phrases). If a bhikṣu, being untrue and lacking such qualities himself, should say of himself:
"I have attained the state of a superior person; I have attained dhyāna; I have attained liberation;
I have attained meditative concentration; I have attained the four formless absorptions; I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat..."
“O Han-kuo, when devas, nāgas, and yakṣas come to make offerings to me, they will say: ‘He is neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya. It is like this analogy:

I dedicate all these merits from the sublime practice of receiving the precepts and all boundless, supreme blessings,

To all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and to all honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas:

The Precepts. This is the medium-grade precept. Third, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, when there is no Dharma master within a thousand *li*, one should take the vow to receive the precepts before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; this is the inferior-grade precept.

Seventh, the Bodhisattva Preceptor who bestows the four unbreakable faiths strikes the sounding block and says:

"The *Sūtra on the Adornment of the Buddha’s Necklace* states: 'Having paid homage to the Three Jewels, one is further instructed to receive the four unbreakable faiths and to rely upon the four reliances.
As for what are called the four unbreakable faiths: the fundamental nature inherited by all people is one; yet, regarding this single essence..."

Because within this [nature] are fully present the Treasures of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as the precepts. In the Sanskrit language, *buddha*; in the Chinese language, "Awakened" (*jue*).

This refers to the nature-body (*svabhāvakāya*) which is spiritually awakened, clearly illuminating that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent; this is called the inherently possessed Treasure of the Buddha.

*Dharma* (fa) carries the meaning of "that which maintains the norm. This refers to the quiescent nature of reality (*dharmatā*), wherein the ocean-like qualities of inherent virtue can all be maintained as norms;
this is called the originally endowed Jewel of Dharma. *Saṃgha*: in Sanskrit, the full term is *saṃgha*; in Chinese, it means "harmonious assembly.
This refers to the ocean-like sublime virtues in which essence and appearance are non-dual, and principle and phenomena are in harmony; this is called the originally endowed Saṃgha.
It is a treasure. As for the precepts, they refer to the Vajra Radiance Treasure Precepts.

They are the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of the Buddha-nature within all sentient beings; this is called the inherently possessed nature-precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*).
From this day forward, you must believe that your own mind is the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts, throughout the entirety of future kalpas.

Because they are neither forgotten nor lost, they are called the "four unbreakable faiths. Although it is said that their essence is inherently endowed with true permanence, there is nonetheless the necessity of cultivation and realization.

As it is said: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. One should take refuge in and dwell within the Triple Gem, receive the pure and wondrous precepts, and rely upon them for practice;
only then can one fully accomplish the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. Now, in contrast to this—

however, fearing that you may be unable to do so, follow what I say.

Dharma. I (so-and-so),

The eighth method for repenting transgressions: The Bodhisattva Precept Master strikes the sounding-block and says:

"O children of the Buddha! As clarified in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, those who currently manifest the commission of the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) are not permitted to receive the precepts.
Last night, the Karmācārya already examined each of you in detail; fortunately, you are all free from such offenses, and thus you may receive the precepts."

Now, according to the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* (瓔珞經), once one has received the four unbreakable faiths (*akṣayaśraddhā*), one should next be instructed in the repentance of the offenses of the three periods of time.

Regarding what is called the "three periods of time" in reference to these offenses: it means that the seeds of past ignorance serve as the cause of karmic offenses, while their manifestation in the present life serves as the condition for those karmic offenses.
Through this present manifestation, it perfumes the karma accumulated since beginningless time in the past.
Through the convergence of various causes and conditions, the karma one has created is brought to fruition; furthermore, it serves as the evil cause for future sinful karma.
Thus, through this mutual reinforcement, saṃsāra continues without interruption.

Now, before the presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I feel shame and remorse for my transgressions. If I can contravene the active manifestations of this present life, then [the cycle of suffering will be broken].
The seeds of past karma have withered away, and the causes of future karma will naturally perish. As for these words of repentance, you ought to speak them yourself;
yet fearing that you may not be able, I shall speak them according to my own path.
I (so-and-so), regarding the ten non-virtuous offenses of body, speech, and mind committed in the past, pray that they may never arise again for as long as the limits of the future endure.
I (so-and-so), regarding the ten non-virtuous offenses of body, speech, and mind committed in the present, pray that they may never arise again for as long as the limits of the future endure.
[End. I, [Name], regarding the ten non-virtuous offenses of body, speech, and mind that I may commit in future lives, vow that they shall never arise again.
Until the end of the future, each person shall recite the words of the teacher clearly and perform three repentances followed by three prostrations.

The ninth section clarifies the method for making vows according to the *Yingluo jing* and the *Jie mo jing*, both of which lack this portion. Now, from within the currently practiced *Śīla-sūtra*, fourteen vows are excerpted to supplement them.
The Bodhisattva Precept Master strikes the sounding block and says:
O sons of the Buddhas, having finished repenting for our transgressions, the three karmas are purified, like clear lapis lazuli shining through from both inside and out.
Next, you should give rise to the fourteen kinds of great vows and practice accordingly to bring those merits to fulfillment.
Even if a hot iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of my head, I would never, because of such suffering, retreat or abandon the vows I have made. Now, before [the assembly]...
Before the seats of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, each of these has been proclaimed three times for your sake. You should now proceed before the seats of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
with mind focused and words spoken, each of you shall declare it for yourselves, reciting the Dharma names one by one (having finished the recitation).
Strike the sounding-block once. First:
From this moment until the end of the future, will you all be able to constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha and draw near to spiritual friends? (They answer: We can draw near.
"Second, from this time forth until the end of the future, will you all be able to constantly abandon and distance yourselves from all evil associates?
[They] replied, "We can abandon them."
"Third, from this time forth, for as long as your bodies shall endure until the end of the future, even at the cost of losing your lives, will you not violate the precepts?
(They answer: "We shall not violate them."

"Fourth, from this time forth until the end of the future, will you all be able to constantly read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, and inquire about their profound meanings? (They answer: "We can."
"Fifth, from this time forward until the end of the future, will you all be able to constantly give rise to faith in unsurpassed bodhi? (They answer: We can."
